10000foot.title: 10000 Foot
10000foot.html: These figures come from Tacitus, Annals 14.38.

1017.title: sounded the Nobility
1017.html: Milton's margin here has: "1017." See Cnut the Great.

1019.title: Edward the Elder
1019.html: Milton's margin here has: "1019." See the Flores Historiarum for 1022 CE. But see also Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.11.

1028.title: above ten years
1028.html: Milton's margin here has: "1028. Sim. Dun." See Simeon, Historia Regum for 1027 CE. See also his entry for 1028 CE: "L. navibus magnis Nerregam devectus, Olavum regem de illa expulit."

1043.title: Easter following
1043.html: Milton's margin here has: "1043." See Edward the Confessor.

115th.title: the 115th
115th.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an." The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle has no entry for 974 CE, nor does it mention the two superannuated monks of Croyland.

12days.title: 12 days
12days.html: Milton's margin here has: "651." The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records the deaths of King Oswald and Bishop Aidan under 651 CE.

13years.title: 250 Sail
13years.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 893 CE.

16years.title: 16 years
16years.html: Milton's margin here has: "Malms." See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.8.

1yearafter.title: one year after
1yearafter.html: Milton's margin here has: "753." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for the year 753 CE.

21years.title: 21 years
21years.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun. Eccles. L. 2." See Simeon of Durham's Historia Regum for 758 CE.

230000.title: 200 and 30 thousand
230000.html: This figure comes from Dio, Roman History 62.8.

24years.title: founded so firmly
24years.html: Milton's margin here has: "The Kingdom of West-Saxons." See Wessex.

2bishops.title: two Bishops
2bishops.html: Milton's margin here has: "Malms." See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.2.

2flight.title: to flight
2flight.html: Milton's margin here has: "Bed. Nin." See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 1.15, and Nennius, Historia Brittonum 48 (search for "put them to flight"); this was a much later event than that described by Bede.

2yearsafter.title: two years after
2yearsafter.html: Milton's margin here has: "743." The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records in the year 743 that Æthelbald of Mercia and Cuthred of Wessex made battle against the Welsh at Gwent and Powys.

30friends.title: Aldra
30friends.html: Milton's margin here has: "Camd." See Camden, "Somersetshire" 9.6.

30ships.title: 30 Ships
30ships.html: See Geoffrey, History of the Kings of Britain 3.12.

30times.title: a place
30times.html: Milton's margin here has: "Camden." See Camden, "Northumberland" 25.10: " Leedes, in the Saxon tongue Loytes , which became a house of the Kings when Cambodunum was by the enemy burnt to the ground, now a rich towne by reason of clothing, where Oswy King of Northumberland put flight Penda the Mercian".

310hides.title: 310 Hides
310hides.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." See Simeon of Durham, Historia Regum for 1008 CE.

38years.title: 38 years
38years.html: Milton's margin here has: "746." Saelred of Essex reigned from 709 CE to 746. Saelred was succeeded by Swithred.

3after.title: three after
3after.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 860 CE.

3rdyearafter.title: third year after
3rdyearafter.html: Milton's margin here has: "765." See Malmesbury, in Chronicle of the Kings of England book 1.3.

3sons.title: three Sons
3sons.html: Milton mentions Locrine as the nymph Sabrina's father in A Mask at Ludlow. According to Geoffrey, Albanactus founded Albania or Alban, also known as Scotland. Camber was a legendary King of Cambria, or Wales.

50.title: Ostorius
50.html: Milton's margin here has: "50." Publius Ostorius Scapula was appointed the second Roman governor of Britain (succeeding Aulus Plautius) in 47 CE.

50daughters.title: fifty daughters
50daughters.html: Raphael Holinshed tells this story in his Chronicles (1587) 1.3. Danaus gave up his daughters in marriage quite reluctantly, supplying each with a sword and instructions to murder their husbands on their wedding night. One, Hypermnestra, allowed her husband, Lynceus, to live because he allowed her to remain a virgin; he revenged his brothers by killing Danaus.

53.title: when first the Romans came
53.html: Today, the generally accepted date of Julius Caesar's invasion of Britain is 55 BCE.

5consuls.title: five Consuls
5consuls.html: Milton's margin here has: "Ingulf." The Pseudo-Ingulf, Historia states that Ludeca reigned for two years and was assassinated by a band of East Angles (486v). See also the See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 823-824 CE.

5yearsafter.title: Five years after
5yearsafter.html: Milton's margin here has: "855," probably a misprint for 865.

5yearsmore.title: five years more
5yearsmore.html: Milton's margin here has: "774. Sim. Dun." See Simeon of Durham's Historia Regum for 774.

60ships.title: 60 Ships
60ships.html: Milton's margin here has: "Malms." See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.13. See also Florence, Chronicron ex Chronicis for 1066, and Simeon, Historia Regum.

615ships.title: 615 Ships
615ships.html: Milton's margin here has: "Florent. Sim. Dun." See the Flores Historiarum for 937 CE. It is Simeon of Durham who mentions the 615 ships: Historia Regum for 937. See also the Battle of Brunanburh.

683.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an." The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle dates this as 685 CE. See also Cædwalla of Wessex.

689.html: Milton's margin here has: "689." See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 5.7: "IN the third year of the reign of Alfrid, Caedwalla, king of the West Saxons, having most honorably governed his nation two years, quitted his crown for the sake of our Lord and his everlasting kingdom, and went to Rome, being desirous to obtain the peculiar honor of being baptized in the church of the blessed apostles."

705.title: the next year
705.html: Milton's margin here has: "705." See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 5.24. See also Osred I of Northumbria.

740.title: built a Library
740.html: Milton's margin here has: "740." See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 1.3. See also Ecgbert of York and Eadberht of Northumbria.

741.html: Milton's margin here has: "741." The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records the passing of Æthelheard of Wessex and the accession of Cuthred in 741 CE.

753bc.title: about the time
753bc.html: The traditional date for the "birth" of Rome is April 21, 753 BCE.

79.title: his last year
79.html: Milton's margin here has: "79." Gnaeus Julius Agricola became governor in 77 CE, but 79 CE was indeed Vespasian's last year as emperor.

794.title: the year following
794.html: Milton's margin here has: "794." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 784 CE and for 794.

7kingdoms.title: 7 absolute Kingdoms
7kingdoms.html: Also known as the Anglo-Saxon Heptarchy.

7yearsafter.title: 7 years after
7yearsafter.html: Milton's margin here has: "704." See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 5.24.

80.title: Summer following
80.html: Milton's margin here has: "80." Milton follows Tacitus very closely here (Life of Agricola 20-21). Milton apparently thought that Agricola arrived in Britain in 79 CE, but he actually arrived in 77. His advance to the Firth of Tay took place in the summer of 79, which would have been his third summer in Britain. Titus was Roman emperor from 79 to 81 CE.

800.title: year 800
800.html: Milton's margin here has: "800." The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle and Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.1 record Beorhthric's death in 800, but the actual date was 802 CE.

808.title: after whom
808.html: Milton's margin here has: "808." See Eanred of Northumbria.

809.title: year following
809.html: Milton's margin here has: "809." See Buchanan, History of Scotland 5.51. See also Legendary kings of Scotland.

819.title: deceas'd
819.html: Milton's margin here has: "819." See Coenwulf of Mercia.

82.title: fourth Summer
82.html: Milton's margin here has: "82." Agricola's fourth summer in Britain was 80 CE (77,78,79,80). Domitian became Roman Emperor in 81 CE.

825.title: two years
825.html: Milton's margin here has: "825." Ludeca was king of Mercia from 826-827 CE.

827.title: year 827
827.html: Milton's margin here has: "827." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 827 CE.

828.title: Tributary
828.html: Milton's margin here has: "828." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 828 CE.

83.title: his fift year
83.html: Milton's margin here has: "83." Agricola's fifth year in Britain was 81 CE.

84.title: Summer
84.html: Milton's margin here has: "84." More likely 82 CE. See Tacitus, Life of Agricola 25. "Forelay" means "To lay obstacles in the way of; to plot or take action against; to embarrass, frustrate, hinder, interfere with" (OED).

85.title: following Summer
85.html: Milton's margin here has: "85." The Battle of Mons Graupius took place in 83 CE. Tacitus's account in Life of Agricola 29-37 is much longer.

8mile.title: 8 Mile
8mile.html: Caesar writes of "seven miles." See Commentaries 4.23.

8years.title: 8 years
8years.html: Milton's margin here has: "527." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle: the battle of "Cerdices-Leaga."

902.title: sent back
902.html: Milton's margin here has: "902." See the Flores Historiarum.

956.title: instigated
956.html: Milton's margin here has: "956." The date of Dunstan's banishment. See also Oda of Canterbury.

973.title: the 30. of his Age
973.html: Milton's margin here has: "973." On Edgar's coronation, see Coronation at Bath.

974.title: soon after
974.html: Milton's margin here has: "974." See the Pseudo-Ingulf Historia: "Swarlingus completis annis vitae suae 142" and "Turgaras venerabilis senex completis annis vitae suae 115."

975.title: year following
975.html: Milton's margin here has: "975." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 975 CE.

979.title: second Son
979.html: Milton's margin here has: "979." The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle dates the accession of Æthelred in 978 CE; so does Simeon of Durham, Historia Regum. See also Æthelred the Unready.

9years.title: dissol'd
9years.html: Milton's margin here has: "748." See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 1.6.

abouteaster.title: strong Castle
abouteaster.html: Milton's margin here has: "Asser." See Asser, Life of Alfred.

aboutthewest.title: about the West
aboutthewest.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 877 CE.

aboutthistimeit.title: About this time
aboutthistimeit.html: Milton's margin here has: "Malms." See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.13.

abouttime.title: the same time
abouttime.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." See Simeon of Durham, Historia Regum.

aboveothers.title: above others
aboveothers.html: Milton's margin here has: "Eadmer. Malms." See Eadmer, Historia novorum in Anglia. See also Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.10, and Ælfheah of Canterbury.

abstaining.title: saith Dion
abstaining.html: Milton's margin here has: "Dion." See Dio's Roman History 77.12.

accompanied.title: accompanied
accompanied.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." See Simeon, Historia Regum for 1043 CE. See also Leofric, Earl of Mercia and Siward, Earl of Northumbria.

accordingtonen.title: according to Nennius
accordingtonen.html: See Nennius, Historia Brittonum 43-44. See also Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 1.1.

accountedking.title: accounted King
accountedking.html: Milton's margin here has: "Ethelwerd. Malmsb. Witichind. gest. Sax. L. 1. p. 3." See Æthelweard's Anglo-Saxon Chronicle page 4: "Vurthern". For Malmesbury, see Chronicle of the Kings of England book 1.1. Widukind was an 8th-century leader of the Saxons. Milton refers here to book 1, page 3 of the Witichindi Saxonis Rerum, published in Basle in 1532. Camden repeats the full text of this letter in his Britannia, "English-Saxons" 2 (search for "Witichindus").

acknowledgehim.title: acknowledge him
acknowledgehim.html: Milton's margin here has: "Spelman. concil. pag. 108." Sir Henry Spelman was the author of Concilia Ecclesiastica Orbis Britannici (1639). See page 122 of the edition by Arthur West Haddan (1869). See also St. Dinooth.

actedemperor.title: acted the Emperor
actedemperor.html: For this account of Constantine's demise, see Olympiodorus, in chapter 80 of the Biblioteca of Photios: "Constantius and Ulphilas are sent by Honorius against Constantine; having reached Arelate [Arles], where Constantine was living with his son Julian, they lay siege to it. Constantine takes refuge in a church and is ordained priest, having been solemnly promised that his life should be spared. The city gates are thrown open to the besiegers, and Constantine and his son taken to Honorius. But the emperor, bearing a grudge against them for the murder of his cousins by Constantine, orders them to be put to death in violation of his oath, thirty miles from Ravenna." See also Sozomenus, in Ecclesiastical History 9.14-15.

addicted.title: addicted to devotion
addicted.html: Milton's margin here has: "Mat. West." See the Flores Historiarum.

addresses.title: addresses
addresses.html: Milton's margin here has: "Strabo L. 4." See The Geography 4.5.3.

addsthat.title: adds that
addsthat.html: See Gildas, The Ruin of Britain 24.

adigression.title: a digression
adigression.html: Milton refers to a passage inserted into the Leges Edouardi Regis in William Lambarde's Archaionomia (1644) on page 148 that makes this claim regarding Ina's reign.

adminius.title: Adminius
adminius.html: Adminius, son of Cunobelinus, was a ruler of the Catuvellauni, an Iron Age British tribe.

adulteries.title: private adulteries
adulteries.html: This story comes from Dio, Roman History 77.16.4-5.

aedui.title: Æduans
aedui.html: The Aedui were a Gallic people of northern Gaul.

aelfric.title: Alfric
aelfric.html: See Ælfric Puttoc. See also Godwin, Earl of Wessex.

aethelwolf.title: Ethelwolf
aethelwolf.html: Æthelwulf became king of Mercia in 839 CE See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.2.

affirmed.title: Annals
affirmed.html: See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 871 CE.

afflicted.title: by the Annals
afflicted.html: Milton's margin here has: "652." The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records the battle at "Bradanfordam" for 652 CE. See also Æthelweard, Anglo-Saxon Chronicle: "Four years after [after 648] he fought a battle against his own people, at a place called Bradford."

after2years.title: after two years
after2years.html: Milton's margin here has: "750." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for the year 750 CE See also Eadberht of Northumbria.

after4years.title: after 4 years
after4years.html: Milton's margin here has: "307." Constantine joined his father in York in the spring of 305 CE. His father died in July 306. By winter 307, he was in Gaul, and returned to Britain in the summer of 307. In 308, he was crossing the Rhine near Cologne.

afterthis2.title: they in Northumberland
afterthis2.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim Dun." See Simeon of Durham's Historia Regum for 798 CE. See also Langho and Anglo-Saxon fires of London.

afterthreeyears.title: After three years
afterthreeyears.html: Milton's margin here has: "697." See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 5.24: "In the year 697, Queen Ostritha was murdered by her own people, that is, the nobility of the Mercians." See also Osthryth, and the Flores Historiarum.

afterwardsemperor.title: afterwards Emperor
afterwardsemperor.html: Milton's margin here has: "Camden." See Camden, Britannia, "Romans 2" 4.81: "At this time, the Generall of all the warre-forces thorowout Britaine was Gratianus surnamed Funarius , the father of Valentinian the Emperour." Camden also asserts that Magnentius had "a Britan to his father."

afterwhich.title: after which
afterwhich.html: Milton's margin here has: "709." See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 5.24. See also Coenred of Mercia.

againsther.title: against her
againsther.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." See Simeon of Durham's Historia Regum for 802 CE.

againsthim.title: Against him
againsthim.html: Milton's margin here has: "340." That is, Magnentius rose against Constantius II in 340 CE.

againstthescots.title: against the Scots
againstthescots.html: Milton's margin here has: "Prosper. Aquitanic. chron." Prosper of Aquitaine was the author of Epitoma chronicon. According to French Fogle (Yale Prose 5, Part 1, 120), this chronicle says nothing about a campaign against the Picts and Scots; he speculates that Milton my have trusted James Ussher's chronology.

agreatbattel.title: a great Battel
agreatbattel.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun. Mat West." See Simeon of Durham's Historia Regum for 759. See also the Flores Historiarum, which records the killing of Oswin in both 759 CE and 762.

alban.title: Alban
alban.html: Along with fellow Saints Julius and Aaron, Alban is one of three named martyrs recorded at an early date from Roman Britain.

albiongiant.title: Albion
albiongiant.html: Milton's source for this story of Albion the Giant, son of Neptune is John Bale, Illustrium Maioris Britanniae scriptorum (1548) folio 8: "Albion Gigas, potentissimi illius Neptuni."

albrightclito.title: Albright
albrightclito.html: See Florentius for 725 CE. See also the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 725 CE: "Aldbrithum."

alclud.title: Alclud
alclud.html: In Scotland (Albania), the town now called Dumbarton, then known as Alt Clut, or high rock.

alcuinmonk.title: learned monk
alcuinmonk.html: Alcuin of York was a monk, scholar, teacher, and poet.

aldulf.title: we find
aldulf.html: See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 1.5.

algiva.title: Algiva
algiva.html: "Ælfgifu of Northampton (c. 990 – after 1036 CE) was the first wife of Cnut the Great, King of England and Denmark, and mother of Harold Harefoot, King of England. She was regent of Norway from 1030 to 1035 CE."

alipius.title: Alipius
alipius.html: For Alypius of Antioch, see Ammianus Marcellus, Roman History 23.1.3.

allobruges.title: Seginus Duke of the Allobruges
allobruges.html: The Allobroges were a Gallic tribe of ancient Gaul.

allover.title: all over England
allover.html: Milton's margin here has: "Florent." See Flores Historiarum for 1002 CE. See also Simeon of Durham, Historia Regum for 1002 CE.

allowsbutone.title: allows but one
allowsbutone.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. ann." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 917 CE See also the Flores Historiarum.

allowthreeyears.title: allow three years
allowthreeyears.html: Milton's margin here has: "Eumen." After murdering Carausius, Allectus ruled for three years from 293-296 CE.

allprovision.title: all provision
allprovision.html: Milton's margin here has: "Leges Ed. Conf. Tit. deduct. Norman." See William Lambarde's Archaionomia (1644) where, directly following the Leges Edouardi Regis, or The Laws of Edward the Confessor, we find an article entitled "De Ducibus Normannorum in Neustria, quae modo vocatur Normannia," which traces the line of Norman dukes from Rollo to William the Bastard. It reports that Cnut entered the Thames "magna cum classe," with a great fleet.

allright.title: Government relapsing
allright.html: Milton's margin here has: "Procopius vandalic." Procopius of Caesarea was author of the History of the Wars. In book 3.2, he writes that "while Honorius was holding the imperial power in the West, barbarians took possession of his land."

allsummer.title: all the Summer
allsummer.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." See Simeon of Durham's Historia Ecclesiae for 870 CE.

allthehorse.title: all the Horse
allthehorse.html: Milton's margin here has: "Florent." See the Flores Historiarum.

allthekings973.title: all the Kings
allthekings973.html: See King Edgar's council at Chester.

alltherest.title: above others
alltherest.html: Milton's margin here has: "Bed. Malms." See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 1.25 and Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 1.1. See also Æthelberht of Kent.

allthirforces.title: a certain King
allthirforces.html: Milton's margin here has: "Annal. omn. Huntingd. Camden." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle; Huntingdon, Historia Anglorum 2.13, and Camden, "Hantshire" 2.

alltyranny.title: Tyranny
alltyranny.html: See Gildas, The Ruin of Britain 27.

alstan.title: Alstan
alstan.html: Eahlstan was Bishop of Sherborne in the 9th century CE.

alyn.title: river Allen
alyn.html: The River Alyn is in northeast Wales, a tributary of the River Dee.

ambrosiusaurelianus.title: Ambrosius Aurelianus
ambrosiusaurelianus.html: Ambrosius Aurelianus (Welsh: Emrys Wledig; Anglicised as Ambrose Aurelian and called Aurelius Ambrosius in the Historia Regum Britanniae and elsewhere) was a war leader of the Romano-British.

amityandleague.title: amity and league
amityandleague.html: Milton's margin here has: "Malms." See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 1.1.

anassembly.title: Assembly
anassembly.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." See Simeon of Durham, Historia Regum for 1015 CE: "perfidus dux Edricus Streone." See also Eadric Streona; Milton's Edric of Streon is probably a mistake.

anation.title: Nation more remote
anation.html: Milton's margin here has: "Malms. l. 1. c. 3." See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 1.3 for the story of Archdeacon Gregory (later Pope Gregory I) and the Northumbrian slave boys.

ancienter.title: ancienter
ancienter.html: Milton's margin here has: "Pontan. hist. Dan." See Pontanus, Rerum Danicarum Historia book 4.

andaprovince.title: and a Province
andaprovince.html: Milton's margin here has: "Bed. l. 4. c. 13. Camd." See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 4.13, and Camden, "Hampshire" 10.13. See also Æthelwealh of Sussex.

andate.title: Andate
andate.html: Andraste, an Icenic war goddess. See Dio, Roman History 62.5-6.

anddivide.title: Deorhirst
anddivide.html: Milton's margin here has: "Camd." See Camden "Gloucestershire" 13.6.

andeager.title: they came
andeager.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." See Simeon, Historia Regum for 1051 CE. Simeon specifically mentions "Suthweorce," but other details come from Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.13: Wulfnoth Godwinson as "a hostage.".

andotherssay.title: and others
andotherssay.html: Milton's margin here has "Huntingd. Mat West." See Henry of Huntingdon, Historia Anglorum and Flores Historiarum See also Asser, Life of Alfred.

andtwoyears.title: and two years
andtwoyears.html: Milton's margin here has: "735." The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records Bedes death under the year 734 CE. Symeon dates his passing, and a bloody-spotted moon, as 735 CE (Historia in Twysden).

andvows.title: and vows
andvows.html: Milton's margin here has: "Gildas." See Gildas, The Ruin of Britain 15.

anewfleet.title: a new Fleet
anewfleet.html: Milton's margin here has: "286." Carausius joined Maximian's campaign in Gaul in 286 CE; he learned of Maximian's order for his execution in late 286 or 287 CE and then fled to England where he built new ships and began minting coins with his own image.

anewfleetdanes.title: a new Fleet
anewfleetdanes.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 918 CE.

anglesey.title: Anglesey
anglesey.html: An island off the northern coast of Wales.

anglesey2.title: Mona
anglesey2.html: Anglesey, an island off the northern coast of Wales.

annal784.title: Saxon Annals of 784
annal784.html: See Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 784 CE. See also Ealhmund of Kent.

annalscall.title: Annals call
annalscall.html: See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 794 CE: "Eadbrihtus alias Præn nuncupatus." See also Eadberht III Præn.

anoldcoine.title: an old coine
anoldcoine.html: Milton appears to be following Camden here; see "Coins of Britain" 8 [III]: "But what should be the meaning of an halfe ship in this coine, with this inscription, Metropolis Etiminii regis? Certes, I cannot for certaine affirme who that Etiminius was, unlesse a man list to imagine him to have beene the very same Adiminius, King Cunobelinus sonne, of whom Suetonius reporteth that he ran away unto C. Caligula."

anotheradversity.title: Another adversity
anotheradversity.html: See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 4.19. See also Æthelthryth.

anothercause.title: another cause
anothercause.html: See Huntingdon, Historia Anglorum 6. See also Flores Historiarum for 1065 CE.

anothercity.title: another City
anothercity.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 921 CE. See also Towcester.

anotherfault.title: Another fault
anotherfault.html: The following story also comes from Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.8. This may be the same woman Malmesbury refers to as Wulfritha on the facing page. See also Flores Historiarum: "Wlfrida concubina."

anothersaxon.title: another Saxon
anothersaxon.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an. omn. Huntingd." The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle dates the arrival of Port and his sons, Bleda and Magla, as 501 CE: "Her cwom Port on Bretene 7 his .ii. suna Bieda 7 Mægla mid .ii. scipum on þære stowe þe is gecueden Portesmuþa 7 ofslogon anne giongne brettiscmonnan, swiþe æþelne monnan." See also Huntingdon, Historia Anglorum 2.12. The place where Port landed came to be known as Portsmouth.

anotherstoryedgar.title: Another story
anotherstoryedgar.html: Once again, from Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.8.

anotherwall.title: another Wall
anotherwall.html: Milton's margin here has: "Capitolin. vit. Anton. 144." Julius Capitolinus was one of the supposed "six scriptores" of the Augustan History; see "Life of Antoninus Pius" 11.2. Quintus Lollius Urbicus was governor of Britain from 139 to 142 CE. The Antonine Wall was a turf fortification that ran from the Firth of Forth to the Firth of Clyde. It was begun in 142 CE and took about 12 years to complete.

aparthur.title: Geoffrey ap-Arthur
aparthur.html: Another name for Geoffrey of Monmouth, based on the assumption, dubious, that his father's name was Arthur.

aplacecalled.title: a place called
aplacecalled.html: Milton's margin here has: "Bede. Ethelwerd." See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 1.15; and Æthelweard, Anglo-Saxon Chronicle page 6: "Ægelsthrep."

aplaceontheedge.title: a place on the edge
aplaceontheedge.html: The location of this first meeting between Augustine and the British bishops is still a matter of dispute. See Augustine's Oak. See also Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 2.2.

apostlerule.title: Apostles rule
apostlerule.html: See 1 Corinthians 7:1-9. See also Milton's idiosyncratic interpretation of this bible passage in his Doctrine and Discipline of Divorce.

appointedasynod.title: appointed a Synod
appointedasynod.html: Milton's margin here has: "359." The Council of Ariminum met in July 359 CE and adopted what some considered to be an Arian-friendly creed. Milton follows the account of Sulpicius Severus, in his Chronicle 2.51.

appointedtime.title: appointed time
appointedtime.html: Milton's margin here has: "Calvisius." Calvisius's Opus Chronologicum confuses St. Brice (or Bricius) with St. Brictius, whose feast day is indeed July 9; hence Milton was misled about the date of the massacre which is generally understood to have been November 13.

appoints.title: appoints
appoints.html: Milton's margin here has: "Cæsar Com. 5." See Commentaries 5.1.

aprey.title: a prey
aprey.html: Milton's margin here has: "Malms." See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England 1.1.

aprimesoldier.title: Trajan was Emperor
aprimesoldier.html: Milton's margin here has: "Spartianus in vit. Hadrian." The Augustan History is a collection of Roman biographies traditionally assigned to six authors or "scriptores;" one of them was said to be Aelius Spartianus. Milton refers to the "Life of Hadrian" 5.2.

archigallo.title: Archigallo
archigallo.html: Also called Archgallo or Arthgallo; see Geoffrey, History of the Kings of Britain 3.17.

archpriesthood.title: archpriesthood
archpriesthood.html: Milton's margin here has: "Cæsar." See Commentaries 6.13.

areconjectured.title: are conjectured
areconjectured.html: Milton's margin here has: "Camden." See Camden's Britannia, "Romans in Britaine" 4.69 for his account of the "thirty tyrants."

arhetorician.title: a Rhetorician
arhetorician.html: Milton's margin here has: "Paneg. 2." A panegyric delivered to Constantius Chlorus attributed to Eumenius claims that the name "Picts" came into use "about the time of Maximian and Dioclesian."

ariver.title: a River
ariver.html: The Medway. The tribes Milton names are mentioned in Dio's Roman History 60.20. The Boduni are probably the Dobunni; the Catuvellauni were a neighboring Celtic tribe.

armorica.title: Armorica
armorica.html: Armorica or Aremorica was the ancient name given to nothern Gaul and the Brittany Penninsula.

armoricans.title: Armoricans
armoricans.html: Camden, in Britannia, "Romans 2" 4.88: "But those Britans who tooke part with Maximus, as some writers doe record, forcibly invaded Armorica in France, and there planted themselves."

arriandoctrine.title: Arrian Doctrine
arriandoctrine.html: Milton's margin here has: "Ammian." See Ammianus Marcellus, Roman History 20.1-3. Arianism asserts that the Son of God is not coeternal with God the Father, and is subordinate to Him.

arthurp.title: Arthur
arthurp.html: As promised in his introduction, Milton recounts legendary stories of Arthur Pendragon, even though he doubts any such person ever existed.

artrius.title: Quintus Atrius
artrius.html: Our copytext misprints his name as "Artrius" here; see Britain (1671) 43. "All in Poste" means in great haste as in Shakespeare's Lucrece, line 1.

arviragusking.title: Arviragus
arviragusking.html: See Juvenal, Satires 4.125-27, where he spells the name "Aruiragus."

asbefore.title: as before
asbefore.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 840 CE.

asbromton.title: Others
asbromton.html: John Brompton was the supposed author of an Historia included in Roger Twysden's edition of ten historical authors, Historiae Anglicanae Scriptores X. At column 936-938 we find an account of Godwin's flight, return, and reconciliation to Edward.

aschool.title: a School
aschool.html: Though Sigeberht did found a school in East Anglia, it was not Cambridge University; see Sigeberht. The legend of his founding Cambridge comes from Camden, "Cambridgeshire" 17.4: "The report goeth that Cantaber, a Spaniard, 375 yeeres before the nativity of Christ, first began and founded this University. Also that Sebert King of the East-Angles restored it againe in the yeere after Christs birth 630." See also the history of Cambridge University.

asclepiodotus.title: Asclepiodutus
asclepiodotus.html: Julius Asclepiodotus was a Roman praetorian prefect.

asharsh.title: as harsh
asharsh.html: Milton's margin here has: "Malms." See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.13. See also Wherwell.

asisreported.title: as is reported
asisreported.html: Milton's margin here has: "Usser. Primord p. 333." See James Ussher, De Primordiis (Dublin, 1639) 333. Flintshire is a district in northern Wales.

asissaid.title: as is said
asissaid.html: Milton's margin here has: "Huntingd." See Huntingdon, Historia Anglorum 2.25.

asisthought.title: as is thought
asisthought.html: Milton's margin here has: "Camd." See Camden, "Dorset" 8.54.

asisthoughtf.title: as is thought
asisthoughtf.html: Milton's margin here has: "Florent." See the Flores Historiarum for 1006 CE. See also Ælfhelm of York.

aslicentious.title: as licentious
aslicentious.html: Milton's margin here has: "Cæsar." See Caesar's Commentaries 5.14.

assaultandfire.title: assualt and fire
assaultandfire.html: Milton's margin here has: "Bed. l. 3. c. 16. Camd." Bede's Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 3.16, reports Penda's attack on Bamburgh (Bebbanburg), but see 3.24 for the rest of the story. Camden identifies Bebbanburgh as "Bamborrow": "Northumberland" 29.23.

assendune.title: Assendune
assendune.html: The Battle of Assandun (or Essendune) was fought between Danish and English armies on 18 October 1016.

assentnot.title: assent not
assentnot.html: Milton's margin here has: "Gildas." See Gildas, The Ruin of Britain 20-21. Germanus of Auxerre made his first anti-pelagian visit to Britain in 429; he may have made a second visit in the mid 430s or 440s which would align with the letter to Aetius.

assomesay3.title: some say
assomesay3.html: See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 1.4. See also Beornred of Mercia.

assomethink.title: as some think
assomethink.html: Milton's margin here has: "Camden." See Camden, "Hantshire" 2.11-12: "For who would ever make doubt that Saresbirig proceeded from Sorbiodunum by addition of the Saxon word byryg , which signifieth a Burg or town." Camden dates Kinric's attack on 553 CE.

assomewritemalms.title: some write
assomewritemalms.html: See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.8: "Scarcely does a year elapse ... in which he did not perform something great...in which he did not build some new monastery."

astrongnavy.title: a strong Navy
astrongnavy.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." See Simeon, Historia Regum for 1045 CE.

atafeast.title: at a Feast
atafeast.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." See Simeon, Historia Regum for 1042 CE. See also Osgod Clapa and Tovi the Proud.

atbedanford.title: at Bedanford
atbedanford.html: Milton's margin here has: "Camden. Annal omn." See Camden, "Bedfordshire"14.3: "Bedford, in the Saxon-tongue Bedanford....Cuthwulf the Saxon, about the yeere of our salvation 572 beneath this towne so vanquished the Britans in an open pitcht field that they presently upon it, finding themselves over matched, yeelded up many townes into his hands." The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle identifies the towns (in Latin) as Liganburh (Limbury), Egelesburh (Aylesbury), Bensingtun (Bensington), and Ignesham (Eynsham).

atfirst.title: at first
atfirst.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an. Huntingd." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 710 CE and Huntingdon, Historia Anglorum 4.

athelwald.title: Earl Athelwold
athelwald.html: Æthelwald was a ealdorman of East Anglia.

athenaeus.title: Athenaeus
athenaeus.html: Lucius Aurunculeius Cotta was one of Caesar's officers in Gaul; See Commentaries 5.24-37. Athenaeus of Naucratis was a Greek author of the Deipnosophistae, or The Learned Banqueters; see book 6. 273b.

athisgate.title: at his Gate
athisgate.html: See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 3.6.

athisreturn.title: at his return
athisreturn.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." See Simeon, Historia Regum for 1020 CE. See also Cirencester.

atribune.title: a Tribune
atribune.html: Milton's margin here has: "Amm. L. 29." See Ammianus Marcellus, Roman History 29.4.7 where he is called "Fraginarius."

atstamfordbridge.title: at Stamford-bridge
atstamfordbridge.html: Milton's margin here has: "Camd." See Camden "Yorkshire: East and North Ridings" 26.31: "Stanford Bridge." See also Battle of Stamford Bridge.

attendedthem.title: attended them
attendedthem.html: Milton's margin here has: "Malms." See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.10.

atthattime.title: at that time
atthattime.html: Milton's margin here has: "Zozim. L. 6." See Zosimus, New History book 6: "Honorius, having sent letters to the cities of Britain, counselling them to be watchful of their own security, and having rewarded his soldiers with the money sent by Heraclianus, lived with all imaginable ease, since he had acquired the attachment of the soldiers in all places."

atthattime2.title: at that time
atthattime2.html: Milton's margin here has: "Camd." See Camden "Gloucestershire" 13.6.

atthefeast.title: at the feast
atthefeast.html: Milton's margin here has: "Malms." See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.2. See also Burgred of Mercia.

atthepraier.title: at the Praier
atthepraier.html: Milton's margin here has: "Nin. ex legend St. Ger. Galfrid. Monmouth." See Nennius, Historia Brittonum 47: "The saint, as usual, followed him there, and with his clergy fasted and prayed to the Lord three days, and as many nights. On the third night, at the third hour, fire fell suddenly from heaven, and totally burned the castle. Vortigern, the daughter of Hengist, his other wives, and all the inhabitants, both men and women, miserably perished." See a different account in Geoffrey of Monmouth, History of the Kings of Britain 8.2.

atyrantsimeon.title: a Tyrant
atyrantsimeon.html: See Simeon of Durham, Historia Regum for 1013 CE: "si jure queat rex vocari qui fere cuncta tyrannice faciebat."

aulusatticus.title: Aulus Atticus
aulusatticus.html: Aulus Atticus is mentioned by Tacitus in his Life of Agricola, but he remains unidentified.

austin.title: Austin
austin.html: Milton's margin here has: "601." See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 5.epitome: "In the year 601, Pope Gregory sent the pall into Britain, to Augustine, who was already made bishop."

aviolentdeath.title: a violent Death
aviolentdeath.html: Milton's margin here has: "685." See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 4.26: "The same year, being the 685th from the incarnation Of our Lord Lothere, king of Kent, died on the sixth of February, when he had reigned twelve years after his brother Egbert." See also Hlothhere of Kent.

ayearafter.title: a year after
ayearafter.html: Milton's margin here has: "676." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 676 CE.

badencester.title: Badencester
badencester.html: Milton's margin here has: "584." The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records the battle at "Fethanleage" and the death of Cutha. The site is disputed but may possibly be Stoke Lyne.

bangor.title: Monastery of Bangor
bangor.html: Now the site of Bangor Cathedral in Wales, St. Deiniol's Monastery was established around 530 CE.

baramdown.title: Baram down
baramdown.html: See Camden, Britannia "Kent", where he claims to have seen a tablet, hanging on a wall in Dover Castle, that reported Caesar arrived in Deale and the "discomfited the Britans at Baramdowne."

barbarouscruelty.title: barbarous cruelty
barbarouscruelty.html: See Florence of Worcester, and his Chronicron ex Chronicis for 1049 CE.

batavian.title: Batavian
batavian.html: For Tacitus's account of the Batavians and Tungrians, see Life of Agricola 36.

battlepoem.title: extravangant fansies and metaphors
battlepoem.html: Probably because he did not understand Old English, Milton failed to recognize the story interpellated in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle of the Battle of Brunanburh as a poem. Wheeloc, the maker of the Latin translation, notes "Idioma, hic & ad annum 942. & 975, perantiquum, & horridum, Lectoris candorem, & diligentiam desiderat." (Since the style used here and in the annals for 942 and 975 is both rough and highly archaic, perspicuity and industry on the part of the reader are required.) See also the poem "Battle of Brunanburh."

becamedivided.title: became divided
becamedivided.html: Milton now begins to summarize Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 3. See also Eanfrith of Bernicia and Oswald of Northumbria.

beda.title: Beda
beda.html: Milton's margin here has: "Bed. l. 1. c. 22." See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 1.22 where Bede cites Gildas.

bedarelates.title: he relates
bedarelates.html: Bede, in his Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 1.2, decribes the remains of these stakes in his own day (673-735 CE): "the remains of these are to be seen to this day, apparently about the thickness of a man's thigh, and being cased with lead, remain fixed immovably in the bottom of the river."

bedatestifies.title: Beda testifies
bedatestifies.html: Milton's margin here has: "L. 5. c. 9." See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 5.8. See also Bede, 5.24 for the year 725. Bede names the three sons in 5.23.

beforeeaster.title: before Easter
beforeeaster.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." See Simeon of Durham, Historia Regum for 1012 CE.

beforeflood.title: before the Flood
beforeflood.html: The biblical story of the flood may be found in Genesis 6 and 7. The "effectual words" of God to which Milton refers are probably those in Genesis 1:28, addressed to Adam and Eve. Genesis 5 details the generations of Adam before the flood

beforethistime.title: before this time
beforethistime.html: Milton's margin here has: "350." Gratian the Elder was made comes of Britain in the early 340s CE and may have campaigned there with Constans I.

belinusbrennus.title: Belinus and Brennus
belinusbrennus.html: Also known as Balinus and Brennius. Geoffery, History of the Kings of Britain 3.1.

bellogallico.title: Caesar, whose Autority
bellogallico.html: Milton refers to Caesar's Commentarii de Bello Gallico or Commentaries on the Gallic War.

bellovaci.title: Bellovaci
bellovaci.html: The Bellovaci were largest of Belgian tribes of north-eastern Gaul. See Commentaries on the Gallic War 2.14 and 4.20.

bergomas.title: Jacobus Bergomas
bergomas.html: Giacomo Filippo Foresti da Bergamo, an Augustinian monk, was the author of Supplementum chronicarum (1483). Milton probably knew his work, and that of Jacobus Lessabeus, second hand from the works of Holinshed and John Stow. Holinshed in his Chronicle 2.5.

bernicia.title: Bernicia
bernicia.html: Bernicia was an Anglo-Saxon Kingdom located in an area that now lies in southeastern Scotland and North East England.

berossus.title: of oldest seeming
berossus.html: The historical works of Berrosus, or more accurately, Pseudo-Berossus, were an elaborate hoax perpetrated by Annius of Viterbo in 1498. More than a few English historians relied on the forgery.

berossus2.title: forg'd Berosus
berossus2.html: The historical works of Berrosus, or more accurately, Pseudo-Berossus, were an elaborate hoax perpetrated by Annius of Viterbo in 1498. More than a few English historians relied on the forgery. See also a List of legendary kings of Britain.

besideshunting.title: besides hunting
besideshunting.html: Milton's margin here has: "Dion." See Cassius Dio's Roman History 77.12.

bestpoets.title: best Poets
bestpoets.html: Such poets include, of course, Edmund Spenser who in his Faerie Queene twice mentions the battle of Goëmot: book 2, canto 10, stanza 10 and 3.9.50.

betterauthors.title: better Authors
betterauthors.html: Milton's margin here has: "Mat. West." See the Flores Historiarum for 808 CE and 810.

birthofchrist.title: Denmark
birthofchrist.html: Milton's margin here has: "Nennius. Malms." See Nennius, Historia Brittonum 37, where Hengist is said to come from the Island of Oghgul in Scythia (search for "Oghgul"). See also Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 1.1, pages 9-10.

bishopofauxerre.title: Bishop of Auxerre
bishopofauxerre.html: Milton's margin here has: "429." The date of the first mission to Britain by Bishops Germanus and Lupus.

bithric.title: Bithric
bithric.html: Probably a typo for Brithric; see Simeon of Durham, Historia Regum.

bladud.title: Bladud
bladud.html: Bladud or Blaiddyd was a legendary British king.

blazingstar.title: blazing Star
blazingstar.html: See Florence, Chronicron ex Chronicis for 1066. See also Halley's Comet for 1066.

blegabredus.title: Blegabredus
blegabredus.html: See Geoffrey, History of the Kings of Britain 3.19: "Blegabred."

boadicea.title: Boadicea
boadicea.html: Dio has Buduica (Roman History 62.2); Tacitus, Boudicea (Annals 14.31). See also Boudica.

booty.title: bootie
booty.html: "That which is taken from an enemy in war; the collective plunder or spoil" (OED).

borehimnot.title: Assembly at Oxford
borehimnot.html: Milton's margin here has: "Huntingdon. Mat. West. Mat West." See Huntingdon, Historia Anglorum 6. See also the Flores Historiarum for 1035 CE. See also Harold Harefoot: Paternity.

boresti.title: Horestians
boresti.html: Tacitus has "Boresti" (Life of Agricola 38). The Boresti may have been an ancient Celtic tribe of Caledonia (now Scotland).

borninmenapia.title: in Menapia
borninmenapia.html: Milton's margin here has: "Aurel. victor. de Cæsar." Sextus Aurelius Victor wrote Liber de Caesaribus (Book of the Caesars) sometime about 360 CE. In book 39, about Diocletian, we find "Carausius, Menapiae civis." Menapia was the chief town of the Belgic tribe called Menapii.

bornofhissister.title: born of his sister
bornofhissister.html: See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 2.3: "At that time, Sabert, nephew to Ethelbert by his sister Ricula, reigned over the nation, though he was under subjection to Ethelbert, who, as has been said above, had command over all the nations of the English as far as the river Humber." See also Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 1.6, and Sæberht of Essex.

branford.title: Branford
branford.html: See Battle of Brentford (1016). See also Camden "Middlesex" 15.3.

brennus.title: Brennus
brennus.html: Our copytext has an unncorrected misprint here: "Bren-Brennus." See EEBO.

brieflyspake.title: briefly spake
brieflyspake.html: Milton translates the speech as recorded in Tacitus, Annals 12.37.

bringall.title: bring all thir goods
bringall.html: Milton's margin here has: "Dion." See Dio's Roman History 62.2. Catus Decianus was procurator of Roman Britain. Lucius Annaeus Seneca was a stoic philosopher who was alleged to have engaged in high-interest lending in the provinces.

britishauthor.title: British Author
britishauthor.html: Milton refers, somewhat disparagingly, to Geoffrey of Monmouth. See his History of the Kings of Britain 4.1-10. Despite Milton's skepticism about his work, Geoffrey was Milton's chief source in book 1.

britomarus.title: Britomarus
britomarus.html: A third-century BCE Celtic chieftain "whom classical authors, including Plutarch, mention fighting the Romans under Marcellus" (John E. Curran Jr., Roman Invasions [2002] 143).

brokein.title: broke in
brokein.html: Milton's margin here has: "407." The Vandals crossed the Rhine in 406 CE and soon after reached the northern coast of Gaul.

brompton.title: Bromton
brompton.html: John Brompton was a 15th-century abbot of Jorvaux, and a supposed chronicler.

brotherkeola.title: Brother Keola
brotherkeola.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an. Malms." The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for the year 597. And see Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 1.2. See also Ceolwulf of Wessex.

brotherofkeaulin.title: Brother of Keaulin
brotherofkeaulin.html: Milton's margin here has: "571." The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records Cuthulf's battle against the Britons at Bedanford. The Flores Historiarum identifies Ceawlin as Cuthulf's brother, but other genealogies identify Ceawlin as Cuthulf's grandfather.

brotherto.title: brother to
brotherto.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." See Simeon, Historia Regum for 1053 CE. See also Gruffydd ap Llywelyn and Macbeth, King of Scotland.

broughttoanend.title: brought to an end
broughttoanend.html: Milton's margin here has: "Herod. L. 3." See Herodian, History 3.14. Severus travelled to Britain in 208 CE.

brutusconsul.title: Brutus the Consul
brutusconsul.html: Nennius in his Historia Brittonum 1.7-11, identifies Brutus, founder of Britain, as a Roman consul.

brutusline.title: Brutus
brutusline.html: William Camden tells the story of Brutus in his Britannia 2.8.

buchwrites.title: Buchanan
buchwrites.html: See Buchanan, History of Scotland 5.30-31: "Aidanus the son of Goranus came into Scotland by the persuasions of Columba, who two years before had come out of Ireland."

builderandrestorer.title: builder and restorer
builderandrestorer.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an. Huntingd. Mat West." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 925 CE See also Huntingdon, Historia Anglorum 5, and the Flores Historiarum who both record King Edward's death in 924 CE.

buildingswithin.title: buildings within
buildingswithin.html: Milton's margin here has: "Strabo." Strabo was a first-century Greek geographer and author of Geographica. Milton refers here to The Geography 4.5.2.

buildsawall.title: builds a Wall
buildsawall.html: Milton's margin here has: "Spartianus in Sever." See Augustan History, "Life of Septimus Severus" 18.2. Severus is generally credited with restoring and reinforcing Hadrian's Wall.

builtatown.title: built a Town
builtatown.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 924 CE.

builtcarlisle.title: built in the North
builtcarlisle.html: See Geoffrey, History of the Kings of Britain 2.9.

buriedhuntingdon.title: Huntingdon
buriedhuntingdon.html: See Henry of Huntingdon, Historia Anglorum and the Flores Historiarum.

buriedregally.title: buried regally
buriedregally.html: Milton's margin here has: "Asser." A hand other than Asser's reported the death of Alfred in the year 900 CE See the edtorial notes in Asser, Life of Alfred. See also the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 899 CE and Alfred the Great.

bydescentabritan.title: by descent a Britan
bydescentabritan.html: Milton's margin here has: "Vapisc. in Bonos." Flavius Vopiscus Syracusanus was one of the supposed "six scriptores" of the Augustan History; see "Lives of Firmus, Saturninus, Proculus and Bonosus" 14.

byhisnobles.title: by his Nobles
byhisnobles.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." See Simeon of Durham's Historia Regum for 790 CE.

byhisrelation.title: his relation
byhisrelation.html: See the Encomium Emmae Reginae 3.2-6. The forged letter appears in paragraph 3, beginning, "Emma tantum nomine regina, filiis Aeduardo et Alfrido materna impertit salutamina."

byintrusion.title: by intrusion
byintrusion.html: Milton's margin here has: "Ethelwerd." See Æthelweard's Anglo-Saxon Chronicle pages 3-4.

bymildness.title: His Son
bymildness.html: Milton's margin here has: "Bed. L. 2. c. 5." See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 2.5: "Orric, surnamed Oisc, from whom the kings of Kent are wont to be called Oiscings. His father was Hengist, who, being invited by Vortigern, first came into Britain, with his son Oisc, as has been said above."

bymonks.title: by Monks
bymonks.html: Milton's margin here has: "Mat. West." See Flores Historiarum for 959 CE.

bytheinscription.title: by the Inscription
bytheinscription.html: Milton's margin here has: "Camd. Cumber." See Camden's Britannia, "Cumberland" 13 which transcribes a Roman inscription from the time of Gordian that refers to "Nonnius Philippus Lieutenant generall of Britaine."

bythemunderstood.title: by them understood
bythemunderstood.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun. Sax. an." See Simeon of Durham, Historia Regum for 1016 CE. See also the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 1017 CE.

bytheriver.title: by the River
bytheriver.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 833 CE.

caerleon.title: Caerlegion
caerleon.html: Now the city of Chester on the Welsh border. See also the Battle of Chester.

calaterforest.title: Forest of Calater
calaterforest.html: Or Calaterium, see Geoffrey, History of the Kings of Britain 3.17.

caledonians.title: Caledonians
caledonians.html: Caledonia was a Latin name the Romans gave to what today is Scotland. This account follows Tacitus, Life of Agricola 26-27.

calgacus.title: Galgacus
calgacus.html: Calgacus was a chieftain of the Caledonian Confederacy.

calldhimback.title: Pacatianus
calldhimback.html: Milton's margin here has: "Camd." See Camden, Britannia, "Romans 2" 4.77: "Pacatianus was the Vicarius of Britaine."

caln.title: at Caln
caln.html: See Camden, "Wiltshire" 10.5: "an old little towne situat upon a stony ground, having in it a faire Church to commend it: at which place when great adoe there was between the Monkes and Priests about single life, a frequent [crowded] Provinciall Councell or Synod was holden in the yeere of our redemption 977."

calphurnius.title: Calphurnius Agricola
calphurnius.html: Sextus Calpurnius Agricola was was made governor of Britain in 161 or 162 CE by Marcus Aurelius. Marcus Aurelius's son, Lucius Aurelius Commodus, became sole emperor in 180 CE.

camalodunum.title: Camalodunum
camalodunum.html: Camulodunum is the ancient Roman name for present-day Colchester in Essex.

camden.title: Deal in Kent
camden.html: Milton's margin here has: "Camden." William Camden (1551-1623) was an English antiquarian most famous for his Britannia (1586). See Camden, Britannia "Kent".

camdenconjectures.title: The place
camdenconjectures.html: See Camden's comments about "Caer Cardoc" in his Britannia, "Shroppshire" 3.

camdenproves.title: Camden
camdenproves.html: See Camden, Britannia, "Stirling" 30 for records of Roman inscriptions concerning the wall.

camefirst.title: authentic Writers
camefirst.html: Milton's margin here has: "Ethelward. Sax. an. Bede Epit. in the year 565 and Bede, L. 2. c. 4." Æthelweard, elder brother of Alfred the great, was the author of a Latin version of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle. His first book (page 3) identifies the Picts as a northern tribe and the Scots "in the west." On page 8, he identifies 565 CE as the year Columba came from Ireland ("Scotia") "to preach the word of God to the Picts." See also See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 5.24. Bede also calls Ireland "Scotland" here. Columba founded the first Christian community in Scotland on the Isle of Iona in 563 CE.

camesafe.title: came safe
camesafe.html: Milton's margin here has: "597." See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 5.epitome: "In the year 597, the aforesaid teachers arrived in Britain; being about the 150th year from the coming of the English into Britain."

caracalla.title: Antoninus
caracalla.html: Marcus Aurelius Severus Antoninus Augustus was also known as Caracalla; that is how Herodian refers to him in History 3.15.

caradocrelates.title: Caradoc relates
caradocrelates.html: Milton's margin here has: "Caradoc. Llancarvon. vit. Gild." Caradoc of Llancarfan was probably the author of a Life of Gildas in Latin; see paragraphs 10-11: Gildas "put in at Glastonia, at the time when king Melvas was reigning in the summer country." See also Monmouth, History of the Kings of Britain 12.20.

cartismandua.title: Cartismandua
cartismandua.html: Also known as Cartimandua, Queen of the Brigantes.

cassibelan.title: Cassibelan
cassibelan.html: In Caesar's Commentaries 5.11 he is called Cassivellaunus.

casually.title: casually
casually.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun. Hoved." See Simeon of Durham, Historia Regum for 982 CE. See also Roger of Hovedon, Chronica for 982 CE.

catus.title: Catus Decianus
catus.html: Catus Decianus was the procurator of Roman Britain 60 or 61 CE.

causeofthis.title: cause of this expedition
causeofthis.html: Malmesbury makes this remark about an earlier battle at "a place called Dacor" in 926 or 927 CE: Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.6.

cavils.title: cavils
cavils.html: OED: [cf. Latin cavilla.] A flout, gibe, jeer.

certainnobles.title: returning from
certainnobles.html: Milton's margin here has: "Eccles. L. 2." Simeon of Durham's Historia Ecclesiae for 792 CE reports that Osred fled to the Isle of Man.

chariots.title: Chariots
chariots.html: The Celtic chariot was a two-horsed biga, open in the front. See also Caesar's Commentaries 4.33.

cheulphus.title: Ceulphus the Morine Duke
cheulphus.html: Also known as Cheulphus, general of the Morini, a Belgic tribe of northern Gaul.

chiefcommanders.title: chief Commanders
chiefcommanders.html: Milton's margin here has: "Labanius in Basilico." Labanius authored an oration entitled "Basilicus, seu Panegyricus Constanti et Constantio Impp. Dictus" which implies the two brothers visited Britain.

chosncompany.title: two Brothers
chosncompany.html: Milton's margin here has: "Bede." See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 1.15. Hengist and Horsa are legendary brothers said to have led the Angles, Saxons, and Jutes into Britain in the 5th century CE. Woden, or Odin, is a pagan god of Germans and Norse.

chr-1641.title: In 1641
chr-1641.html: This is somewhat misleading, since most of Milton's criticism of the Long Parliament has to do with matters that occurred long after that date. Perhaps the editor chose that date as a way of naming the Parliament by a date near its beginning. The Assembly was not officially commissioned until 1643. Milton probably composed this portion of his History in 1649.

chr-beginningplace.title: Character
chr-beginningplace.html: The never-published manuscript version of the Digression includes two pages (one leaf) of text before this place where the 1681 Character begins. Those two pages introduce Milton's theme of comparing the failure of 5th-century Britons to make good use of a rare opportunity to establish lasting liberty following the retreat of the Romans to what he regards as a similar failure of the Long Parliament following the defeat of King Charles I. He rejects Gildas's opinion that the Britons were weak in arms.

chr-bosoms.title: covetous Bosoms
chr-bosoms.html: French Fogle, in Yale Prose 5.1 (455 n22), identifies a number of Assembly members who benefitted in some of the ways Milton here enumerates. Anthony Tuckney, vicar of Boston in Lincolnshire, accepted appointment as Master of Emmanuel College, Cambridge; he also prospered after the Restoration. Herbert Palmer, who later became one of the most vocal opponents of Milton's Doctrine and Discipline of Divorce, held a vicarage in Hertfordhsire and was made Master of Queens, Cambridge in 1644. Lazarus Seaman, rector of Allhallows, Bread Street (London) where Milton was baptized, became Master of Peterhouse in 1644. Thomas Young, once Milton's tutor, was vicar of St. Peter and St. Mary at Stowmarket, and was appointed Master of Jesus College, Cambridge in 1644; he was expelled from that position in 1650.

chr-character.title: CHARACTER of the Long Parliament
chr-character.html: This version of the Digression first appeared in 1681 as a quarto pamphlet. Including the title page, it runs about 12 pages. It appears to have been prepared for the press by Roger L'Estrange, a Tory pamphleteer and persistent critic of Milton, probably working from a manuscript now lost, but perhaps similar to the 17th-century manuscript now held by the Harvard College Library (Harvard MS Eng 901 Lobby XI.2.69). He appears to have abbreviated the text significantly. The Long Parliament sat from 1640 until December 1648, when it was purged of members unwilling to put King Charles I on trial for treason by Army Colonel Thomas Pride. In its "Rump" form, it lasted until 1660 and the restoration of monarchy and bishops. The Westminster Assembly of Divines was commissioned by Parliament in 1643 to restructure the English Church along Presbyterian, non-episcopal, principles. The idea of appointing such a body was first proposed in Parliament in 1641, and was resisted by the King until Parliament acted without royal consent.

chr-divines.title: Divines were called
chr-divines.html: In 1643, Parliament appointed the Westminster Assembly of Divines, or clergymen, to deliberate on reform of the English Church. Delegates were chosen by counties and by regions and from the two universities, but Milton sounds less than sanguine about the process of selection.

chr-honoured.title: honoured
chr-honoured.html: The 1681 edition misprints this word as "hononred", probably a matter of an inverted letter.

chr-integrity.title: some indeed men of Wisdom and Integrity
chr-integrity.html: Just whom Milton might consider belonging to such a group calls for some speculation. French Fogle in the Yale Prose edition (volume 5, part 1, 452 n. 11) lists the following with "some confidence:" Henry Vane the Younger, John Selden, John Hampden and Oliver Cromwell. Among the Lords, he suggests Robert Greville, Lord Brooke. Milton wrote, but posthumously published, a sonnet in celebration of Henry Vane.

chr-latetroubles.title: late Troubles
chr-latetroubles.html: Milton refers to the civil wars between Parliament and King Charles I during the 1640s. Like the 5th-century Britons, the New Model Army had plenty of military force to prosecute its war against the king.

chr-money.title: many
chr-money.html: The 1681 edition, due either to a misprint or simple editorial error, here appears to have changed "money" to "many."

chr-ownprofit.title: his own profit
chr-ownprofit.html: One of the first acts of the new Parliament was the Triennial Act of 1641, which required that Parliament meet for at least 50 days in a 3-year period. Charles I had ruled for 11 years without calling a Parliament. Parliament got a bit bogged down in its efforts to address abuses of monopolies and excise taxes.

chr-parliamentcalled.title: a Parliament being call'd
chr-parliamentcalled.html: After 11 years of royal government without parliament and a brief fiasco of a "Short Parliament" in the spring of 1640, a parliament was summoned by royal order on 24 September 1640. Elections were held in October. What came to be known (much later) as the Long Parliament first sat on the 3rd of November 1640.

chr-personalestate.title: Personal Estate
chr-personalestate.html: The editor, Roger L'Estrange, believes that Milton, like many supporters of Parliament's war against King Charles I, invested his own private wealth in the cause, and failed ever to recover it due to waste, fraud, and failure to honor the "Publick Faith." Milton also complains about similar corruption in his sonnet to Fairfax, probably composed in the summer of 1648. That sonnet was not included in the 1673 Poems, for reasons similar to those that prompted the omission of what we now call the Digression in 1670.

chr-pluralities.title: Pluralities
chr-pluralities.html: Early on, Milton had joined the Presbyterian attacks on pluralism, the practice of holding multiple ecclesiastical offices and appointemnts at one time. Here he charges that they have proved hypocrites by indulging in the practice themselves.

chr-publickfaith.title: The Publick Faith
chr-publickfaith.html: This term had a very specific meaning in the ordinance of the 9th of June 1642. By this ordinance (and several succeeding ordinances), Parliament raised funds to wage an expensive war against King Charles I. Milton refers to the breach of this Public Faith—"Publick Fraud"—in his posthumously published sonnet to Fairfax.

chr-salary.title: Publick Salary
chr-salary.html: The act that established the Assembly of Divines (12 June 1643) also stipulated that "That for the Charges and Expences of the said Divines, and every of them in attending the said Service, there shall be allowed unto every of them that shall so attend, during the time of their said attendance, and for ten days before and ten days after, the sum of Four Shillings for every day, at the charges of the Commonwealth, at such time and in such manner as by both Houses of Parliament shall be appointed."

chr-seasonable.title: seasonable for these times
chr-seasonable.html: This most likely refers to the period known now as the Exclusion Crisis (1679-81), an attempt by parliamentary Whigs to exclude James, Duke of York (later James II), from succession to the English throne because he was a Roman Catholic. L'Estrange and Tory readers took delight in using Milton's criticisms of the revolutionary Long Parliament to advance their cause in support of James in 1681.

chr-shopsand.title: from Shops and Ware-houses
chr-shopsand.html: Milton did not think well of the merchants and tradesmen elected to Parliament. He assumed they were motivated by their own ambitions for profit.

chr-suchservice.title: performing such service
chr-suchservice.html: Milton, appointed in March 1649 by the Council of State as Secretary for Foreign Tongues, performed many services for the Commonwealth, including writing Eikonoklastes against the king's book, Eikon Basilike, and his monumental Latin defenses of the English People. The editor here, probably Roger L'Estrange, suggests that Milton performed such "services" merely to repair his lost wealth.

chr-tenderness.title: tenderness to a Party
chr-tenderness.html: From at least 1645 on, Milton was hardly a supporter of the Presbyterian "party" in Parliament. However, in 1670, when preparing his History for the press, he may have thought further criticism of a parliament now more than ten years out of power was superfluous, or he may have given way to other persuasions, or even, as Nicholas von Maltzahn suggests, threats (Milton's History of Britain 16).

chr-theirsubstance.title: with their substance
chr-theirsubstance.html: This passage led Roger LeStrange, the editor and publisher of the 1681 Character, to suppose that Milton was one of those who lent much of his "Personal Estate" to aid the cause of Parliament and then never recovered it. There is precious little, if any, evidence for this supposition.

chr-thesun.title: Sun which we want
chr-thesun.html: As late as Paradise Lost (1667 and 1674), Milton still advanced the speculative notion that cold northern climates may be bad for arts and sciences of many kinds; see PL 9.44-46.

chr-whichplace.title: which place
chr-whichplace.html: According to the manuscript version of the Digression, the place where the Digression originally began was in book 3, after the words, "from one misery to another." When first published together with the History, by Thomas Birch in 1738, the Digression (the 1681 version) was inserted after the first sentence of Book 3.

christiansubjects.title: Christian Subjects
christiansubjects.html: Milton's margin here has: "Gildas." See Gildas, The Ruin of Britain 9-11.

churlishly.title: Emma, his Sister
churlishly.html: Milton's margin here has: "Malms." See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.10 for the story of Queen Emma's visit to her brother, Richard II, Duke of Normandy.

cicerowrites.title: Cicero writes
cicerowrites.html: Milton's margin here has: "Cic. Att. L. 4. Ep.17." See Marcus Tullius Cicero, Letters to Atticus 4.16 (not 17), where Cicero writes of "astonishing masses of cliff," which Milton calls "moles."

citesacharter.title: cites a Charter
citesacharter.html: See Camden, "Ireland" 32.14: "Unto whom God of His gracious favour hath granted together with the Empire of England dominion over all the Kingdomes of the Isles lying in the Ocean, with the most stout and fierce Kings even as farre as to Norway, yea and to subdue under the English Empire the greatest part of Ireland with her most noble City Dublin."

cityofrochester.title: City of Rochester
cityofrochester.html: Milton's margin here has: "Bed. l. 4. c. 12." See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 4.12.

civilwar.title: late civil broils
civilwar.html: Milton refers here to both the first and the second of the English Civil Wars between 1642 and 1648, which culminated with the execution for treason of King Charles I on January 30, 1649.

civilwarr.title: Civil Warr
civilwarr.html: Milton's margin here has: "Ammian. L. 20. & in eum Valesius." Ammianus Marcellinus was the author of Res Gestae or Roman History; see book 20.1-3. See also Valesius's account. See also Constantine II.

civilwars.title: Civil Warrs
civilwars.html: Caesar's civil war pitted Julius Caesar against Pompey and was the last political-military conflict before the advent of the Roman Empire and the end of the Roman Republic.

clearthedoubt.title: clear the doubt
clearthedoubt.html: Milton's margin here has: "Idem vit. Auth. ignot. Euseb. Const." See The Anonymous Valesius's account and Eusebius, Life of Constantine 1.8.

cleersnot.title: could not be
cleersnot.html: There is reason to believe that Milton's copy of Simeon of Durham included a tract by another author that introduced conflicting dates.

coaps.title: Coaps
coaps.html: A cope is a liturgical vestment. So is a pall or pallium.

comeforth.title: come forth
comeforth.html: Milton's margin here has: "Asser." See Asser, Life of Alfred.

cometoage.title: come to Age
cometoage.html: Milton's margin here has: "Ethelwerd." See Æthelweard, Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 4.8.

comingtoreigne.title: coming to Reigne
comingtoreigne.html: Milton's margin here has: "Ninn." See Nennius, Historia Brittonum 43-44 for the story of "Vortimer, the son of Vortigern."

comingtorequire.title: coming to require
comingtorequire.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 800 CE, but also for 836 concerning the exile of Egbert in France. See also Ecgberht, King of Wessex.

comingtotreaty.title: coming to treaty
comingtotreaty.html: See Simeon, Historia Regum for 1052 CE.

comius.title: Comius of Arras
comius.html: That is, Caesar made Comius King of the Atrabates. See Commentaries 4.21.

commandedhim.title: commanded him
commandedhim.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. ann." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 784 CE, but also fuller details of the story under 755.

commandedhome.title: commanded home
commandedhome.html: Milton's margin here has: "86." Gnaeus Julius Agricola was recalled from Britain in 85 CE.

commendedmuch.title: commended much
commendedmuch.html: See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 3.14. See also Oswine of Deira.

committed.title: committed
committed.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an. Malms." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 819 CE See also Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.13, and the Flores Historiarum for 821 CE. See also the Legend of Saint Kenelm.

commonfame.title: common fame
commonfame.html: See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.10.

commonsort.title: common sort
commonsort.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 897 CE.

commonverse.title: verse in Lucan
commonverse.html: For Lucan, see his The Civil War 2.645.

compelldnone.title: compell'd none
compelldnone.html: Milton's margin here has: "Bed. l. 2. c. 5." See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 2.5. Why Milton refers to this passage is unclear. It says nothing about either Æthelbert's favoring of converts to Christianity nor of his tolerance of non-converts. Bede dates Æthelbert's death accurately in 616 CE, but that was 19, not 21, years following the arrival of Augustine's mission. But see also Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 1.26:"Their conversion the king so far encouraged, as that he compelled none to embrace Christianity, but only showed more affection to the believers".

computation.title: truer computation
computation.html: Tacitus, in his Annals 12.36 reports nine years, but Milton may here accept the editorial comment made by Lipsius in his edition of Tacitus (1627), or the dates asserted by Calvisius in his Opus Chronologicum (French Fogle, Yale Prose 5 [1] 71).

conanus.title: Conanus
conanus.html: For Aurelius Conanus, see Gildas, The Ruin of Britain 30.

concludeapeace.title: conclude a Peace
concludeapeace.html: Milton's margin here has: "Victor. Eutrop." See Aurelius Victor's Liber de Caesaribus 39 and Eutropius's Abridged History of Rome 9.22.

concludedpeace.title: concluded peace
concludedpeace.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 907 CE.

confederatebrother.title: confederate Brother
confederatebrother.html: Milton's margin here has: "Malms." See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.11.

constantinescot.title: Constantine
constantinescot.html: Constantine II was King of Alba from 900 to 943 CE.

contemptible.title: contemptible
contemptible.html: Milton's margin here has: "Ann. omn." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for an entry recording the defeat of Æthelberht by Ceawlin and Cutha at a place called "Wibban-dune."

continualpreaching.title: continual preaching
continualpreaching.html: Milton's margin here has: "Prosp. Aquit." See Prosper of Aquitaine, Prosper's Chronicum (search for "Germanus" and "Lupus").

continualsupplies.title: continual supplies
continualsupplies.html: See Nennius, Historia Brittonum 56: "And while they were being defeated in all the battles, they were seeking assistance from Germany and their numbers were being augmented many times over without interruption."

continualvictories.title: continual Victories
continualvictories.html: Milton's margin here has: "Bed. l. 1. c. 25." See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 1.25. See also Bertha of Kent.

conversion.title: conversion
conversion.html: Milton's margin here has: "Florent. Genealog." See the Flores Historiarum.

convertedalso.title: converted also
convertedalso.html: See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 2.16.

converting.title: converting
converting.html: Milton's margin here has: "Bed. l. 2. c. 1." See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 2.1.

cordelia.title: Cordelia
cordelia.html: Cordelia of Britain was a legendary queen of the Britons.

corineus.title: Corineus
corineus.html: A legendary British warrior and giant slayer, Corineus was considered the eponymous founder of Cornwall. Goffarius Pictus, according to this story, was the King of Aquitainia.

corsecastle.title: Corfe Castle
corsecastle.html: See Camden, "Dorset" 9.4. See also Corfe Castle.

countryabove.title: Country above
countryabove.html: That is, what Milton calls "Anglen" above, also known as Angeln. See also Wuffa of East Anglia.

crossesthesea.title: crosses the Sea
crossesthesea.html: Milton's margin here has: "367." Theodosius the Elder Was raised to the rank of comes and sent to Britain in 368 CE.

cruellbattel.title: cruell Battel
cruellbattel.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 715 CE.

cullen.title: Cullen
cullen.html: Cologne (in Latin, Agrippina), where, according to Eutropius's Abridged History of Rome 9.17, Bonosus and Proclus were defeated by Probus.

cunedagius.title: Cunedagius
cunedagius.html: A legendary king of the Britons, Cunedagius was the son of Henwinus.

cuneglas.title: Cuneglas
cuneglas.html: See Gildas, The Ruin of Britain 32. See also Cuneglasus.

cuthahisson.title: Cutha his son
cuthahisson.html: Milton's margin here has: "568." The son of Ceawlin was Cuthwine, and Cuthwine's son was Cutha, or Cuthwulf.

dangerousopinions.title: dangerous Opinions
dangerousopinions.html: Milton's margin here has: "405." Pelagianism denied that original sin tainted human nature, rendering human will incapable of choosing good over evil without the assistance of divine (prevenient) grace. Augustine (St. Austin), in his Christian Doctrine, wrote against Pelagian notions of the human will.

danishhistory.title: History
danishhistory.html: Johan Isaaksz Pontanus was a Dutch historian and author of Rerum Danicarum historia (Amsterdam, 1631; Fensburg, 1637).

danishtax.title: Danish Tax
danishtax.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." See Simeon, Historia Regum for 1051 CE. See also Danegeld.

deathofoffa.title: strenuous
deathofoffa.html: Milton's margin here has: "Malms." See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 1.4. The letter from Charles (Charles the Great, or Charlemagne) to Offa appears on pages 85-86.

dedicated.title: dedicated
dedicated.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." See Simeon, Historia Regum for 1032 CE. See also Bury St. Edmunds Abbey.

dee.title: River Dee
dee.html: The Dee is a principal river in Wales.

defending.title: defending
defending.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." See Simeon of Durham, Historia Regum for 1001 CE.

degsastan.title: Degsastan
degsastan.html: "The Battle of Degsastan was fought around 603 between king Æthelfrith of Bernicia and the Gaels under Áedán mac Gabráin, king of Dál Riada."

deira.title: Deira
deira.html: See the ancient Anglian Kingdom of Deira.

deserted.title: deserted
deserted.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sozom. L. 9." Sozomenus, in Ecclesiastical History 9.13, tells the gruesome story of Gerontius's grisly end with more detail an commentary than others.

deservebelief.title: deserve belief
deservebelief.html: See Gildas, The Ruin of Britain 21.

deservedlysomesay.title: deservedly
deservedlysomesay.html: See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 1.3.

desirdbanishment.title: desir'd banishment
desirdbanishment.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." and repeated a second time. See Simeon of Durham's Historia Regum for 792 CE. This entry also records Æthelred's marriage to Offa's daughter, Elfledam.

destitute.title: destitute
destitute.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 895 CE.

destruction.title: Kyules
destruction.html: Milton's margin here has: "Gildas." See Gildas, The Ruin of Britain 23: "A multitude of whelps came forth from the lair of this barbaric lioness, in three cyuls, as they call them, that is, in their ships of war." Cyuls are Keels.

didius.title: Aulus Didius
didius.html: Aulus Didius Gallus, an imperial legate under Claudius. See Tacitus, Annals 12.40.

differsinthename.title: differs in the name also
differsinthename.html: See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.6: "Anlaf, the son of Sihtric, then fled into Ireland, and his brother Guthferth into Scotland."

digression.title: to another
digression.html: According to the manuscript version (Digression-MS), the Digression follows this paragraph.

digression1681.title: great undertakings
digression1681.html: Following these words, Thomas Birch, in his edition of A Complete Collection of the Historical, Political, and Miscellaneous Works of John Milton (1738), inserts the Digression from the 1681 text of Mr. John Miltons Character of the Long Parliament and Assembly of Divines.

dike.title: Dike
dike.html: "A ridge, embankment, long mound, or dam, thrown up to resist the encroachments of the sea, or to prevent low-lying lands from being flooded by seas, rivers, or streams." (OED).

diligentesthistorian.title: diligentest Historian
diligentesthistorian.html: Milton refers to Johan Isaaksz Pontanus, a Dutch historian and author of Rerum Danicarum Historia (Amsterdam, 1631; Fensburg, 1637).

diodorus.title: Diodorus
diodorus.html: Diodorus of Sicily's Bibliotheca historica, or "Universal History," included many accounts of events attested only by poets.

dionaffirms.title: Dion affirms
dionaffirms.html: See Cassius Dio's Roman History 40.3.

disdainedsight.title: disdained sight
disdainedsight.html: Tacitus reports Agrippina's sitting in state as "a novelty, quite alien to ancient manners:" Annals 12.37; Milton adds the misogynist "disdain."

disquietedboth.title: things in peace
disquietedboth.html: Milton's margin here has: "Bed." See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 4.26: "till the lawful king, Wictred, the son of Egbert, being settled in the throne, by his piety and zeal delivered his nation from foreign invasion."

diverspassages.title: in Tacitus
diverspassages.html: For Tacitus, see his The Life of Julius Agricola 13.

diviat.title: Divitiacus
diviat.html: Diviciacus or Divitiacus was a druid of the Aedui tribe who lived in Gaul during the 1st century BCE.

divineworship.title: divine worship
divineworship.html: Milton's margin here has: "598." Æthelbert is generally supposed to have converted within one year of Gregory's arrival. See also St. Martins Church.

dms-12ages.title: 12 ages and more
dms-12ages.html: The 12 centuries and more between the departure of the Romans sometime around 410 CE and the defeats of King Charles I, first in 1645, and then more permanently in January 1649.
