dms-after.title: after
dms-after.html: French Fogle, in his edition of the digression in the Yale Prose (5.1.441), supplies the letter "r" for the word "after."

dms-anough.title: anough
dms-anough.html: French Fogle, in his edition of the digression in the Yale Prose, supplies the letters "gh" for the word "anough."

dms-asgildas.title: as Gildas reportes
dms-asgildas.html: See Gildas, On the Ruin of Britain 14-20.

dms-authoritie.title: authoritie
dms-authoritie.html: French Fogle, in his edition of the digression in the Yale Prose, supplies the letter "e" for the word "authoritie."

dms-authority.title: authoritie
dms-authority.html: French Fogle, in his edition of the digression in the Yale Prose, supplies the letters "ie" for the word "authoritie."

dms-becomes.title: becomes
dms-becomes.html: French Fogle, in his edition of the digression in the Yale Prose, supplies the letter "s" for the word "becomes."

dms-bosoms.title: covetous bosomes
dms-bosoms.html: French Fogle, in Yale Prose 5.1 (455 n22), identifies a number of Assembly members who benefitted in some of the ways Milton here enumerates. Anthony Tuckney, vicar of Boston in Lincolnshire, accepted appointment as Master of Emmanuel College, Cambridge; he also prospered after the Restoration. Herbert Palmer, who later became one of the most vocal opponents of Milton's Doctrine and Discipline of Divorce, held a vicarage in Hertfordhsire and was made Master of Queens, Cambridge in 1644. Lazarus Seaman, rector of Allhallows, Bread Street (London) where Milton was baptized, became Master of Peterhouse in 1644. Thomas Young, once Milton's tutor, was vicar of St. Peter and St. Mary at Stowmarket, and was appointed Master of Jesus College, Cambridge in 1644; he was expelled from that position in 1650.

dms-integrity.html: Just whom Milton might consider belonging to such a group calls for some speculation. French Fogle in the Yale Prose edition (volume 5, part 1, 452 n. 11) lists the following with "some confidence:" Henry Vane the Younger, John Selden, John Hampden and Oliver Cromwell. Among the Lords, he suggests Robert Greville, Lord Brooke. Milton wrote, but posthumously published, a sonnet in celebration of Henry Vane.

dms-latetroubles.title: late troubles
dms-latetroubles.html: Milton refers to the civil wars between Parliament and King Charles I during the 1640s. Like the 5th-century Britons, the New Model Army had plenty of military force to prosecute its war against the king.

dms-ofthese.html: With these words the 1681 edition of the Digression, Milton's Character of the Long Parliament, begins.

dms-once.html: French Fogle, in his edition of the digression in the Yale Prose (5.1.443), supplies the letter "e" for the word "once."

dms-ownprofit.title: his owne profit
dms-ownprofit.html: One of the first acts of the new Parliament was the Triennial Act of 1641, which required that Parliament meet for at least 50 days in a 3-year period. Charles I had ruled for 11 years without calling a Parliament. Parliament got a bit bogged down in its efforts to address abuses of monopolies and excise taxes.

dms-parliamentcalled.title: a parliament being call'd
dms-parliamentcalled.html: After 11 years of royal government without parliament and a brief fiasco of a "Short Parliament" in the spring of 1640, a parliament was summoned by royal order on 24 September 1640. Elections were held in October. What came to be known (much later) as the Long Parliament first sat on the 3rd of November 1640.

dms-period.title: period
dms-period.html: French Fogle, in his edition of the digression in the Yale Prose, supplies the period here.

dms-period2.title: period
dms-period2.html: French Fogle, in his edition of the digression in the Yale Prose, supplies the period here.

dms-pluralities.title: pluralities
dms-pluralities.html: Early on, Milton had joined the Presbyterian attacks on pluralism, the practice of holding multiple ecclesiastical offices and appointemnts at one time. Here he charges that they have proved hypocrites by indulging in the practice themselves.

dms-principles.title: principles
dms-principles.html: French Fogle, in his edition of the digression in the Yale Prose, supplies the letter "s" for the word "principles."

dms-publickfaith.title: the publick faith
dms-publickfaith.html: This term had a very specific meaning in the ordinance of the 9th of June 1642. By this ordinance (and several succeeding ordinances), Parliament raised funds to wage an expensive war against King Charles I. Milton refers to the breach of this Public Faith—"Publick Fraud"—in his posthumously published sonnet to Fairfax.

dms-related.title: related
dms-related.html: French Fogle, in his edition of the digression in the Yale Prose, supplies a colon here; I reckon a semi-colon makes more sense and is more in keeping with Milton's punctuation practice.

dms-salary.title: public salarie
dms-salary.html: The act that established the Assembly of Divines (12 June 1643) also stipulated that "That for the Charges and Expences of the said Divines, and every of them in attending the said Service, there shall be allowed unto every of them that shall so attend, during the time of their said attendance, and for ten days before and ten days after, the sum of Four Shillings for every day, at the charges of the Commonwealth, at such time and in such manner as by both Houses of Parliament shall be appointed."

dms-shopsand.title: from shops & warehouses
dms-shopsand.html: Milton did not think well of the merchants and tradesmen elected to Parliament. He assumed they were motivated by their own ambitions for profit.

dms-teachers.title: teachers
dms-teachers.html: French Fogle, in his edition of the digression in the Yale Prose, supplies the letter "h" for the word "teachers."

dms-theirsubstance.title: with thir substance
dms-theirsubstance.html: This passage led Roger LeStrange, the editor and publisher of the 1681 Character, to suppose that Milton was one of those who lent much of his "Personal Estate" to aid the cause of Parliament and then never recovered it. There is precious little, if any, evidence for this supposition.

dms-thesewords.title: these words
dms-thesewords.html: This refers to the first edition of The History of Britain, book 3, page 110 (image 57). The brackets are in the original MS. Nothing from the first two pages of this MS appears in the 1681 Character.

dms-thesun.title: sunn, which we want
dms-thesun.html: As late as Paradise Lost (1667 and 1674), Milton still advanced the speculative notion that cold northern climates may be bad for arts and sciences of many kinds; see PL 9.44-46.

dms-they.title: they
dms-they.html: French Fogle, in his edition of the digression in the Yale Prose, supplies the letter "y" for the word "they."

dms-us.title: us
dms-us.html: French Fogle, in his edition of the digression in the Yale Prose, supplies the word "us" here.

dms-were.html: French Fogle, in his edition of the digression in the Yale Prose, supplies the letter "e" for the word "were."

dms-weretoseeke.title: were to seeke
dms-weretoseeke.html: That is, if they were indeed somewhat unpracticed in the arts of war, which Milton rather doubts.

dms-wisdom.title: wisdom
dms-wisdom.html: French Fogle, in his edition of the digression in the Yale Prose, supplies the letter "m" for the word "wisdom."

donenothing.title: done nothing
donenothing.html: Milton's margin here has: "Huntingd." See Huntingdon, Historia Anglorum 6.

doroverne.title: Doroverne
doroverne.html: See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 1.25: "Dedit ergo eis mansionem in ciuitate Doruuernensi, quae imperii sui totius erat metropolis." Dorovernum Cantiacorum was a Roman name for Canterbury.

dosomething.title: do something
dosomething.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sueton." See Suetonius's Lives of the Caesars, "The Life of Claudius" 17.1.

doubtsnot.title: doubts not
doubtsnot.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." Simeon of Durham's Historia Regum for the year 744 CE. speaks of a battle between Picts and Britons.

dreading.title: rejected
dreading.html: Milton's margin here has: "Hoved." See Roger of Hoveden's Annals for 950 CE.

drivenout2.title: driv'n out
drivenout2.html: Milton's margin here has: "Ingulf." Ingulf was a Benedictine abbot of Crowland, or Croyland. In Milton's day he was widely credited with being the author of the Historia Monasterii Croylandensis or the Croyland Chronicle; the Chronicle has since been exposed as a medieval forgery. The Pseudo-Ingulf, Historia dated Cenwulf's death in 819 CE (page 486). See also Ceolwulf I of Mercia.

drovethemback.title: drove them back
drovethemback.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 837 CE.

drovethemonks.title: drove the Monks
drovethemonks.html: Milton's margin here has: "Florent. Sim. Dun." See the Flores Historiarum, and Simeon of Durham, Historia Regum. See also Byrhtnoth.

druids.title: Druids
druids.html: Ancient sources, including Caesar and Tacitus, describe the Druids as philosophers, political advisors, legal experts, physicians, and religious leaders. Although literate, even using Greek letters, sources report that they avoided recording their knowledge in written form, especially their doctrines and beliefs. References to Druids date from the 4th century BCE. Milton refers here to Caesar's Commentarii de Bello Gallico (50s BCE) in which Caesar mentions that Druids believed it unlawful to commit their doctrines to writing. They memorized it in oral, probably poetic, forms. See Caesar's Commentaries on the Gallic War 6.13-14. The part to which Milton refers comes from 6.14.

dueadministration.title: due administration
dueadministration.html: Milton loosely follows Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 2.16.

dulcitius.title: Dulcitius
dulcitius.html: A Roman governor of Macedonia who may have been brought to Britain in 369 CE by Theodosius the Elder.

dunfeoder.title: Dunfeoder
dunfeoder.html: Dunfeoder is now called Dunnottar and Wertermore remains unidentified. Cathness is in northern Scotland on the North Sea.

dunwallo.title: Dunwallo Molmutius
dunwallo.html: Also known to the Welsh as Dyfnwal Moelmud, Dyfnwal the Bald and Silent. See Geoffery, History of the Kings of Britain 2.17.

durus.title: Quintus Laberius Durus
durus.html: Quintus Laberius Durus died in August 54 BCE. See Caesar Commentaries 5.15.

dwellings.title: thir dwellings
dwellings.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." See Simeon of Durham's Historia Regum for 886 CE.

dyingorslain.title: dying or slain
dyingorslain.html: Milton's margin here has: "Bed. l. 5. c. 24." See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 5.23.

eadmerandsimeon.title: Eadmer and Simeon
eadmerandsimeon.html: See Eadmer, Historia novorum in Anglia, 4-5, and Simeon, Historia Regum for 1066 CE. See also Harold Godwinson: in Northern France.

earlbaldwin.title: Earl Baldwin
earlbaldwin.html: See Baldwin V, Count of Flanders and Tostig Godwinson.

easiestpassage.title: Marcus
easiestpassage.html: Milton's margin here has: "Zozim. L. 6." See Zosimus, New History book 6: "When Arcadius was reigning, Honorius being consul the seventh time and Theodosius the second, the troops in Britain revolted and promoted Marcus to the imperial throne, rendering obedience to him as the sovereign in those countries."

ebranc.title: Ebranc
ebranc.html: In Geoffrey he is called Ebraucus (History of the Kings of Britain 2.7).

ecbert.title: Ecbert
ecbert.html: See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 4.1. See also Ecgberht of Kent.

ecferth.title: Ecferth
ecferth.html: Ecgfrith was king of Mercia from 29 July to December 796 CE.

eclips.title: Eclips
eclips.html: See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 3.27 and 5.24 (the epitome).

edan.title: Edan
edan.html: Milton's margin here has: "603." See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 5.epitome: "In the year 603, a battle was fought at Degsastane." See also Áedán mac Gabráin.

edelburga.title: Edelburga
edelburga.html: See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 2.9. See also Æthelburh of Kent.

edinburgnowstands.title: Edinburg now stands
edinburgnowstands.html: Milton's margin here has: "Bede. L. 1. c. 2." See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 1.12.

edreddead.title: was buried
edreddead.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." See Simeon of Durham, Historia Regum for 955 CE.

edwinofmercia.title: Edwin
edwinofmercia.html: See Edwin of Mercia, Morcar of Northumbria, and Malcolm III of Scotland.

elder.title: his elder
elder.html: That is, Elidure, whom he overthrew with his other brother's help.

eldestson.title: eldest Son
eldestson.html: See Edward the Martyr. Milton cobbles the following accounts from Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.9, together with some bits from the Flores Historiarum (for 964 and 975 CE) and Simeon of Durham, Historia Regum for 964 and 975 CE.

electedking.title: without the Regal Habiliments
electedking.html: Milton's margin here has: "Encom. Em." See the Encomium Emmae Reginae 3.1 where Harold is referred to aas "filium falsa" and we read that Archbishop "Aelnotum" refused to consecrate him as king. See also Ælnoth of Canterbury.

elfrida.title: Elfrida
elfrida.html: The following story comes from Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.8. See also Ælfthryth, wife of Edgar.

elidurus.title: Elidure
elidurus.html: Elidurus the Pious, or Dutiful. See Geoffrey, History of the Kings of Britain 3.17.

embraceit.title: Paulinus
embraceit.html: Milton's margin here has: "625." The date Bede records for the ordination of Bishop Paulinus. See also the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle under the year 625 CE. See also Paulinus of York.

eminentperson.title: some eminent person
eminentperson.html: Milton closely follows Bede's account here: Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 1.16. Bede indicates that the Briton's leader at this time was a "a modest man," a Roman named Ambrosius Aurelius.

emperorinperson.title: Emperor in person
emperorinperson.html: Milton's margin here has: "122." Hadrian was in Britain from approximately 121 to 122 CE. The second Roman-Jewish war broke out in 132 CE. Evidently Milton is mistaken about Hadrian's reason for visiting Britain.

emperourdispleasd.title: Emperour displeas'd
emperourdispleasd.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." See Simeon, Historia Regum for 1049 CE. See also Baldwin V, Count of Flanders. Milton's account deviates significantly from Simeon's.

enchantments.title: enchantments
enchantments.html: Milton's account follows Bede's quite closely, but see Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 1.25. Milton suggests that the sung litanies may have increased Æthelbert's suspicions.

endofelfwald.title: end of Elfwald
endofelfwald.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun. Malms." See Simeon of Durham's Historia Regum for 788 CE. See also Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 1.3.

endowd.title: Archbishop
endowd.html: Milton's margin here has: "Bed. l. 1. c. 27." See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 1.27.

englishbishops.title: English Bishops
englishbishops.html: Milton's margin here has: "Bed." See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 3.25-26. See also Synod of Whitby.

englishtongue.title: English Tongue
englishtongue.html: French Fogle, editor of the Yale Prose edition (volume 5, page 41) paraphrases this sentence: "The only authors we have of British matters during the Roman epriod in Britain are Roman authors, and there are those who in English have already brought together from them as much as or more than is necessary for a history of Britain."

enniaunus.title: Enniaunus
enniaunus.html: Enniaunus was another legendary king of the Britons.

enrichinghimself.title: enriching himself
enrichinghimself.html: Milton's margin here has: "Eutrop. Oros." Eutropius's Abridged History of Rome 9.21-23 and Orosius's Against the Pagans 7. 25 supply most of Milton's details about Carausius.

ensigns.title: Ensignes
ensigns.html: "A military or naval standard; a banner, flag" (OED).

entreataid.title: entreat aid
entreataid.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." See Simeon, Historia Regum for 1047 CE.

epitomist.title: Epitomist Florus
epitomist.html: Lucius Annaeus Florus was a Roman historian who compiled an epitome of Livy's History of Rome.

estrildis.title: Estrildis
estrildis.html: According to the English chronicler Geoffrey of Monmouth, Estrildis was the beloved mistress of King Locrine, though he was married to Queen Gwendolyn. Milton retells a version of her story in A Mask at Ludlow.

ethelhardus.title: Edelard
ethelhardus.html: See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 728 CE: "Ethelhardus."

ethelmund.title: Ethelmund
ethelmund.html: See Æthelmund and the Battle of Kempsford. See also Weohstan.

ethelred7.title: Ethelred
ethelred7.html: Æthelred was King of Mercia from 675-704 CE. His Queen, Osthryth, was murdered in 697 CE.

ethelric.title: Ethelric
ethelric.html: Milton's margin here has: "559." See Æthelric of Bernicia; his father, Ida of Bernicia, died in 559 CE.

eugenius.title: Eugenius
eugenius.html: Buchanan in his History of Scotland 4.51-52, names Eugenius the 39th King of the Scots.

everytenthspared.title: every tenth
everytenthspared.html: See Simeon of Durham, Historia Regum for 1011 CE.

example.title: example of Roman Emperors
example.html: See a history of Roman law.

expectedtheevent.title: expected the event
expectedtheevent.html: Looked out for or waited for the event.

expresswords.title: express words
expresswords.html: See Gildas, The Ruin of Britain 25; and Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 1.16.

fagan.title: two religious doctors
fagan.html: Faganus and Deruvianus, legendary evangelical bishops and saints, alleged to have been sent to Britain to baptise the nation. See also Matthew, The Flowers of History 4.

fainatlength.title: fain at length
fainatlength.html: Milton's margin here has: "Capitolin. in Pert." Julius Capitolinus was one of the supposed "six scriptores" of the Augustan History; see "Life of Pertinax" 13.4-9.

fairhouse.title: fair house
fairhouse.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun. Camden." See Simeon, Historia Regum for 1065 CE. See also Camden "Monmouthshire" 23.5.

fallingonhishands.title: falling on his hands
fallingonhishands.html: See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.13.

fargreater.title: far greater
fargreater.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." See Simeon of Durham, Historia Regum for 1009 CE. See also Thorkell the Tall.

farotherwise.title: far otherwise
farotherwise.html: See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.7. For what follows, Milton relies chiefly on the Flores Historiarum, and Roger of Hovedon, Chronica for 957 CE.

farsuperior.title: far superior
farsuperior.html: See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 2.5: "The first who had the like Sovereignty was Elli, king or the South-Saxons; the second, Celin, king of the West-Saxons, who, in their own language, is called Ceaulin; the third, as has been said, was Ethelbert, king of Kent; the fourth was Redwald, king of the East-Angles, who, whilst Ethelbert lived, had been subservient to him. The fifth was Edwin, king of the nation of the Northumbrians." See also Rædwald of East Anglia.

faustus.title: Faustus
faustus.html: Nennius, in his Historia Brittonum 48, names the son produced by Vortigern's incest with his daughter, Faustus.

feasting.title: feasting
feasting.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an. Camden." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 946 CE. See also Camden, "Gloucestershire" 13.10. The story of Edmund's murder is told by the Flores Historiarum.

fellout.title: fell out
fellout.html: Milton's margin here has: "758." According to the Flores Historiarum, Eadbehrt resigned his kingdom and became a monk in 757 CE. See also Osmund of Sussex and Swithred of Essex.

felltosedition.title: fell to sedition
felltosedition.html: Milton's margin here has: "Lamprid. in comm." Aelius Lampridius was one of the supposed "six scriptores" of the Augustan History; see "Life of Commodus Antoninus" 4.5 to 6.3.

femalegovernment.title: Female Government
femalegovernment.html: Milton's margin here has: "674." See the Flores Historiarum. Milton ignores Malmesbury's praise for Queen Seaxburgh in Chronicle of the Kings of England book 1.2.

fewwords.title: few words
fewwords.html: Milton's margin here has: "446." The date Milton posts here may come from Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 1.13, who says the letter was sent to Flavius Aetius in the "twenty-third" year of the reign of Theodosius II which Bede dates as beginning in 423.

fidler.title: habit of a fidler
fidler.html: See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.4.

finisindex.title: FINIS
finisindex.html: In the 1671 edition, there follows an Index of Chief Persons.

firstcall.title: first call
firstcall.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 944 CE. Milton's "Anlaf" is Olaf Guthfrithson, not the son of Sihtric, who was his cousin (also named Olaf).

firstcoming.title: first coming
firstcoming.html: Milton's margin here has: "866." See Æthelred of Wessex.

firstlast.title: the first shall be last
firstlast.html: Matthew 19:30, Mark 10:31, and Luke 13:30 for the sources of Jesus's words.

firstmotion.title: first motion
firstmotion.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 876 CE.

firstwifesister.title: first wife
firstwifesister.html: See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.13.

firstyear.title: first year
firstyear.html: Milton's margin here has: "450." Marcian, or Flavius Marcianus Augustus, was emperor of the Eastern Roman Empire from 450 to 457 CE.

fisburg.title: Fisburg
fisburg.html: Apparently Milton's edition of Simeon misprinted "Fyburgenses" as Fisburgenses (Historia Regum). The "Five Boroughs" are Lincoln, Stamford, Leicester, Nottingham, and Derby; see also Five Boroughs of the Danelaw. Also see Uhtred the Bold.

fledoversea.title: fled over Sea
fledoversea.html: Milton's margin here has: "Primord. pag. 418." See James Ussher, De Primordiis (Dublin, 1639) 418.

followingin.title: year following
followingin.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 838 CE.

forage.title: forage the Country
forage.html: Milton's margin here has: "Asser." See Asser, Life of Alfred.

forhostage.title: for hostage
forhostage.html: Milton's margin here has: "Florent." See the Flores Historiarum for 933 CE.

formerlyking.title: formerly King
formerlyking.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." See Simeon of Durham's Historia Regum for 791 CE.

formerresolution.title: former resolution
formerresolution.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." See Simeon, Historia Regum. But see also Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.13.

formerstory.title: former story
formerstory.html: Milton's margin here has: "Leges Ed. Conf. Tit. Lex Noricor." See William Lambarde's Archaionomia (1644) where, on page 150, directly following the Leges Edouardi Regis, or The Laws of Edward the Confessor, we find an article entitled "Lex Noricorum, & Danorum in Brytannia," where we are told that "Rex autem Edwardus ut cognovit gentis suae nequitam, & praecipue superbiam filiorum Godwini, scilicet Haraldi, qui postea regnum invasit, Tosti, Gurti, Leofwini, & aliorum fratrum suorum, comperit non posse fore stabile vel ratum quod proposuerat de Edgaro Ethelinge, adoptavit Wilhelmum ducem Normannorum in regnum."

fortheempire.title: for the Empire
fortheempire.html: Milton's margin here has: "Herod. L. 3." Herodian, History 3.7, says that Albinus was defeated and beheaded in Gaul in 197 CE.

fortified.title: fortifi'd
fortified.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 920 CE.

fortifying.title: Fortifying
fortifying.html: Milton's margin here has: "Mela." Pomponius Mela was the earliest Roman geographer. See his The Situation of the World (translated by Arthur Golding 1585) 78-79. Milton recommends Mela in Of Education.

fortreasonsaith.title: for treason
fortreasonsaith.html: See Huntingdon, Historia Anglorum 6. See also Ælfgar, Earl of Mercia.

foundmeans.title: found means
foundmeans.html: Milton's margin here has: "Did. Jul. Spartian. in Sever. Herod. L. 3." See Augustan History, "Life of Septimus Severus" 6.6 and Herodian, History 3.5-6.

foundoccasion.title: found occasion
foundoccasion.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun. Malms." See Simeon, Historia Regum for 1021 CE, and Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.11.

fourmonths.title: four Months
fourmonths.html: Milton's margin here has: "Oros. L. 7." Orosius, in his Against the Pagans 7.40, calls Gratian "a townsman of Britain" and says that "He was later slain and in his place Constantine, a man from the lowest ranks of the soldiery, was chosen simply from confidence inspired by his name and without any other qualifications to recommend him."

fouryears.title: Four years
fouryears.html: Milton's margin here has: "489." The Flores Historiarum page 42 dates Hengist's death in 488 CE. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle implies Hengist's death by noting that "Esc" became king in 488.

fowrekings.title: fowr Kings
fowrekings.html: See these names in Caesar, Commentaries 5.22.

freshinvasion.title: fresh invasion
freshinvasion.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an. Huntingd." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 866 CE See also Huntingdon, Historia Anglorum 5.

frith.title: frith
frith.html: Or firth; OED: "An arm of the sea; an estuary of a river."

froda.title: old Army
froda.html: Huntingdon apparently misread the Old English "froda" (aged one) as a proper name, and so invented the "ductor Normannus." See Huntingdon, Historia Anglorum 5: "Froda ductor Normannus." Wheeloc's Latin version also identifies "Froda" as a "Dux Normannicus" in his margin. See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle.

fromanexpedition.title: from an expedition
fromanexpedition.html: Milton's margin here has: "Author ignot. post Marcellin. valesii." Milton refers to The Anonymous Valesius's account of Constantius and Galerius. Constantius died at York in 306 CE, and was succeeded by his son, Constantine the Great.

frontinus.title: Julius Frontinus
frontinus.html: Sextus Julius Frontinus succeeded Quintus Petillius Cerialis as governor of Rome. In what year is not exactly clear. He was succeeded by Gnaeus Julius Agricola, the father-in-law of the famous historian Tacitus, in 77 CE.

gabius.title: Gabius and Porsena
gabius.html: Geoffrey indeed writes of Gabius and Porsenna as "two consuls of Rome," (History 3.9) but the name Gabius has not been found in any Roman records, and Lars Porsenna was an early Etruscan king (6th century CE) of Clusium, a city in Tuscany. The exiled Tarquinius Superbus recruited Porsenna to lead an army against Rome in an unsuccessful bid to retore the monarchy and his dynasty.

gaiusv.title: Caius Volusenus
gaiusv.html: Gaius Volusenus served under Julius Caesar for ten years, including in the Gallic wars. See Commentaries 4.21.

galfred.title: Galfred
galfred.html: "Galfred" looks like a misprint for "Geoffrey," but there is no correction in the errata, and I have seen a German edition of the Historia attributed to "Galfred von Monmouth." The History of the Kings of Britain 5.3-4 represents Carausius as a tyrant over the Britons.

galfredofmonmouth.title: made himself strong
galfredofmonmouth.html: Milton's margin here has: "Buchanan." Buchanan's History of Scotland 4.46 speaks of "Carantius, a Roman exile, one of mean descent but a good soldier," who reconciled the Scots and Picts and avoided numerous Roman attempts on his life.

gallio.title: Gallio
gallio.html: Milton's margin here has: "Blond." Flavio Biondo (Latin Flavius Blondus), an Italian historian, wrote Historiae Ab Inclinatione Romanorum Imperii (Basel 1531). See Decade 1, book 2. Camden, in Britannia, "Romans 2" 4.91 mentions Gallio as leader of the Roman legion who helped with the wall.

gangani.title: Cangians
gangani.html: The Gangani were a tribe of ancient Ireland, but there was also a tribe of the same name in northwest Wales.

gaul.title: Gaule
gaul.html: Gaul was a region of Western Europe that encompassed what today is France, Belgium, and Switzerland. The Romans named the territory Gaul.

gavehimawife.title: gave him a Wife
gavehimawife.html: See William Lambarde's Archaionomia (1644) where, on page 150, directly following the Leges Edouardi Regis, or The Laws of Edward the Confessor, we find an article entitled "Lex Noricorum, & Danorum in Brytannia," where we are told that Edward "(timore Chnuti regis) aufugit ad regum Rugorum, quod nos melius vocamus Russiam. Quem rex terrae Malesclotus nomine, ut cognovit quis esset, honeste retinuit. Qui de nobili progenie ibidem duxit uxorem, de qua natus est ei Edgarus Ethelinge, & Margareta quae fuit postea regina Scotiae, & Christina soror ejus."

gavenotleave.title: run to the Palace
gavenotleave.html: Milton's margin here has: "Malms. L. 1." See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 1.1. Vortigern was possibly a 5th-century British king.

gavesister.title: gave him his sister
gavesister.html: Milton's margin here has: "Malms. Mat. West." See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.6, and the Flores Historiarum for 925 CE. See also Eadgyth.

generalrevolt.title: general revolt
generalrevolt.html: Milton's margin here has: "259." Gallienus lost control over Britain (and other provinces) due to the revolt of Posthumus in 259 or 260 CE.

geofend.title: Geffrey Monmouth
geofend.html: Milton closes this first book at the same point in history Geoffrey winds up his third book, chapter 20.

germandead.title: German
germandead.html: That is, Germanus of Auxerre, who died in 448 CE.

gerontiusbriton.title: Gerontius
gerontiusbriton.html: Gerontius was a general of the Western Roman Empire.

gildasaffirms.title: confidently affirms
gildasaffirms.html: See Gildas, The Ruin of Britain 8.

gildasaffirms2.title: Gildas affirms
gildasaffirms2.html: See Gildas, The Ruin of Britain 4.

gildasboudica.title: Gildas
gildasboudica.html: See Gildas, The Ruin of Britain 6: "that deceitful lioness."

gildaspoet.title: Gildas
gildaspoet.html: Gildas Sapiens, or Gildas the Wise was a 6th-century monk, known for his polemical writings.

girdtheempire.title: gird the Empire
girdtheempire.html: Milton's margin here has: "Spartianus ibid." See the Augustan History "Life of Hadrian" 11.2.

givelaws.title: Woman should give Laws
givelaws.html: See the Son's rebuke to Adam in Paradise Lost 10.145-55.

giveoutsaith.title: give out
giveoutsaith.html: See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.13.

glaive.title: Glaves
glaive.html: A glaive is A slender, pointed, straight, thrusting sword; a rapier" (OED).

glamorganshire.title: a religious man
glamorganshire.html: Milton's margin here has: "Gildas." See Gildas, The Ruin of Britain 25.

glota.title: Dunbritton
glota.html: Glota was an early name for the Clyde; Dunbarton Castle overlooks the Firth of Clyde on the north side. Bodotria is now known as the Firth of Forth, dominated by the City of Edinburgh.

gmonmouth.title: Geoffrey of Monmouth
gmonmouth.html: Geoffrey of Monmouth was one of the pioneers of British historiography. His Historia Regum Britanniae (c. 1136) or History of the Kings of Britain was subject to a great deal of dispute about reliability and authenticity.

gogmagog.title: Gogmagog Hills
gogmagog.html: See Camden, "Cambridgeshire" 17.7. See also Huntingdon, Historia Anglorum 6, and Gog Magog Hills.

gomer.title: Gomer
gomer.html: Genesis 10:1-5 lists the sons of Japheth, Noah's youngest son, and suggests that from these sons are born the "gentiles," or "the nations." William Camden, in his Britannia, derives the various peoples of Europe from these sons; for example, the Spaniards come from Tubal, and from Meschech, the Muscovites. The sons of Gomer, or "Gomerians," he surmises, are the ancient "Cimbrians" or "Cimmerians" of Germany, Gaul, and Wales (Cymru). See Britannia 2.17.

goodlaws.title: good Laws
goodlaws.html: Ine is noted for his code of laws (leges Inae or "laws of Ine"), which he issued in about 694. These laws were the first issued by an Anglo-Saxon king outside Kent. See Anglo-Saxon law.

goodrecord.title: good record
goodrecord.html: Milton's margin here has: "Notitiæ imperii." The Notitia Dignitatum (Latin for "The List of Offices") is a document of the late Roman Empire that details the administrative organization of the Eastern and Western Empires. See Part V: "Litoris Saxonici per Britannias" or "Saxony along the shores of Britain."

goodwriters.title: good Writers
goodwriters.html: Milton's margin here has: "Florent. Wigorn. ad an. 370." Milton refers to Florence of Worcester's Chronicon. Another "good" writer may be William Camden, in Britannia, "English-Saxons" 3-4: "that conceit of the best learned Germans may seeme worthy of acceptance and to be preferred before the rest, who suppose that the Saxons descended from the Sacae, a most noble Nation and of much worth in Asia, and so called, as one would say, Sacosones, that is, the sonnes of the Sacae: and that out of Scythia, or Sarmatia Asiatica."

gorboduc.title: Gorbogudo
gorboduc.html: Also known as Gorboduc, eponymous hero of the play Gorboduc (1561).

gorroghs.title: Gorroghs
gorroghs.html: OED: " A small boat made of wickerwork covered with hides, used from ancient times in Scotland and Ireland; a coracle."

government.title: Government
government.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an. Malms." The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records under the year 611 CE: "Hic Cinegelfus & Cuichelmus regnum occuparunt," but it identifies only "Cinegelfus" as the son of Ceola. Malmesbury, in his Chronicle of the Kings of England book 1.2, has both Cynegils and Cuichelm as sons of Ceolric. But see also Cynegils.

greatacts.title: great Acts
greatacts.html: Milton's margin here has: "Primord. p. 468. Polychronic. L. 5. c. 6." See Ussher, De Primordiis 5.13. Milton also refers to Ranulf Higden, author of the Polychronicon; again, Milton quotes from Ussher, De Primordiis 5.13.

greatalms.title: Romscot
greatalms.html: Milton's margin here has: "Huntingd." See Huntingdon, Historia Anglorum 6. See also Rome-payment (Romscot).

greatbattail.title: great Battail
greatbattail.html: Milton's margin here has: "Zozimus." See Zosimus, New History book 1: Probus "made war on the Burgundi and the Vandili."

greatdanger.title: great danger
greatdanger.html: Milton's margin here has: "Suet. Vesp. Dio. L. 60." See Lives of the Caesars, "The Life of Vespasian" 4.1-2. See also Dio, Roman History 61.30.

greaterfleet.title: greater Fleet
greaterfleet.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." See Simeon of Durham, Historia Regum for 994 CE.

greatestpart.title: greatest part
greatestpart.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an." The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records Peada's death under 657 CE, but says nothing about Oswiu and the Mercians under the following year. Bede's Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 3.24 tells with the story of Oswiu's gift of South Mercia to Peada and his death by murder the following year, 659 CE.

greatfamin.title: great Famin
greatfamin.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." See Simeon of Durham, Historia Regum for 1005 CE.

greatforces.title: great Forces
greatforces.html: Milton's margin here has: "343." Constans visited Britain in the early months of 343 CE.

greatforcesedward.title: great forces
greatforcesedward.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 910 CE.

greatmortality.title: Siger
greatmortality.html: Milton's margin here has: "Malms." See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 1.6. See also Sighere of Essex and Sæbbi of Essex.

greatnumber.title: great number
greatnumber.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." See Simeon, Historia Regum for 1054 CE.

greatoffence.title: great offence
greatoffence.html: Milton's margin here has: "Amm. L. 28. Zozim. L. 4." See Ammianus Marcellus, Roman History 28.3.3-6 and Zosimus, New History book 4: "About this time, a person named Valentinian for some offence was banished to the island of Britain, and endeavouring there to render himself absolute, was at once deprived of his life and his hopes."

greatpuissance.title: great Puissance
greatpuissance.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an. Sim. Dun." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 934 CE. See also Simeon of Durham's Historia Regum for 937.

greatslaughter.title: build a Wall
greatslaughter.html: Milton's margin here has: "Diaconus. L. 14." Paul the Deacon was author of Historia Romana; Milton refers to book 14.

greatsupplies.title: great supplies
greatsupplies.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 871 CE See also Huntingdon, Historia Anglorum 5.

greatvictory.title: great Victory
greatvictory.html: Milton's margin here has: "744." See Huntingdon's account of the alliance and battle in Historia Anglorum 4.

greatvictory1.title: great Victory
greatvictory1.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." See Simeon, Historia Regum for 1055 CE.

greatwealth.title: to his great wealth
greatwealth.html: See the Flores Historiarum for 1003 CE.

greedy.title: greedy
greedy.html: See Gildas, The Ruin of Britain 12, where he speaks of "the Arian treason."

greekhistorian.title: Greek Historian
greekhistorian.html: Milton's margin here has: "Dion." See Dio, Roman History 62.2-6. Dio's account of Boudica is mostly positive; the defensive misogynistic tone—"the rankest note of Barbarism, as if in Britain Woemen were Men, and Men Woemen"—is entirely Milton's.

greekishmonk.title: Greekish Monk
greekishmonk.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an." The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records the ordination of Theodore as Archbishop in 668 CE. See also Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 4.1-2: "He was ordained by Pope Vitalian, in the year of our Lord 668, on Sunday, the 26th of March, and on the 27th of May was sent with Hadrian into Britain.".

gregorygreat.title: Gregory
gregorygreat.html: Later Pope Gregory the Great, he was an archdeacon when he first met the enslaved British boys.

greifofhim.title: greif of him
greifofhim.html: Milton's margin here has: "Bede." See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 3.14: "Not long after, the bishop's prediction was fulfilled by the king's death, as has been said above. But Bishop Aidan himself was also taken out of this world, twelve days after the king he loved, on the 31st of August, to receive the eternal reward of his labours from our Lord."

grewfamous.title: had a hand
grewfamous.html: Milton's margin here has: "Malms." See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.9; Malmesbury actually does not allege that Ælfhere had a hand in Edward's death, though he was indeed an ally of Ælfthryth, Edward's stepmother and assassin. See also Ælfhere, Ealdorman of Mercia.

gudfrid.title: Gudfrid
gudfrid.html: See Simeon of Durham's Historia Regum for 927 CE. See also Olaf Guthfrithson.

guilttherof.title: guilt therof
guilttherof.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." See Simeon, Historia Regum for 1031 CE.

guitheline.title: Guitheline
guitheline.html: Spenser mentions Guitheline in the Faerie Queene 2.10.42. See also Geoffrey, History of the Kings of Britain 3.13.

guorangonus.title: Guorangonus
guorangonus.html: Milton treats this as a proper name, but Camden regards it as a title, meaning "Freed man"; see "Kent" 3 (search for "guorong"): "when the Romanes were departed quite out of Britaine, Vortigern, who bare soveraine rule in the greatest part of Britaine, placed over Kent a guorong , that is to say, a Vice Roy or Freed man under him, and unwitting to him, he forthwith freely graunted this region, as Ninnius and William of Malmesburie write, unto Hengist the Saxon for his daughter Rowens sake, upon whom he was exceedingly enamoured." Nennius also treats this as a proper name, but "Guoyrancgonus" (37, search for "Guoyrancgonus").

guortimer.title: Guortimer
guortimer.html: Malmesbury names Vortigern's son Vortimer; see Chronicle of the Kings of England book 1.1, page 10.

gurgant.title: Gurguntius Barbirus
gurgant.html: Also known as Gurguit Barbtruc. See Geoffrey, History of the Kings of Britain 3.11.

habitofamonk.title: Habit of a Monk
habitofamonk.html: See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 4.11.

hadavictory.title: had a Victory
hadavictory.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an. omn." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle: the battle of "Cerdices-Fordam." See also Æthelweard, Anglo-Saxon Chronicle: "the river Avene," and Camden, "Hantshire" 2.

haddecreed.title: had decreed
haddecreed.html: Milton's margin here has: "Asser." See Asser, Life of Alfred.

hadsetup.title: had set up
hadsetup.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." See Simeon of Durham's Historia Regum for 867, 872, 873, 876, and 894 CE for records of these Northumbrian kings.

hadwar.title: had War
hadwar.html: Milton's margin here has: "Malms." See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.10 where the letter appears in full.

hardbeset.title: hard beset
hardbeset.html: Milton's margin here has: "Dion." See Dio, Roman History 75.5.

hardecnutedead.title: Hardecnute dead
hardecnutedead.html: See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.13. See also Godwin, Earl of Wessex.

harmless.title: harmless Nation
harmless.html: See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 4.26: "IN the year of our Lord's incarnation 684, Egfrid, king of the Northumbrians, sending Beort, his general, with an army, into Ireland, miserably wasted that harmless nation, which had always been most friendly to the English."

hastedthenext.title: the next year
hastedthenext.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." See Simeon of Durham, Historia Regum for 1003 CE.

hastilykill.title: hastily kill
hastilykill.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sozom. L. 9." Salminius Hermias Sozomenus was a Greek church historian. See his Ecclesiastical History 9.11: " The soldiers in Britain were the first to rise up in sedition, and they proclaimed Mark as tyrant. Afterwards, however, they slew Mark, and proclaimed Gratian. Within four months subsequently they killed Gratian, and elected Constantine in his place."

hastings.title: Hestings
hastings.html: Simeon spoke of "Hestingorum," probably meaning the people of Hastings in East Sussex.

hathbeensaid.title: hath been said
hathbeensaid.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for the year 709 CE.

havefought.title: have fought
havefought.html: Milton's margin here has: "Camd." See Camden, "Dorset-shire" 10.2: "Byndon, in the Saxon tongue Beandun , which also had a monasterie where Kinegilfus in the yeere 614 in a doubtfull and dangerous battell vanquished the Britans."

haveitlater.title: have it later
haveitlater.html: See Huntingdon, Historia Anglorum 2.18, where he dates the beginning of Sleda's reign to 604 CE. See also Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 1.6, page 90.

haveslain.title: second year following
haveslain.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an." The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records under 616 CE the death of Æthelberht. See also Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 2.5.

havinglost.title: while after
havinglost.html: Milton's margin here has: "62." 62 CE. For Suetonius's lost vessels and resigning his command to Publius Petronius Turpilianus, see Tacitus, Annals 14.39

heagain.title: he again
heagain.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." See Simeon, Historia Regum for 1058 CE.

heardbefore.title: Venusius
heardbefore.html: Milton's margin here has: "74." In 74 CE, Venutius was King of the Brigantes when Quintus Petillius Cerialis, the Roman governor, campaigned against them.

heavythraldome.title: two young Sons
heavythraldome.html: Milton's margin here has: "Bed. l. 4. c. 16." See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 4.16: "two royal youths, brothers to Atwald, king of the island" rather than "sons" as Milton has it. See also Arwald.

hebuilt.title: he built
hebuilt.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 923 CE.

hecame.title: he came
hecame.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 922 CE.

hedgeout.title: hedge out
hedgeout.html: Milton's margin here has: "Capitolin. Marc. Ant. Philos. 162." See the Augustan History, "Life of Antoninus Pius" 11.2 which mentions that Sextus Calpurnius Agricola "was sent" against the Britons; he was made governor of Britain in 161 or 162 CE.

heforgets.title: Secandune
heforgets.html: Milton's margin here has: "Camd." See Camden, "Warwickshire" 20.15 where he identifies "Secandunum" with Seckinton or Seckington.

hegave.title: the slaughter
hegave.html: Milton's margin here has: "Malms." See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 1.1 and 2.13.

hegave2.title: or Son
hegave2.html: Milton's margin here has: "Mat. West." See the Flores Historiarum.

heldacastle.title: Simeon writes
heldacastle.html: See Simeon, Historia Regum for 1051 CE. See also Leofric, Earl of Mercia and Siward, Earl of Northumbria.

heldofhim.title: held of him
heldofhim.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an. Asser." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 853 CE See also Asser, Life of Alfred.

heldthem.title: held them
heldthem.html: Milton's margin here has: "Calvis. Tacit. Hist. 3. & vit. Agric." "Held them tack" means "to be a match for; to hold at bay" (OED). Milton points to Sethus Calvisius, whose Opus Chronologicum (Leipzig, 1605) he consulted for dates. See also Histories 3.45 and Life of Agricola 17.

helenus.title: Helenus King Priams son
helenus.html: Helenus was famous as a seer and as a son of King Priam of Troy.

heli.title: Heli
heli.html: Also known as Beli Mawr, or Beli the Great.

helptobuild.title: help to build
helptobuild.html: Milton's margin here has: "Bede ibid." See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 1.12.

helvius.title: Helvius Pertinax
helvius.html: Pertinax was emperor of Rome for the first 3 months of 193 CE.

herblood.title: her blood
herblood.html: Milton's margin here has: "Mat. West." See the Flores Historiarum.

herson.title: her Son
herson.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." See Simeon, Historia Regum for 1039 CE.

herunning.title: he running
herunning.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 874 CE.

hesubdued.title: he subdu'd
hesubdued.html: Milton's margin here has: "47." The accepted date for this conquest is 43 CE.

hewasable.title: he was able
hewasable.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." See Simeon, Historia Regum for 1066 CE. See also Westminster Abbey.

hidingforhaste.title: hiding for haste
hidingforhaste.html: Milton's margin here has: "Ethelwerd. annal. Sax." See Æthelweard's Anglo-Saxon Chronicle page 6: "418. In the ninth year also after the sacking of Rome by the Goths, those of Roman race who were left in Britain, not bearing the manifold insults of the people, bury their treasures... and taking a portion,...seek an exile on the shores of Gaul."

himofmonmouth.title: Monmouth
himofmonmouth.html: See Geoffrey of Monmouth, History of the Kings of Britain 6.5-6.

himsucceeded.title: him succeeded
himsucceeded.html: Milton's margin here has: "Florent. Genealog. Bed. L. 2. c. 15." See the Flores Historiarum for the genealogy of the East Saxon kings. See also Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 2.15.

hisappointment.title: improbable Letter
hisappointment.html: Milton's margin here has: "181." One traditional date for the conversion of King Lucius is 181 CE; another is 179 CE.

hisbirth.title: his Birth
hisbirth.html: Milton's margin here has: "Malms." See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.1.

hisbrother.title: his Brother
hisbrother.html: Milton's margin here has: "Hoved." Roger of Hovedon, Chronica for 957 CE.

hischaplain.title: his Chaplain
hischaplain.html: Milton's margin here has: "Ingulf." See Pseudo-Ingulf, Historia. When Robert of Jumièges was made the first Norman Archbishop of Canterbury, Ulfus Normanus was made Bishop of Dorcester, and William was made Bishop of London.

hischronicle.title: his Chronicle
hischronicle.html: Sigebert of Gembloux was the author of a Chronicon sive Chronographia, or universal chronicle.

hisclerks.title: his Clerks
hisclerks.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." See Simeon, Historia Regum for 1056 CE. See also Leofgar of Hereford.

hiscommand.title: those Provinces
hiscommand.html: Milton's margin here has: "Bed. L. 1. c. 15. & L. 2. c. 5." See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 1.15, and Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 2.5.

hisdaughter.title: his daughter
hisdaughter.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 912 CE.

hisflight.title: his flight
hisflight.html: Milton's margin here has: "Olympiodor. apud Photium." Olympiodorus of Thebes was a Greek historian and poet. His history of the Western Roman Empire is lost except for an extract preserved in chapter 80 of the Biblioteca of Photios I of Constantinople, where we read: "Gerontius, on the arrival of Constantius and Ulphilas, takes to flight, and is seized by his mutinous troops, who resented his severe discipline. The house where he seeks refuge is set on fire, but he offers a brave resistance to the mutineers, together with one of his servants, an Alan by birth. At last, he slays the Alan and then his wife, at their earnest request, and then stabs himself."

hisforces.title: his Forces
hisforces.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 894 CE.

hisfriends.title: his friends
hisfriends.html: Milton's margin here has: "409." Maxiumus of Hispania may have been the son of Gerontius, who after his mutiny against Constans, installed Maximus in his place in te summer of 410 CE.

hisgeneral.title: his General
hisgeneral.html: See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 1.1: "Ambrosius...quelled the presumptuous barbarians by the powerful aid of warlike Arthur."

hishead.title: his head
hishead.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." See Simeon, Historia Regum for 1064 CE, which actually says that Griffin was killed by his own men, not by another person named Griffin. See also Gruffydd ap Llywelyn which dates his death in 1063 CE.

hisinnocence.title: his innocence
hisinnocence.html: Milton's margin here has: "Malms." See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.6.

hislasttime.title: his last time
hislasttime.html: Milton's margin here has: "Eutrop. Eumen. idem Auth. ignot." See Eutropius, Abridged History of Rome 10.1-2, Eumeius, "Panegyricus" 7, and The Anonymous Valesius's account.

hismanner.title: slaying of a few
hismanner.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an. omn." The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle says "in Wightgara-burgo multos interfecit"; "many were killed at Wightgara-burgh." But see Æthelweard, Anglo-Saxon Chronicle page 7-8: "they took the Isle of Wight,...but they did not kill many of the Britons."

hisnotist.title: or his notist
hisnotist.html: James Ussher, in his De Primordiis (Dublin 1639) 5.13, quotes an annotation from a manuscript of Nennius that reads, "Mab uter Britannice, Latine filius horriblis: quoniam a pueritia sua crudelis fuit. Arthur Latine translatum, sonat ursum horribilem." Translation: The British (or Welsh) "Mab uter" is "horrible son" in Latin, for he was a cruel child. Arthur, in Latin, sounds like a bear.

hisobedience.title: Baptism
hisobedience.html: Milton's margin here has: "Bed. L. 2 c. 15." Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 2.15.

hisoldenemy.title: his old Enemy
hisoldenemy.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an." The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records an Easter-time battle between Cenwahl and Penda at "Possentes-burgam." See also Æthelweard, Anglo-Saxon Chronicle: "A. 661 After three years Kenwalk again fought a battle near the town of Pontesbury." "Eskesdun" is modern Ashdown.

hisown.title: his own
hisown.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." See Simeon of Durham's Historia Regum for 796 CE.

hispedigree.title: his Pedigree
hispedigree.html: Milton's margin here has: "Huntingd." See Huntingdon, Historia Anglorum 2.26. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records a genealogy from Penda (grandson of Creoda) back to Woden.

hispredecessor.title: departs not
hispredecessor.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sabellic." Marcus Antonius Coccius Sabellicus was a Venetian historian and author of Enneades sive Rhapsodia Historiarum. See Buchanan History of Scotland 7.3-4. See also Hector Boece, History of the Scottish People 7.28

hissepulchre.title: Hagustald
hissepulchre.html: Milton's margin here has: "Camd." Camden, in "Northumberland" 29.11, identifies the town as Hexham in Northumberland.

hisson.title: was buried
hisson.html: Milton's margin here has: "544." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle: "Hic Wihtgar obiit, & in Wihtgara-burgo sepultus est."

hissonalfrid.title: his Son
hissonalfrid.html: See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 3.25.

hisswiftness.title: Harefoot
hisswiftness.html: Milton's margin here has: "Florent. Bromton." See the Flores Historiarum for 1035 CE. John Brompton was the supposed author of an Historia included in Roger Twysden's edition of ten historical authors, Historiae Anglicanae Scriptores X. At column 932 we find the nickname "Haraldus Harefot." See also Harold Harefoot.

hisuncle.title: his Uncle
hisuncle.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." See Simeon, Historia Regum for 1057 CE. See also Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.13, and Edward the Exile.

holinshed.title: find not in him
holinshed.html: Milton's margin here has "Holinshed." Holinshed cites Nennius as the source of this story of Danaus and his daughters (Chronicles (1587) Historie I. 5) but Milton here claims he can find no such story in the copy of Nennius he has read. No known surviving manuscript of Nennius includes this story. For more on this matter, see Constance Nicholas.

homageofmalcolm.title: homage of Malcolm
homageofmalcolm.html: Milton's margin here has: "Huntingd." See Huntingdon, Historia Anglorum 6. See also Malcolm II of Scotland.

hopeofprey.title: hope of prey
hopeofprey.html: Milton's margin here has: "Ethelwerd." See Æthelweard, Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 4.4. See also Cambridge, Gloucestershire.

hovedenrecords.title: Hoveden records
hovedenrecords.html: See Roger of Hoveden's Annals for 902 CE.

howeverplaced.title: however plac'd
howeverplaced.html: Milton's margin here has: "Bed. l. 4. c. 12." Bede, in Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 4.12 speaks of the province of Lindsey in 678 CE as "newly subdued" by Ecgfrith, "having overcome and vanquished Wulfhere," but Bede elsewhere (book 5) dates Wulfhere's death at 875. So does the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle . So Milton reckons the battle as happening in 673 or 674 CE.

hungus.title: Hungus
hungus.html: Óengus mac Fergusa (Angus MacFergus) was King of the Picts from 820 until 834 CE.

huntingdon1.title: All of them
huntingdon1.html: Milton's margin here has "Henry of Huntingdon. Matthew of Westminster." Henry of Huntington was Archdeacon of Huntingdon and author of the Historia Anglorum, or History of the English People. It was first published in Henry Savile's 1596 collection of early English histories (after Bede's): Rerum Anglicarum Scriptores post Bede, which also included histories by William of Malmesbury, Roger Hovedon, Ethelwerd, and Ingulf of Croydon. Matthew of Westminster was thought to be the author of the Flores Historiarum, but since 1826 has been regarded as never having existed. The Flores Historiarum has since been attributed to Matthew Paris.

huntingdon2.title: Huntingdon
huntingdon2.html: Milton's margin here has "Huntingd. L. I." Henry of Huntingdon was archdeacon of Huntingdon and author of Historia Anglorum (1129, 1154). Milton refers here to book (Liber) 1 of that work, where Lud is mentioned as "Liud regis fortissimi, qui multas insulas maris bellis occupaverat."

huntingdonmarriageerror.title: Huntingdon relates
huntingdonmarriageerror.html: See Huntingdon, Historia Anglorum 6, who dates Alfred's visit in 1042. CE.

icenians.title: Icenians
icenians.html: The Iceni or Eceni were a Brittonic tribe of Eastern Britain.

ifthetruth.title: if the truth
ifthetruth.html: Milton's margin here has: "868." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 868 CE.

illegitimate.title: illegitimate
illegitimate.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." See Simeon of Durham's Historia Regum for 933 CE. The story as Milton tells it appears to come from others, though. See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.6, and the Flores Historiarum for 934 CE.

imitation.title: 7 year after
imitation.html: Milton's margin here has: "Year before the Birth of Christ, 25." The year was 27 BCE.

impaled.title: impal'd
impaled.html: Impaled; OED: "To enclose with pales, stakes, or posts; to surround with a palisade; to fence in."

impiousson.title: impious Son
impiousson.html: Milton's margin here has: "Spartianus in Sever." See Augustan History, "Life of Septimus Severus" 19-20. Here Severus's eldest is called "Antoninus Bassianus."

ina.title: Ina
ina.html: See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 5.7: "When Cædwalla went to Rome, Inn succeeded him on the throne, being of the blood royal." See also Ine of Wessex.

inaletter.title: in a letter
inaletter.html: Malmesbury reproduces portions of the letter from Boniface, Archbishop of Mainz, in Chronicle of the Kings of England book 1.4. Æthelbald's predeccesor was Ceolred, whom Boniface also claims was a "debaucher of nuns."

incensingthepeople.title: incensing the people
incensingthepeople.html: Milton's margin here has: "Huntingd. Huntingd." See Huntingdon, Historia Anglorum 4.20.

incourage.title: in courage
incourage.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 942 CE, another poetic tribute, this time to Edmund.

ingulfnomention.title: no mention
ingulfnomention.html: See Pseudo-Ingulf, Historia: "De successione autem regni spes adhuc, aut mentio nulla facta inter eos fuit."

inhisroom.title: in his room
inhisroom.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." See Simeon of Durham's Historia Ecclesiae for 792 CE. See also Ælfwald II of Northumbria.

inhisroom1.title: in his room
inhisroom1.html: Milton's margin here has: "718." In other words, in his place.

inhisstead.title: in his stead
inhisstead.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an." The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records the accession of "Kenwalchius" as King of the West-Saxons in 643 CE. See also Cenwalh of Wessex.

inlycia.title: Lycia
inlycia.html: See Simeon, Historia Regum for 1052 CE. See also Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.13.

inmanybattels.title: in many Battels
inmanybattels.html: Milton's margin here has: "Camd. ex Firmico." See Camden, Britannia, "Romans 2" 4.81: "When Constantine was dead, Britaine fell unto his Sonne Constantine: who upon an ambitious humour and desire of rule, breaking into the possessions of other men, was slaine by his brother Constans. With which victorie he was so puffed up, that he seized Britaine and the rest of the Provinces into his owne hands, and with his brother Constantius came into this Island." "Firmico" refers to Julius Firmicus, quoted by Camden in this same place.

inmarriage.title: in marriage
inmarriage.html: See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.12. See also Henry III, Holy Roman Emperor and Gunhilda of Denmark.

innogen.title: Innogen
innogen.html: . See Geoffrey, History of the Kings of Britain 1.11: "his eldest daughter, Ignoge."

innorthumberland.title: in Northumberland
innorthumberland.html: Milton's margin here has: "738." "Malms." See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 1.3. See also Ceolwulf of Northumbria.

inoneday.title: in one day
inoneday.html: Milton's margin here has: "Huntingd." See Huntingdon, Historia Anglorum 5. See also St. Brice's Day massacre.

insuchplace.title: in such place
insuchplace.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sigon. Gildas." See Sigonius, Historiarum de occidentali imperio for the year 448 CE. See also Gildas, The Ruin of Britain 22.

inswarms.title: in swarms
inswarms.html: Milton's margin here has: "Gildas. Bede." See Gildas, The Ruin of Britain 19, and Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 1.12.

intelligence.title: Merantun
intelligence.html: Milton's margin here has: "Camd." Camden, in "Surrey" 11.9, identifies the town as Merton in Surrey.

intereign.title: intereign
intereign.html: Or interregnum: "Temporary authority or rule exercised during a vacancy of the throne or a suspension of the usual government" (OED). Nicholas von Maltzahn (both 1991 and 1993) has convincingly argued that Milton refers here to the period immediately following the trial and execution for treason of King Charles I on January 30, 1649, and presumably before the appointment of a new executive on February 14, 1649, known as the Council of State.

inthecity.title: in the City
inthecity.html: Milton's margin here has: "Asser." See Asser, Life of Alfred.

inthefield.title: in the field
inthefield.html: Milton's margin here has: "Asser." See Asser, Life of Alfred.

intoexile.title: into exile
intoexile.html: See Nennius, Historia Brittonum 31: "three vessels, exiled from Germany, arrived in Britain. They were commanded by Horsa and Hengist, brothers, and sons of Wihtgils."

intofavour.title: Burford
intofavour.html: Milton's margin here has: "Camden." See Camden, "Oxfordshire" 13.3.

intohisplace.title: Bericus
intohisplace.html: Milton's margin here has: "Dion." See Dio's Roman History 60.19.

intooxfordshire.title: into Oxfordshire
intooxfordshire.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun. Florent." See Simeon of Durham, Historia Regum for 1010 CE. See also the Flores Historiarum for 1010 CE.

intothecapitol.title: into the Capitol
intothecapitol.html: Milton's margin here has: "Suet. Claud. 5.24." See Lives of the Caesars, "The Life of Claudius" 24.3.

inweapons.title: in Weapons
inweapons.html: Milton's margin here has: "Dion." See Cassius Dio's Roman History 39. 50-53 and 40.2-3.

inwiltshire.title: in Wiltshire
inwiltshire.html: Milton's margin here has: "Florent." The Flores Historiarum calls the town "Wodnesburch," a town on the borders of Wiltshire and Berkshire; see Camden, "Wilshire" 10.2: "And neere unto this Dike standeth Wodensburge , a little Village where Ceauline, the most warlike King of the West-Saxons, in the yeere of grace 590, whiles he defended his Marches in a bloodie fight, received such a foile and overthrow by the Britans and Englishmen that hee was forced to flie his countrey, and to end his daies in exile."

iricthedane.title: Iric
iricthedane.html: See Eiríkr Hákonarson and his part in the Conquest of England. See also William of Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.10: "Eric."

irishpirates.title: Irish pirats
irishpirates.html: See Florence of Worcester, Chronicron ex Chronicis for 1049 CE. See also Gruffydd ap Llywelyn.

itwasusual.title: it was usual
itwasusual.html: This bit comes from Tacitus, Annals 14.35. Dio, on the other hand, says nothing about this claim; see Roman History 62.8.

jarumannus.title: Jarumannus
jarumannus.html: Jaruman was the fourth Bishop of Mercia.

joiningforces.title: joining Forces
joiningforces.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 835 CE.

josephexeter.title: Geoffrey ap-Arthur
josephexeter.html: Joseph of Exeter was a 12th-century Latin poet whose most famous poem is Daretis Phrygii Ilias De bello Troiano or The Iliad of Dares the Phrygian: On the Trojan War (c. 1184), a Latin epic in six books.

juliadomna.title: Julia
juliadomna.html: Julia Domna was Severus's second wife and empress.

julian.title: by Julian
julian.html: Milton's margin here has: "In Cæsarib." Flavius Claudius Julianus wrote a satire called The Caesars (362 CE); he ridicules a boastful Julius Caesar in The Caesars.

juliusauthor.title: Julius Caesar
juliusauthor.html: Now in Book 2, Caesar replaces Geoffrey as Milton's chief source: Commentarii de Bello Gallico or Commentaries on the Gallic War.

jutesdef.title: Jutes
jutesdef.html: Jutes were an ancient Germanic people who lived in what is now Denmark.

kelred.title: Kelred
kelred.html: See Ceolred of Mercia and Offa of Mercia.

kerdic.title: Kerdic
kerdic.html: Cerdic of Wessex was allegedly the founder and first king of Saxon Wessex.

kingalfred.title: King Alfred
kingalfred.html: Also known as Alfred the Great (849-899 CE).

kingleir.title: Leir
kingleir.html: The source for Shakespeare's King Lear. Milton follows Geoffrey fairly closely (History of the Kings of Britain 2.11-15).

kingnennius.title: Nennius
kingnennius.html: Not to be confused with the Welsh monk and chronicler whom Milton calls Ninnius, Nennius is a mythical King of Britain.

kingofthealmans.title: King of the Almans
kingofthealmans.html: Milton's margin here has: "373." Fraomar was briefly the king of the Bucinobantes, an Alamannic tribe, from about 372 to 373 CE.

kinswoman.title: Kinswoman
kinswoman.html: Milton's margin here has: "Mat. West." See Flores Historiarum for 955 CE. See also Ælfgifu, wife of Eadwig. One story reports that King Eadwig took to his bed both a mother and her daughter simultaneously.

known.title: But heer
known.html: Milton's margin here has: "Suetonius. Cæsar Com. L. I." Gaius Asinius Pollio was a Roman historian whom Suetonius cites in his chapter 56 of his "Life of Julius,". Caesar mentions Diviciacus (whom Milton calls Divitiacus) in Commentaries 2.4, not book 1.

kymbeline.title: Kymbeline
kymbeline.html: Cymbeline or Cunobeline was a pre-Roman British King. See Monmouth, History of the Kings of Britain 4.11-12. This is the Cymbeline of William Shakespeare's late play.

labienus.title: Labienus
labienus.html: Titus Labienus was one of Caesar's lieutenants. See Caesar, Commentaries 5.11.

labourers.title: labourers
labourers.html: See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 1.29 (search for "Mellitus").

laicadulteries.title: Laic Adulteries
laicadulteries.html: An odd way of saying that Æthelbald committed adultery with lay persons as well as with nuns.

lamentabledeath.title: lamentable Death
lamentabledeath.html: Milton's margin here has: "Huntingd." Huntingdon, Historia Anglorum 4.

landed.title: where he had landed
landed.html: Milton's margin here has: "Before the Birth of Christ, 52." More precisely, 54 BCE. Caesar specified "that part of the island in which he had discovered the preceding summer, that there was the best landing-place" (Commentaries 5.8).

languedoc.title: Languedoc
languedoc.html: Languedoc is a region in southern France.

lapland.title: Lapland
lapland.html: Lapland is the northernmost region of Finland.

largeletter.title: large letter
largeletter.html: Simeon of Durham omits the letter from his account, but William of Malmesbury includes it: Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.11.

largeletters.title: Letters of exhortation
largeletters.html: Bede "quotes" two letters at length, one to Edwin and another to Æthelburh: Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 2.10-11.

largepossessions.title: large possessions
largepossessions.html: The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records under the year 648 CE that Cenwahl gave to Cuthred "tria millia terrarum juxta Escesdunam."

largeterritory.title: After him
largeterritory.html: Milton's margin here has: "501." The date of the arrival of Port.

latterconflict.title: latter conflict
latterconflict.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for the year 754 CE.

lawmaxim.title: Law-Maxim
lawmaxim.html: See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.13.

lawsofalfred.title: Laws of Alfred
lawsofalfred.html: See the Law Code of Alfred the Great.

lawsofedward.title: Laws of Edward
lawsofedward.html: Milton refers to a passage from the Leges Edouardi Regis in William Lambarde's Archaionomia (1644) page 149.

laythensick.title: Cosham
laythensick.html: Milton's margin here has: "Camd." See Camden, "Wiltshire" 10.6. See also Corsham.

leadingforth.title: leading forth
leadingforth.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." See Simeon of Durham's Historia Regum for 801 CE. See also Coenwulf of Mercia.

leadingnation.title: leading Nation
leadingnation.html: Milton's margin here has: "Zozim L. 6." See Zosimus, New History book 6: "the barbarians beyond the Rhine made such unbounded incursions over every province, as to reduce not only the Britons, but some of the Celtic nations also to the necessity of revolting from the empire, .... In a similar manner, the whole of Armorica, with other provinces of Gaul, delivered themselves by the same means; expelling the Roman magistracies or officers, and erecting a government, such as they pleased, of their own."

leagre.title: leagre
leagre.html: "A military camp, esp. one engaged in a siege" (OED).

learningnot.title: learning not equal
learningnot.html: Milton's margin here has: "Malms." See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.5.

leastpatient.title: Antoninus Pius
leastpatient.html: Milton's margin here has: "Pausan. archad." See Pausanias's Description of Greece, "Arcadia" 43-44. Antoninus Pius was Roman emperor from 138 to 161 CE. For Camden's "Guinethia," see Britannia, "Ordevices" 24.2.

leavesindoubt.title: in doubt
leavesindoubt.html: See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 1.4. See also Simeon of Durham's Historia Regum for 798 CE. See also Coenwulf of Mercia.

leftthesame.title: left the same
leftthesame.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun. Mat. West." I cannot find the place in Simeon of Durham's Historia Regum. But see the Flores Historiarum.

leftunacted.title: left unacted
leftunacted.html: Milton's margin here has: "Dion. L. 62." See Dio, Roman History 62.7.

legion.title: 25000 Foot and 4500 Horse
legion.html: It is generally believed that until the middle of the first century CE, a Roman legion consisted of 5,000 foot and a small unit of cavalry. William Camden, in his Britannia (1586), speaks of "five Legions;" that would amount to 25000 foot.

legiondeparted.title: Legion departed
legiondeparted.html: Milton's margin here has: "Gildas." See Gildas, The Ruin of Britain 16-17.

lessreason.title: others with less reason
lessreason.html: Milton's margin here has: "Eutrop. L.7." Eutropius, in his Abridgement of Roman History 7.13, attributes the triumph over the Orcades (Orkneys) to Claudius. Apparently so did Eusebius in his Chronicle.

letteritself.title: Letter it self
letteritself.html: See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 1.23: "Dated the 23rd of July, in the fourteenth year of the reign of our pious and most august lord, Mauritius Tiberius, the thirteenth year after the consulship of our said lord."

lettersofdischarge.title: Letters of discharge
lettersofdischarge.html: Milton's margin here has: "Calvis. Sigon." Calvisius's Opus Chronologicum dates these letters at 409 CE. Sigonius, in his Historiarum de occidentali imperio page 252-253, concurs. More likely Honorius sent them in 410 CE, the same year as the sack of Rome by the Visgoths, led by Alaric.

letterstoaetius.title: send Letters
letterstoaetius.html: Milton's margin here has: "Gildas. Bede." See Gildas, The Ruin of Britain 20, and Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 1.13.

levitical.title: Levitical
levitical.html: That is, having to do with knotty questions of ritual observance. Milton, like most Puritans of his day, were a bit scornful of what they regarded as a Jewish of Levitical overconcern with the details of "outward observances."

lieunburied.title: lie unburied
lieunburied.html: Milton has been following Simeon of Durham's account up to this point; see Historia Regum for 1017 CE.

ligeris.title: Ligeris in Aquitania
ligeris.html: The Loire River, from Latin Liger, Ligerim, itself a transcription of the native Gaulish name of the river.

lighttarget.title: light Target
lighttarget.html: Milton's margin here has: "Cæsar." See Caesar's Commentaries on the Gallic War 4.24-36 and 5.9-22.

likefelicity.title: Constans
likefelicity.html: Milton's margin here has: "408." Constans II was appointed co-emperor with his father, Constantine III, in 409 CE. Orosius, in his Against the Pagans 7.40, writes "Constantine sent into Spain his son Constans, who, shameful to say, had been transformed from a monk into a Caesar."

likefury.title: like fury
likefury.html: Milton's margin here has: "Ingulf." The Pseudo-Ingulf Historia records this Danish campaign (492r).

likesuccess.title: from the digests
likesuccess.html: Milton's margin here has: "Digest. L. 36." The Digest of Roman law was compiled by order of Justinian I in the 6th century CE. Milton refers to book 36 where Seius Saturninus is described as "Admiral of the Britannic Fleet" (36.1.46). See also Camden, Britannia, "Romans in Britaine" 60.

likewildbeasts.title: like wild Beasts
likewildbeasts.html: Milton's margin here has: "Huntingd." See Huntingdon, Historia Anglorum 6.

lindisfarne.title: Lindisfarne
lindisfarne.html: Lindisfarne was also known as Holy Island, and importnat center of Celtic Christianity.

littlebefore.title: little before
littlebefore.html: Milton's margin here has: "Hoved. Florent." See Roger of Hovedon, Chronica for 1066 CE: "After his burial, the viceroy Harold, son of earl Godwin, whom, before his decease, the king had appointed his successor, was elevated to the throne by all the chief men of England." See also Florence, Chronicron ex Chronicis.

littlebetter.title: overthrew them
littlebetter.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an. Asser." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 851 CE See also Asser, Life of Alfred. Probably the town of Wembury in Devon.

littlecredit.title: little credit
littlecredit.html: See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.12. See also Alfred Aetheling.

littleriver.title: little river
littleriver.html: See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 3.1.

livie.title: Livie
livie.html: Titus Livius, in his Ab urbe condita, or History of Rome, also relied on poetic sources of legendary stories.

llandaff.title: recounts
llandaff.html: The Book of Llandaff, compiled around 1125 CE, was available only in manuscript when Milton wrote his History. He may well have seen references to it in Ussher's Primordiis. See also Tewdrig, king of Glywysing.

logres.title: Loëgria
logres.html: Also called Logres or Lloegyr, the part of England southeast of a line extending from the Humber Estuary to the Severn Estuary.

longafter.title: not long after
longafter.html: Milton's margin here has: "291." Marcus Flavius Valerius Constantius Herculius Augustus became Caesar in 293 CE.

longpeace.title: Valentinus
longpeace.html: Milton's margin here has: "368." Valentinus, exiled to Britain, attempted a rebellion which was suppressed by Theodosius in 369 CE.

losthislife.title: lost his life
losthislife.html: Milton's margin here has: "Florent. Annal. Sax. The Kingdome of Kent." See the Flores Historiarum page 14: "Ailestorp." See also the Wheeloc Latin translation of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle page 508: "Aeillstreu."

lowparentage.title: About which time
lowparentage.html: Milton's margin here has: "284." Carus died in 283 CE, Numerian in 284 CE, and Carinus in 285 CE. Marcus Aurelius Mausaeus Valerius Carausius was of humble origin, a Menapian. He usurped power in 286 and died in 293 CE.

lud.title: Lud
lud.html: King Lud, for whom London (Lud's Town) is named.

ludiken.title: Camelford
ludiken.html: Milton's margin here has: "Camd." See "Cornwall" 8.54 where Camden also names the town as "Gaffelford."

lyingopposite.title: lying opposite
lyingopposite.html: Milton's margin here has: "457." See Anglo-Saxon Chronicle: "Hengestius & Esc."

lynceus.title: Linceus
lynceus.html: According to myth, Lynceus of Argos was spared.

madehisown.title: made his own
madehisown.html: Milton's margin here has: "Eumen. Paneg. 2." "Maximian prepared an invasion of Britain in 288 or 289 to oust him,[5] but it failed. A panegyric delivered to Constantius Chlorus attributes this failure to bad weather, but notes that Carausius claimed a military victory" (Carausius). That panegyric has been attributed to Eumenius.

madeking.title: made King
madeking.html: Milton's margin here has: "Malms. Sax. ann." See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 1.1 and the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 805 CE (should be 807, see Cuthred of Kent).

madenostay.title: made no stay
madenostay.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." See Simeon of Durham, Historia Regum for 1013 CE.

madepeacewith.title: made peace
madepeacewith.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." See Simeon, Historia Regum for 1048 CE. Simeon confuses Harald Hardrada and Harald Fairhair; Milton repeats the confusion.

madethesecond.title: made the second
madethesecond.html: Geoffrey of Monmouth, in his History of the Kings of Britain 4.17-19, tells a version of the King Lucius story in which Lucius is the great grandson of Aviragus. See also Camden, Britannia, "Westmoreland" 1, who scoffs at the notion of Westmaria being names for King Marius: "Let that dream therefore, as touching King Marius, be excluded out of the schoole of reverend antiquity, who, forsooth, as our Chronicles have dreamed, subdued the Picts and called this country after his owne name."

madewar.title: made War
madewar.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an." The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records a battle between "Ceolvulfus" and the South Saxons.

maglocune.title: Maglocune
maglocune.html: See Gildas, The Ruin of Britain 33-36. See also Maelgwn Gwynedd.

magnanimous.title: magnanimous
magnanimous.html: Milton's margin here has: "183." The rebellion of northern tribes was not quelled until 184 CE.

magnificence.title: magnificence
magnificence.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an. Ingulf." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 973 CE. For Pseudo-Ingulf, see the next note.

makingsport.title: making sport
makingsport.html: Milton's margin here has: "Huntingd." See Huntingdon, Historia Anglorum 6.

malmesbury.title: barbarous Invaders
malmesbury.html: Milton's margin here has: "Malins". Most likely a misprint for "Malms." William of Malmsebury was the author, in Latin, of a Chronicle of the Kings of England; in book 1.1 he describes the state of Britain after the Romans left: "Britain, despoiled of the support of its youthful population, and bereft of every useful art, was for a long time exposed to the ambition of neighboring nations."

malmesburyagree.title: agree
malmesburyagree.html: See Simeon, Historia Regum and Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.13 for 1066 CE.

malmsine.title: Malmsbury
malmsine.html: See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England; in book 1.2. See also Ine of Wessex.

mandubratius.title: Mandubratius
mandubratius.html: Also known as Mandubracius in Caesar's Commentaries 5.20. Bede calls him Androgeus in Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 1.2.

manhood.title: manhood
