manhood.html: This sentiment about the relative unmanliness of Britons is Milton's own, not that of Tacitus. The same may be said of his sense of Venutius's indignation towards the Romans for supporting the rebellion af "an adultress."

manliusvalens.title: Manlius Valens
manliusvalens.html: Gaius Manlius Valens, Roman General whose legion was overcome by the Silures. See Tacitus, Annals 12.40.

manypresents.title: presents
manypresents.html: See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 1.32.

manyprinces.title: many Princes
manyprinces.html: Milton's margin here has: "Tacitus." See The Life of Julius Agricola 12.

manytrophies.title: many Trophies
manytrophies.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an. Malms. Ingulf." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 941 CE. And see Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.6, whose praise of Athelstan goes on for pages and includes passages from old poems. The Pseudo-Ingulf's Historia identifies Athelstan's kinsmen (495v).

marchenlage.title: Marchen Leage
marchenlage.html: Merchenlage: the law of the ancient kingdom of Mercia. See also Merchene law in the OED: "The Anglo-Saxon legal code of Mercia".

marchingout.title: marching out
marchingout.html: Milton's margin here has: "Constant. vit. German." See Life of St. Germanus Chapters 17-18.

marchonlondon.title: Suetonius
marchonlondon.html: General Suetonius's march on London comes from Tacitus, Annals 14.33-39.

marcian.title: Chrysanthus
marcian.html: Milton's margin here has: "Socrat. L. 7." Socrates of Constantinople was a Greek historian. See his Church History 7.12 for an account of Chrysanthus as "Bishop of the Novatians at Constantinople."

marganus.title: Marganus and Cunedagius
marganus.html: See the family tree of Brutus of Troy, according to legend.

margincaesar.title: should allege
margincaesar.html: Milton's margin here has "Cæs. 1.6." The passage Milton refers to (in Latin) comes from Commentarii de bello Gallico 6.14; in English, Commentaries on the Gallic War 6.14.

marianus.title: Marianus Scotus
marianus.html: Marian the Scot wrote a Clear Chronicle (Latin: Cronica Clara), which purports to be a universal history from the creation of the world to 1082 CE.

marriesemma.title: marries Emma
marriesemma.html: See Simeon of Durham, Historia Regum for 1002 CE.

martia.title: Martia
martia.html: Queen Marcia, the third female ruler of the Britons.

martialepigrams.title: Martial
martialepigrams.html: Marcus Valerius Martialis in The Epigrams 11.53, praises Claudia Rufina.

martinus.title: Martinus
martinus.html: For the story of Flavius Martinus and Paulus Catena, see Ammianus Marcellus, Roman History 14.5.7.

mataddsthat.title: adds that
mataddsthat.html: See the Flores Historiarum for 946 CE.

matthew.html: Milton's margin here has "Matthew Westmin." Milton signals his marginal notation with a star or asterisk here on page 27. Matthew of Westminster was thought to be the author of the Flores Historiarum, but since 1826 has been regarded as never having existed. Matthew Paris was probably the true author, though much of the work was completed at Westminster Abbey. See Matthew, The Flowers of History 5.25. See also Gorbonianus.

matwest.title: wicked counsel
matwest.html: See the Flores Historiarum for an elaborate story of the malice of Offa's queen toward Æthelberht.

matwest4800.title: by Monks
matwest4800.html: See Flores Historiarum for 975 CE. See also Simeon of Durham, Historia Regum for 975 CE. Simeon reckoned three fleets of 1200 vessels, and Pseudo Matthew 4 fleets of 1200 vessels.

maximusmagnus.title: Maximus
maximusmagnus.html: Magnus Maximus was Western Roman Emperor from 383 (when he slew Gratian) to 388 CE.

meanwhilehunt.title: Mean while
meanwhilehunt.html: See Huntingdon, Historia Anglorum 2. See also Ceolric or Ceol of Wessex and Pybba of Mercia.

meanywhile.title: Mean while
meanywhile.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." See Simeon of Durham's Historia Regum for 802 CE. See also Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.1. See also Ecgberht, King of Wessex.

mela.title: saith Mela
mela.html: Milton's margin here has: "Lucan." See Mela's The Situation of the World (translated by Arthur Golding 1585) 78-79 and Lucan's The Civil War 4.131-35.

melageo.title: Mela the Geographer
melageo.html: Pomponius Mela was the earliest Roman geographer. In his De Situ Orbis Libri III, Pomponius mentions a battle between Hercules and Albion: " it is but a rascall banke all stonie, where the report goeth that Hercules fighting against Albion and Bergion the sonnes of Neptune, and hauing spent all his Artillerie, called uppon his Father Iupiter, who rayned downe stones to helpe him with: and a man would beléeue it had rained stones in déede, there lye so many, and that euerie where, and so farre of" (Arthur Golding, trans., The Worke of Pomponius Mela (1585) 54.

mellitus.title: Mellitus
mellitus.html: Mellitus was the first Bishop of London in Saxon times. Justus was the fourth Archbishop of Canterbury. Paulinus was the first Bishop of York. Rufinianus was a 5th-century Bishop of Bayeux in Normandy; just why Bede includes him in this list of 7th-century missionaries is unclear.

menacing.title: some say menacing
menacing.html: Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 2.2 (search for "threatening").

mentioned.title: forage the Country
mentioned.html: See Asser, Life of Alfred. But see the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 871 CE: "apud Meretune dimicabant."

mercia.title: Mercian Kingdom
mercia.html: Mercia was one of the seven ancient Kingdoms of Anglo-Saxon Britain.

mercianborder.title: Idle
mercianborder.html: Milton's margin here has: "Camden." See Camden, "Nottinghamshire" 20.7: "Out of this wood there spring many riverets that runne into the Trent, but Idle is thought to be the chiefe: upon which neere unto Idleton in the yeare 616 that felicity and prosperous successe which for a long time had accompanied Ethered that most puissant king of the Northumberland, was overtaken and forsooke him quite."

mercianking.title: Mercian King
mercianking.html: Milton's margin here has: "593." The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records the deaths of "Ceaulinus, & Cuichelmus, & Crida:" Ceawlin of Wessex, Cwichelm of Wessex, and Creoda of Mercia. See also Pybba of Mercia (Milton's "Wibba").

merlinambrose.title: Merlin
merlinambrose.html: It is Monmouth who calls this young prophet Merlin; see History of the Kings of Britain 8.1.

metwith4.title: met with four
metwith4.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 882 CE.

midstofsloughs.title: midst of sloughs
midstofsloughs.html: Milton's margin here has: "Dion." See Cassius Dio, Roman History 77.13-17.

militarytumult.title: nine years
militarytumult.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an. Huntingd." The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records the death of Cynric of Wessex in 748 CE, closer to eight rather than nine years after Cuthred's accession in 740, though Simeon of Durham dates it in 739 and John of Worcester in 741. Cynric was slain in a mutiny.

mindsintent.title: not less busied
mindsintent.html: Milton's margin here has: "Bed. l. 2. c. 34." See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 1.34. And see Æthelfrith.

mineauthor.title: mine Author
mineauthor.html: . In this case, presumably Geoffrey of Monmouth. See his History of the Kings of Britain 1.5.

minerva.title: Minerva
minerva.html: Athena in Greek, Minerva was the Roman goddess of wisdom and martial strategy. The ancient Britons called her Sulis.

modernnames.title: modern names
modernnames.html: The ancient names as Milton lists them appear in Caesar's Commentaries 5.21.

molestnomore.title: no more
molestnomore.html: Milton's margin here has: "Huntingd." Huntingdon, Historia Anglorum 5.

molmutine.title: Molmutine Laws
molmutine.html: Among other notable features the Molmutine Laws are said to have established temples and cities as sanctuaries from death and a system of weights and measures.

money.title: brazen pieces
money.html: Milton's margin here has: "Tacitus, Diodor. Strabo." See Tacitus, The Life of Julius Agricola 12; Diodorus of Sicily's The Library of History 5.22; Strabo's The Geography 4.5.3.

monmouthbook.title: Monmouth Booke
monmouthbook.html: See History of the Kings of Britain 4.11.

monmouthstorie.title: Monmouth Storie
monmouthstorie.html: Milton returns to Geoffrey of Monmouth when there is a gap in his Roman sources. See History of the Kings of Britain 4.11. Tenuantius, or Tasciovanus, was the son of King Lud, for whom London was named.

monmouthwriter2.title: Monmouth Writer
monmouthwriter2.html: Milton returns to Geoffrey of Monmouth when there is a gap or conflict in his Roman sources. See History of the Kings of Britain 4.12-16. In his play, Cymbeline, Shakespeare adopts Geoffrey's names.

morecredible.title: more credible
morecredible.html: See Gildas, The Ruin of Britain 26.

moreorless.title: more or less
moreorless.html: Milton's margin here has: "The Kingdom of East-Angles." See Kingdom of East Anglia.

morethenone.title: more then one
morethenone.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 813 CE See also Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.1.

morindus.title: Morindus
morindus.html: . Also known as Morvidus. See also Geoffrey, History of the Kings of Britain 3.14-15.

morini.title: King of the Morines
morini.html: The Morini were a Belgic tribe of northern Gaul.

mostanend.title: most an end
mostanend.html: OED: "almost uninterruptedly, almost always, mostly, for the most part."

muchado.title: much ado
muchado.html: Milton's margin here has: "752." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for the year 752 CE.

muchafter.title: not much after
muchafter.html: Milton's margin here has: "The Kingdom of East-Saxons." See Kingdom of Essex.

muchbooty.title: much booty
muchbooty.html: Milton's margin here has: "Malms." See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.13.

muchexecution.title: much execution
muchexecution.html: Milton follows fairly closely Dio's narrative in Roman History 60.20. Titus Flavius Vespasian, later Emperor, was legate for Claudius. Dio's account also mentions Sabinus, Caratacus, Togodumnus, and Gaius Vitorius Hosidius Geta.

muchtrouble.title: much trouble
muchtrouble.html: Milton's margin here has: "Bed. L. 3. c. 14." See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 3.14. See also Oswiu.

muchtruth.title: much truth
muchtruth.html: Compared, that is, to the legendary nature of his sources in Book 1. Starting in Book 2, Milton fills his margins with references to his sources and regular notations of dates.

mustsurvive.title: must survive
mustsurvive.html: Milton's margin here has: "Malms. gest. pont. l. 1." In his Gesta Pontificum Anglorum, William of Malmesbury reports that Augustine was Archbishop of Canterbury for 15 or 16 years. Counting from 597 CE, that would have him living well past 607, the date of the Bangor massacre according to the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle. Bede dates his death shortly after 604 CE: Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 2.3. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records his death under the year 606 CE.

myauthor.title: my Author
myauthor.html: Again, see Gildas, The Ruin of Britain 21: "Kings were anointed, not according to god's ordinance, but such as showed themselves more cruel than the rest; and soon after, they were put to death by those who had elected them, without any inquiry into their merits, but because others still more cruel were chosen to succeed them."

myauthorwheeloc.title: my Author
myauthorwheeloc.html: Milton apparently follows Wheloc's Latin translation in this regard; see the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle.

myauthour.title: my Authour
myauthour.html: See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.13.

namelessauthor.title: nameless author
namelessauthor.html: See the Pseudo-Brompton's account in Roger Twysden's edition of ten historical authors, Historiae Anglicanae Scriptores X at columns 941-42. "Ordalian Law" refers to trial by ordeal. See also Emma of Normandy.

namestheplace.title: names the place
namestheplace.html: See Camden, "Wiltshire" 10.8: " Avon, thus increased by this riveret, watereth Bradford, in the foregoing times Bradanford (so named of a broad foord) situat upon the descent or fall of an hill, and built of all of stone: where Kenilwacuh King of the West-Britans embrued his sword with bloud in civill war against Cuthred his neere kinsman."

narrowplace.title: place narrow
narrowplace.html: This bit is from Tacitus, Annals 14.34.

nectaridius.title: Nectaridius
nectaridius.html: See Ammianus Marcellus, Roman History 27.8.1 for Nectaridius and Fullofaudes. Milton follows Marcellus for this story.

neglectingcommand.title: neglecting his command
neglectingcommand.html: See Nennius, Historia Brittonum 44: "They imprudently disobeyed this last injunction, and neglected to bury him where he had appointed."

neither.title: neither
neither.html: Milton's margin here has: "Malms." See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 1.6 for Sexred and Saeward as sons of Sæberht of Essex.

nemorum.title: in Verse
nemorum.html: . These are Milton's own translations of Latin verses as they appear in Jerome Commelin's Rerum Britannicarum (Heidelberg 1587) 6. A different version or translation of these verses appears in Geoffrey's History of the Kings of Britain 11.

nennius.title: Elder Ninnius
nennius.html: Nennius was a Welsh monk of the 9th century, credited with authorship of the Historia Brittonum. See the Historia Brittonum in English.

newenden.title: Newenden
newenden.html: Milton's margin here has: "Camden." See "Kent" 40.

newforce.title: new force
newforce.html: Milton's margin here has: "Malms." See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 1.2. See also Eadric of Kent.

newlevies.title: new levies
newlevies.html: Milton's margin here has: "An. omn." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle: "Stuf & Witgar."

newopposition.title: new opposition
newopposition.html: Milton's margin here has: "Ethelwerd." See Æthelweard, Anglo-Saxon Chronicle page 6.

nextage.title: next Age
nextage.html: Milton's margin here has: "Gildas." See Gildas, The Ruin of Britain 26.

nextnextyear.title: next year
nextnextyear.html: Milton's margin here has: "756." See Eadberht of Northumbria.

nextyear2.title: next year
nextyear2.html: Milton's margin here has: "561." See Flores Historiarum: "Eodem anno, Athelbertus, rex magnus Cantuariorum, secundum quosdam regnare incepit."

nextyearpeada.title: next year Peada
nextyearpeada.html: Milton's margin here has: "653." The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records under the year 653 that Mercia became Christian ("RECTAM FIDEM acceperunt") under the kingship of Peada. The story of Peada and Oswiu's daughter comes from Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 3.21.

nighhalf.title: nigh half spent
nighhalf.html: See Caesar's Commentaries 4.36: "the time of the equinox was near."

ninthyear.title: ninth year
ninthyear.html: Milton's margin here has: "Huntingd. L. 2. p. 313-315." See Huntingdon, Historia Anglorum 2.15; Henry dates this at 527 CE. Cerdic reigned in Wessex from 519 to 534 CE.

nobigger.title: no bigger
nobigger.html: Milton's margin here has: "Dion." See Cassius Dio's Roman History 77.12.4.

nogreatbody.title: no great body
nogreatbody.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." See Simeon, Historia Regum for 1062 CE, which says nothing whatever about Harold's exploits.

nokingmalms.title: no King
nokingmalms.html: See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 1.3.

nolessexactness.title: no less exactness
nolessexactness.html: Milton's margin here has: "Buch. L. 5." See Buchanan, History of Scotland 7.3-6.

nolesshostility.title: no less hostility
nolesshostility.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 911 CE. See also the Flores Historiarum and Battle of Tettenhall.

nooccasion.title: next year
nooccasion.html: Milton's margin here has: "626." See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 2.9 for the story of Eumer the assassin. For "assassin" as a transitive verb, see the OED.

northward.title: Northward
northward.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 875 CE.

notabledamage.title: notable damage
notabledamage.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sigon. de regn. Ital. L. 5." See Sigonius, Historiarum de Regno Italiae.

notdisagreeing.title: not disagreeing
notdisagreeing.html: See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records the loss of seven earls, or in Wheloc's translation, "septem Anlavi Duces." Malmesbury reports twelve "earls" killed; see Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.6. He also reports the death of Constantine, king of the Scots, not his escape.

notedleader.title: noted leader
notedleader.html: Caesar names this noted leader as Lugotorix in his Commentaries 5.22.

notlongafter.title: 30 Tyrants
notlongafter.html: Milton's margin here has: "Eumen. Paneg. Const." Eumenius's "Panagyricus Con[s]tantino Augusto" appears in Panegyrici Latini. The Thirty Tyrants were a series of claimants to the imperial throne during the reign of Gallienus.

notlongafter2.title: not long after
notlongafter2.html: Milton's margin here has: "Pontan. L. 3." Johannes Pontanus was a Dutch historian and author of the Rerum Danicarum Historia (Amsterdam 1631). This may be the passage from book 3 Milton refers to.

notmaterialtoinquire.title: not material
notmaterialtoinquire.html: See Simeon, Historia Regum for 1051 CE, and Florence, Chronicron ex Chronicis which uses precisely the same words. See also Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.13.

notoftendestitute.title: not often destitute
notoftendestitute.html: But see Jesus's contrary opinion in Paradise Reagin'd 3.47-67.

notpast.title: not past
notpast.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an. Huntingd." The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records the slaughter of the monks at Chester, numbering the deaths in Latin as "mille ducenti sacerdotes." See also Huntingdon, Historia Anglorum 3.

notread.title: not read
notread.html: So claimed Camden in his "Britans of Armorica" 2: "Before the arrivall of our Britans, this countrey was at first called Armorica , that is, situate by the sea side".

notrecorded.title: no recorded
notrecorded.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Duu." Clearly an inverted letter; see Simeon of Durham, Historia Regum for 1000 CE. See also Flores Historiarum for 1000 CE.

notreturning.title: Armorica
notreturning.html: Milton's margin here has: "Beda. Ninn." See Bede's Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 1.9. And see also Nennius, Historia Brittonum 27: "Unwilling to send back his warlike companions to their wives, children and possessions in Britain, he [Maximus] conferred upon them numerous districts from the lake on the summit of Mons Jovis, to the city called Cant Guic, and to the western Tumulus, that is, to Cruc Occident. These are the Armoric Britons."

notsilent.title: not silent
notsilent.html: Milton's margin here has: "Pontan. hist. Dan. L. 4." See Pontanus, Rerum Danicarum Historia book 4.

notsofond.title: not so fond
notsofond.html: Milton's margin here has: "519." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle: the battle of "Cerdices-Fordam."

notsowell.title: not so well
notsowell.html: Milton's margin here has: "Ethelwerd. Florent." See Æthelweard's Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, which dates Palladius's mission as 430 CE. See also Florence of Worcester, Chronicle.

nottainted.title: Vectius Bolanus
nottainted.html: Milton's margin here has: "Tacit. Hist. 2. & vit. Agric." Marcus Vettius Bolanus became governor of Britain in 69 CE. See Tacitus, Histories 2.65 and 2.97. See also Life of Agricola 16-17 for brief accounts of Bolanus and Quintus Petillius Cerialis as governors of Britain.

notunjustly.title: not unjustly
notunjustly.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an." The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle has no entry for 927 CE but see also Huntingdon, Historia Anglorum 5.

nowashdown.title: now Ashdown
nowashdown.html: Milton's margin here has: "Camden." See Camden "Essex" 16.8.

nowcalld.title: now call'd
nowcalld.html: Milton's margin here has: "Camden." Camden, in "Lancashire" 27.23, identifies the town as Winander-mere (Windermere) in Lancashire.

nowcomedown.title: now come down
nowcomedown.html: Milton's margin here has: "Henry Huntingd." Henry of Huntingdon was archdeacon of Huntingdon and author of Historia Anglorum (1129, 1154). Milton refers here to book (Liber) 2 of that work.

nowhissubjects.title: now his subjects
nowhissubjects.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun. Huntingd. Mat. West." See Simeon, Historia Regum for 1018 CE. See also Huntingdon, Historia Anglorum 6, and the Flores Historiarum for 1018 CE.

nowoswestre.title: now Oswestre
nowoswestre.html: Milton's margin here has: "Camden." See Camden, "Shropshire" 22.14: "It hath the name of Oswald King of the Northumbers (whereas before time it was called Maserfield) whom Penda the Pagan Prince of the Mercians both slow heere and a bloudy battaile, and after hee had slaine him, with monstrous cruelty tare in peeces."

nowsomany.title: Palladius
nowsomany.html: Milton's margin here has: "Prosp. Aquit." Palladius was the first Bishop of Ireland (then called Scotia), sent to Ireland by Pope Celestine in 431 CE. Prosper's Chronicum says, "Palladius was sent by Pope Celestine to the Scots [i.e. Irish] who believed in Christ, and was ordained as their first bishop."

obscureutterance.title: obscure utterance
obscureutterance.html: See Gildas, The Ruin of Britain 26: "the year of the siege of Bath-hill [Badon Hill], when took place also the last almost, though not the least slaughter of our cruel foes, which was (as I am sure) forty-four years and one month after the landing of the Saxons, and also the time of my own nativity." Gildas was born sometime near 500 CE.

octavianus.title: Octavianus Cæsar Augustus
octavianus.html: Milton's margin here has: "Strabo L. 2." See The Geography 2.5.8.

octaviusaugustus.title: Octavianus Caesar Augustus
octaviusaugustus.html: Caesar Augustus, Rome's first emperor.

offaofmercia.title: Offa
offaofmercia.html: See Offa of Mercia. See also Simeon of Durham's Historia Regum for 771 CE.

ofmaximus.title: of Maximus
ofmaximus.html: Milton's margin here has: "Huntingd. L. 1." book (Liber) 1, page 8. See also Constantine the Great.

oisier.title: Oysier
oisier.html: Osier: "Any of several willows with tough pliant branches used in basketwork" (OED).

oldarmy.title: old Army
oldarmy.html: The Old English original, from the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, refers to those of the sons of Edward who escaped the "hamora lafan," the hammer-beaten swords. Milton was probably led astray by Huntingdon's Latin version; see Huntingdon, Historia Anglorum 5: "nobiles ceciderunt, domesticae reliquiae defuncti Edwardi."

oncemore.title: Once more
oncemore.html: Milton's margin here has: "588." See the Flores Historiarum.

onedayattable.title: one day at Table
onedayattable.html: The following story comes from Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.8. See also Kenneth II of Scotland.

onekingdom.title: one Kingdom
onekingdom.html: Milton's margin here has: "Florent. ad ann." See the Flores Historiarum. See Edwin of Northumbria.

oneman.title: One man
oneman.html: Milton's margin here has: "Malms." See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.13.

oneofhissons.title: one of his Sons
oneofhissons.html: Milton's margin here has: "283." Marcus Aurelius Carus Augustus was emperor from 282-283 CE. He was succeeded by his sons Carinus and Numerian.

oneplace.title: one place
oneplace.html: Milton's margin here has: "Camden." See Camden, Britannia, "Surrey": "Otelands."

opendiscord.title: op'n discord
opendiscord.html: Milton's margin here has: "Tacit. Hist. 8.1. & vit. Agric." Probably "8" is a misprint for "L", for Liber. Milton picks up the story as related by Tacitus in Histories 1.60 and Life of Agricola 16. Marcus Roscius Coelius was legate of Legion XX in Britain in 68 CE.

opposition.title: Warlike opposition
opposition.html: Milton's margin here has: "Malms." See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.10.

ordainingbishops.title: ordaining Bishops
ordainingbishops.html: Milton's margin here has: "Bed. l. l. 2. c. 3." See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 2.3. See also Mellitus and Justus.

ordovices.title: Ordovices
ordovices.html: Ordovices: an ancient Celtic tribe of northern Wales.

orosius.title: Orosius
orosius.html: Paulus Orosius, a Gallaecian Chalcedonian priest, historian and theologian was most famous for his Historiarum Adversum Paganos Libri VII, History Against the Pagans in Seven Books (416-17). See book 6, section 9. Milton is still following Caesar's Commentaries 4.29.

orosiusadds.title: Orosius adds
orosiusadds.html: Milton's margin here has: "Eutropii Pean. Oros. l. 7." Flavius Eutropius authored a Abridged History of Rome in Latin. There in book 8, paragraph 19, he reports that the wall was 32 miles long, and that Severus died at York "in the eighteenth year and fourth month of his reign, and was honoured with the title of god." Orosius, in his Against the Pagans 7.17, reports the wall as "one hundred and thirty-two miles" long. Hadrian's wall is 73 miles long between Newcastle-on-Tyne and Carlisle.

otheraffairs.title: 20 Years after
otheraffairs.html: Milton's margin here has: "Year before the Birth of Christ, 32." Augustus planned invasions of Britain in 34, 27, and 25 BCE. The first was called off due to uprisings. Milton's date is two years late.

otherbodies.title: other Bodies
otherbodies.html: Milton's margin here has: "Cæsar." See Commentaries 5.12. For Pythagoras's notion of metempsychosis, see Pythagoras.

otherplacesthere.title: other places
otherplacesthere.html: Perhaps the "other places" include Ceolesegiam and Cuuichelmslawe (Simeon, Historia Regum), now known as Cholsey and Cuckhamsely Knob in Berkshire, but now in South Oxfordshire.

others.title: Others
others.html: Milton's margin here has: "Malms. L. 1. c. 1." Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 1.1, page 6. Armorica is an ancient name for that part of Gaul between the Seine and the Loire.

othersacrament.title: other Sacrament
othersacrament.html: Though the Roman Catholic Church of Augustine's day recognized seven sacraments, Milton (like most reformed Protestants) recognizes only two: baptism and the Lord's Supper.

othersinterpret.title: others interpret
othersinterpret.html: Milton's margin here has: "Huntingd." See Æthelweard, Anglo-Saxon Chronicle. See also Huntingdon, Historia Anglorum 4.

othersnametwo.title: others name two
othersnametwo.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an. Malms." The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records the succession of Æscwine as King of the West Saxons in the year 674 CE. See also Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 1.2. See also Centwine of Wessex.

othersoflatertime.title: Others of later time
othersoflatertime.html: Milton probably refers to antiquarians like John Leland and John Bale, both of whom regarded it as their patriotic duty to assert the truth of Arthur legends.

othersonof.title: other Son
othersonof.html: See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 3.24. See also Wulfhere of Mercia.

othersrelatepurpose.title: Others relate
othersrelatepurpose.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun. Florent." See Simeon of Durham's Historia Regum for 894 CE. See also the Flores Historiarum.

otherssay.title: others say
otherssay.html: Milton's margin here has: "Florent." See the Flores Historiarum.

otherthreeyears.title: other three years
otherthreeyears.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an." The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records the death of Ecgberht of Kent in the year 673 CE. See also Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 4.5.

ottanford.title: Ottanford
ottanford.html: Otford is a village in Kent where King Offa fought the Kentish Saxons in 776 CE.

ourown.title: our own Historians
ourown.html: Geoffrey of Monmouth claims Constantine's British birth in History of the Kings of Britain 5.6. See also William Camden, Britannia, "Romans in Britaine" 4.75. In fact, Flavius Valerius Constantinus "was born in the city of Naissus, (today Niš, Serbia) part of the Dardania province of Moesia on 27 February, probably c. 272" CE.

outlandish.title: out-landish
outlandish.html: See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.8. See also his account of riding circuit at Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.8. For the story of Ludwal and the Welsh wolves, see the previous page; Malmesbury reports that "Judwall" paid the trubute for three years before running out of wolves.

outofbritain.title: out of Britain
outofbritain.html: Milton's margin here has: "418." The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle The Wheloc edition (1644), page 506, records 418 CE as the year some Romans hid treasure and departed for Gaul.

outofhisrealm.title: out of his Realm
outofhisrealm.html: Milton's margin here has: "Huntingd." See Huntingdon, Historia Anglorum 4.28. See also Eardwulf of Northumbria.

outofthefont.title: out of the Font
outofthefont.html: Milton's margin here has: "636." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for the year 636 CE. See also Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 2.15 and 3.18.

overallkent.title: over all Kent
overallkent.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." See Simeon of Durham, Historia Regum for 1006 CE.

overlaies.title: overlaies
overlaies.html: . OED: "To overwhelm, overpower, crush by force (a person, military force, etc.); to press heavily upon, oppress."

overland.title: over land
overland.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 867 CE See also Osberht of Northumbria.

overthrown.title: overthrown
overthrown.html: Milton's margin here has: "Gildas." See Gildas, The Ruin of Britain 13-14.

overthrown2.title: overthrown
overthrown2.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 823 CE The Battle of Ellendun was fought in Wiltshire in 625 CE.

ownyouth.title: at home destitute
ownyouth.html: Milton's margin here has: "Gildas. Beda." See Gildas, The Ruin of Britain 14-15, and Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 1.12.

palaceoftosti.title: Palace of Tosti
palaceoftosti.html: Simeon does not mention the location of this slaughter (see Simeon, Historia Regum for 1065 CE), but see also Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.13. See also Tostig Godwinson: Exile and rebellion.

pannonia.title: Pannonia
pannonia.html: Milton's margin here has: "Dion. L. 49." See Dio's Roman History 49.38. See also Pannonia.

passingthethames.title: passing the Thames
passingthethames.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." See Simeon of Durham, Historia Regum for 1016 CE. See also Cricklade.

paulus.title: Paulus Orosius
paulus.html: Milton's margin here has: "Oros. Lib. 6. c. 7. & 9." Paulus Orosius, a Gallaecian Chalcedonian priest, historian and theologian was most famous for his Historiarum Adversum Paganos Libri VII, History Against the Pagans in Seven Books (416-17). See book 6, sections 7 and 9.

pearlandgold.title: Pearl and Gold
pearlandgold.html: Milton's margin here has: "793." See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 1.4. See also the Flores Historiarum.

pedridan.title: Pedridan
pedridan.html: The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records under 658 CE the battle near Peonum and the flight to Pedridan. Camden identifies Peonum in "Somerset-shire" 9.2 as Pen (now Penselwood).

pelagianismdef.title: Pelagianism
pelagianismdef.html: Pelagianism is a doctrine named for the monk Pelagius which holds that original sin did not thoroughly taint human nature. The Roman Catholic Church deemed the doctrine heretical.

pelmel.title: pelmel
pelmel.html: Pell-mell: "With reference to combatants: without keeping ranks; hand to hand, man to man; in a mêlée" (OED).

perpetuallandings.title: perpetual landings
perpetuallandings.html: Milton's margin here has: "Amm. L. 26. 27." See Ammianus Marcellus, Roman History 26.4.5 ("Atacotti") and 27.8.5 ("Attacotti").

perpetualtribute.title: perpetual tribute
perpetualtribute.html: See Huntingdon, Historia Anglorum 4.20. See also Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 1.4.

pest.title: the Pestilence
pest.html: The first plague pandemic broke out in 541 CE and lasted about 8 years.

petilius.title: Petilius Cerealis
petilius.html: Quintus Petillius Cerialis was a Roman general who fought during Boudica's rebellion.

pettywarrs.title: those Kings
pettywarrs.html: Milton's margin here has: "Bede L. 2. c. 15." See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 2.15.

philosopherthenliving.title: Philosopher then living
philosopherthenliving.html: Milton's margin here has: "Gildas." Gildas, also known as Gildas the Wise, was a 6th-century monk best known for his book, The Ruin of Britain where, in 2.4, he cites Porphyry as saying that "Britain is a land fertile in tyrants."

piousimpiety.title: pious impiety
piousimpiety.html: See Simeon of Durham, Historia Regum for 1012 CE: "impia motus pietate."

piousintention.title: Augustine
piousintention.html: Milton's margin here has: "596." See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 5.epitome and 1.23.

pirrhus.title: Pirrhus
pirrhus.html: Pirrhus is also known as Neoptolemus, son of Achilles.

plentyofcorn.title: plenty of Corn
plentyofcorn.html: Milton's margin here has: "Marcel. l. 18." See Ammianus Marcellus, Roman History 18.10.3.

pliniewrites.title: Plinie
pliniewrites.html: On Druids, magic and mistletoe, see Pliny, The Natural History 16.93-95.

poetsofflood.title: read in Poets
poetsofflood.html: Ovid, for example, tells a story of a pre-historic flood in his Metamorphoses 1.4, a story often compared to that in Genesis 6:12-22. Hesiod, in his Theogony 52 tells of giants, as does Genesis 6:4.

polydore.title: Polydore and Virunnius
polydore.html: Polydore Vergil's Anglia Historia (1513) and Ludovicus Ponticus Virunius, in his six-volume Historiae britanniae (Augsburg 1534, London 1585), also included legendary material in their works.

poniardsdef.title: Poniards
poniardsdef.html: A poniard is a long lightweight dagger.

portents.title: foregoing signes
portents.html: A nearly identical list of signs and portents appears in Tacitus, Annals 14.32. The story of the extraordinary Buduica is from Dio, Roman History 62.2-12.

prasutagus.title: Prasutagus
prasutagus.html: King of the Iceni. For competing accounts of Prasutagus, see Tacitus, Annals 14.31 and Dio, Roman History 62.2-12. Tacitus was born in 56 CE, approximately one year before these events.

preachthegospel.title: preach the Gospel
preachthegospel.html: Milton's margin here has: "694." For Willibrod, see Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 5.10-11. See also Pepin of Herstal.

preface.title: Preface
preface.html: See Histories 1.2, where Tacitus writes that " Britain was thoroughly subdued and immediately abandoned."

priscus.title: Priscus Licinius
priscus.html: Marcus Statius Priscus Licinius Italicus became governor of Britain in about 162 CE.

probuswasemperor.title: Probus was Emperor
probuswasemperor.html: Milton's margin here has: "282." Marcus Aurelius Probus Augustus was emperor of Rome from 276-282 CE.

prosperousgale.title: prosperous gale
prosperousgale.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." See Simeon, Historia Regum.

publiccost.title: public cost
publiccost.html: Milton's margin here has: "Gildas." Gildas, in The Ruin of Britain 18, reports in more detail the parting admonishments of the Romans to the Britons.

publicdisputation.title: public disputation
publicdisputation.html: Milton's margin here has: "Math. West. ad ann. 446." Matthew of Westminster was thought to be the author of the Flores Historiarum, but since 1826 has been regarded as never having existed. Matthew Paris was probably the true author, though much of the work was completed at Westminster Abbey. Verulamium is now St. Albans in Hertfordshire.

purchase.title: purchase
purchase.html: OED: "the action of hunting or seizing prey." For speeches by General Suetonius, see Tacitus, Annals 14.36 and Dio, Roman History 62.9-11

putagain.title: put again
putagain.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." See Simeon of Durham's Historia Regum for 790 CE.

putonthemonk.title: put on the Monk
putonthemonk.html: In other words, he became a monk, resigning his crown.

puttoflight.title: put to flight
puttoflight.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an." The errata list instructs "for flight r. fight" but I have retained flight here. See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 896 CE.

quietedtheiland.title: mouth of Tine
quietedtheiland.html: Milton's margin here has: "Camden." Camden describes the path of the wall and some of the Roman ruins and inscriptions in his Britannia, "Northumberland" 29. He also reports that he had seen "one peece of money of his coining the stampe of an Emperour with three souldiers, whom I judge to represent three Legions, with this Inscription, EXER. BRITANNICVS, and another bearing this inscription, RESTITVTOR BRITANNIAE."

readnothow.title: read not how
readnothow.html: See Simeon of Durham's Historia Regum for 790 CE. Simeon records the event, but offers no explanation of how Eardulf survived.

readyatthetime.title: ready at the time
readyatthetime.html: Milton's margin here has: "Florent." See the Flores Historiarum for 1035 CE.

reiner.title: Reiner
reiner.html: For this story, see Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 1.3, and Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 2.12. See also Oswald of Northumbria.

reingratiate.title: Encomium Emmae
reingratiate.html: Milton's margin here has: "Encom. Em." See Encomium Emmae Reginae. The story of Cnut and his fleet is found in the Second Book. See also Olaf II of Norway. The Swedish king in 1015 CE was Olof Skötkonung.

relateitdone.title: relate it done
relateitdone.html: See Huntingdon, Historia Anglorum 6, and the Flores Historiarum for 1016 CE.

relateshim.title: relates him
relateshim.html: Milton's margin here has: "Bed. l. 3. c. 7." See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 3.7.

relatesthiswar.title: relatesthiswar
relatesthiswar.html: See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.6.

remitted.title: worship'd
remitted.html: Milton's margin here has: "Dion. L. 62." Apparently a misprint, this part of the story comes from Dio, Roman History 60.21-22.

removing.title: removing
removing.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an. Camden." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 873 CE See also Camden, "Derby" 20.3.

reportedmiraculous.title: reported miraculous
reportedmiraculous.html: See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 3.2.

reprehendshim.title: reprehends him
reprehendshim.html: See Buchanan, History of Scotland 5.25: "As to what Geofry of Monmouth attributes to him there, it hath no shadow, much less likelyhood, of truth in it, so that I pass them by as impudently forged, and as causelessly believed."

restorement.title: Restorement
restorement.html: That is, his restoration to the throne.

retaining.title: retaining
retaining.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for the year 632 CE.

returntorome.title: return to Rome
returntorome.html: Milton's margin here has: "Pliny." Pliny the Elder, author of The Natural History; in book 9.57, he tells of a breast-plate made of British pearls which Caesar dedicated to Venus Genetrix.

richard2.title: Richard
richard2.html: See Richard II, Duke of Normandy.

richborrow.title: now Richborrow
richborrow.html: Milton's margin here has: "Camden. Juvenal, sat. 2." Richborough is a port town in northeast Kent, quite some distance from the Firth of Tay. Camden calls it "Richborow" in his Britannia, "Kent" 27, and identifies it (probably mistakenly) with Tacitus's Portus Trutulensis. Milton does not resolve the confusion. Juvenal celebrates the Roman conquest of the Orcades (Orkneys) in Satires 2.159-61.

richlypresented.title: richly presented
richlypresented.html: For this detail, see Pseudo-Ingulf, Historia: "& eum sibi succedere in regnum Angliæ."

richpresents.title: rich presents
richpresents.html: See Flores Historiarum for 975 CE. See also Kenneth II of Scotland.

ringmere.title: Ringmere
ringmere.html: The Battle of Ringmere was fought on 5 May 1010 CE.

riverwinwed.title: the River
riverwinwed.html: See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 3.24: "The battle was fought near the river Vinwed, which then, with the great rains, had not only filled its channel, but overflowed its banks, so that many more were drowned in the flight than destroyed by the sword."

rodes.title: Rodes
rodes.html: Road in OED: " a hostile incursion by mounted men; a foray, raid."

romishrites.title: Romish Rites
romishrites.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an." The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records the death of Oswiu.

roundhouse.title: round House
roundhouse.html: This does little to clear up the confusion about which wall is the "Wall of Severus," that is, which wall did Severus restore. The Carron flows into the Solway Firth not very far from the west end of Hadrian's Wall. Camden, in Britannia, "Romans in Britaine" 4.71 writes, "hee reedified the wal between the mouths of Cluda and Carunus, and fortified the same with 7 castles, and built a round house of polished stone upon the bank of the river Carun."

roundsumme.title: round summe
roundsumme.html: Milton's margin here has: "Malms." See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.12.

ruind.title: much ruind
ruind.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 886 CE.

rutilius.title: Rutilius
rutilius.html: Rutilius Claudius Namatianus was a Roman imperial poet, author of De Reditu Suo (or the A Voyage Home to Gaul). In book 1.103, Ritulius identifies his friend Victorinus as a "Prefect's deputy." "Tolosa" is Toulouse.

sabra.title: Sabra
sabra.html: Milton calles her Sabrina in A Mask at Ludlow. Milton follows Geoffrey's account quite closely in this story; Geoffrey calls her Sabre. See 2.2-5 of History of the Kings of Britain.

saildinto.title: sail'd into Denmarke
saildinto.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." See Simeon, Historia Regum for 1019 CE.

sailingabout.title: sailing about
sailingabout.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." See Simeon of Durham, Historia Regum for 997 CE.

saithbede.title: saith Bede
saithbede.html: Milton's margin here has: "Bed. l. 3. c. 22." See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 3.22. But see also Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 1.6, where Suidelm is called Sigeberht's brother.

saithflorent.title: saith Florent
saithflorent.html: Milton's margin here has: "Malms." See Florentius for 754 CE, and Malmesbury Chronicle of the Kings of England book 1.2.

saithmalms.title: saith Malmsbury
saithmalms.html: See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.6: "elected king by the unanimous consent of the nobility." Malmesbury dates his accession at 924 CE. Some confusion may arise since he was first crowned King of the Anglo-Saxons, then in 927 King of the English.

saithnennius.title: saith Nennius
saithnennius.html: Milton's margin here has: "Ninn." See Nennius, Historia Brittonum 48: "the third was Pascent, who reigned in the two provinces Builth and Guorthegirnaim, after the death of his father. These were granted him by Ambrosius, who was the great king among the kings of Britain."

saiththatthesetwo.title: saith, that these two
saiththatthesetwo.html: See the Flores Historiarum for 1015 CE.

salustius.title: Salustius Lucullus
salustius.html: Sallustius Lucullus remains a bit of an enigma. John Speed, in his Historie of Great Britaine (1611) 215, writes that Agricola "deliuered vp the Prouince in a peaceable estate vnto Salustius Lucullus, and returned to Rome." See also Suetonius, "The Life of Domitian" 10.3.

samebeleef.title: same beleef
samebeleef.html: Milton's margin here has: "632." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for the year 632 CE. See also Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 2.15, and Eorpwald of East Anglia.

samecruelties.title: samecruelties
samecruelties.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." See Simeon of Durham, Historia Regum for 1011 CE.

sameintent.title: Cogidunus
sameintent.html: Milton's margin here has: "Tacit. vit. Agric." Tacitus, in his The Life of Julius Agricola 14, calls him Cogidumnus; Tiberius Claudius Cogidubnus was a 1st-century king of the Regni tribe.

sameplight.title: but for shame
sameplight.html: Milton's margin here has: "Tacit. Hist. 3. Sueton." See Tacitus, Histories 3.45 and Suetonius, Lives of the Caesars, "The Life of Nero" 18.1.

sametime.title: same time
sametime.html: Milton's margin here has: "Huntingdon." See Huntingdon, Historia Anglorum 2.15.

sametimeat.title: banishing Gunhildis
sametimeat.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." See Simeon, Historia Regum for the expulsion of Gunhilda and her sons in 1044 CE, and the expulsion of Osgod Clapa in 1046 CE.

samewood.title: same Wood
samewood.html: Presumably the same wood metioned earlier, near the River Stour in Kent where the Romans chased the Britons off the field of battle and into the woods.

samothes.title: Samothes or Dis
samothes.html: Raphael Holinshed, in his Chronicles (1587) 1.3, identifies Samothes as one of the sons of Japhet (Noah's son), and as the forefather of the Celts, or Samotheans.

samuelprophet.title: Samuel
samuelprophet.html: See Geoffrey, History of the Kings of Britain 2.6.

saxonsdef.title: Saxons
saxonsdef.html: The Saxons were a Germanic people dwelling on the North Sea coast of what is now Germany.

scaeva.title: Scaeva
scaeva.html: Milton's margin here has: "Valer. Max./ Plutarch." Valerius Maximus was author of a collection of historical anecdotes called Facta et Dicta Memorabilia, Memorable Deeds and Sayings. The story of Marcus Caesius Scaeva appears in Facta et Dicta 23a-24a "On Bravery." Plutarch also tells this story in his Caesar, chapter 16.

sconce.title: sconce
sconce.html: OED: "Fortification. A small fort or earthwork; esp. one built to defend a ford, pass, castle-gate, etc., or erected as a counter-fort."

scorastan.title: Scorastan
scorastan.html: See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.10; perhaps Chipping Norton.

scotchorbadenglish.title: Scotch or bad English
scotchorbadenglish.html: See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 3.3: "it was most delightful to see the king himself interpreting the word of God to his commanders and ministers, for he had perfectly learned the language of the Scots during his long banishment."

scottishelders.title: Elders
scottishelders.html: See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 3.3. Milton no doubt preferred the term "Elders" to bishops.

scottishwriters.title: Scottish Writers
scottishwriters.html: Buchanan's History of Scotland 4.37-38 dates the Severus campaign to the reign of Donald 1 (201-219 CE). Another Scottish writer, Hector Boece (or Boethius), in his History of the Scottish People 5.39, writes of an alliance between Fulgentius, a British noble of royal lineage, and "King Donald of Scots" against the Romans. Geoffrey, History of the Kings of Britain 5.2-3 mentions "Fulgenius," but says nothing of Donald.

searsbirig.title: Searsbirig
searsbirig.html: Milton's margin here has: "Annal omn." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle : "Searobyrig."

seaside.title: till'd the ground
seaside.html: Milton's margin here has: "Cæsar." See Caesar's Commentaries 5.12.

seatedthemselves.title: seated themselves
seatedthemselves.html: Milton's margin here has: "Paneg. Sigonius. Carolus Sigonius published Historiarum de occidentali imperio in 1579. He records the death of Carausius at the hands of Allectus in 292 CE on page 22.

seemterrible.title: seeme terrible
seemterrible.html: Milton's margin here has: "Herodian." Also known as Herodianus of Syria, and Herodian of Antioch, he authored an eight-book History of the Roman Empire in Greek. See his History 3.14.6. For woad, see Isatis tinctoria.

seigeofdurham.title: his treatise
seigeofdurham.html: De obsessione Dunelmi, "On the Seige of Durham" was mistakenly attributed to Simeon of Durham in Twysden's Historiae (1652). It was certainly written in Durham in the late 11th or early 12th century. See De obsessione Dunelmi

semblance.title: come to the Ocean
semblance.html: Milton's margin here has: "Dion. Sueton. Cal. An. Dom. 40." See Dio's Roman History 59.25 and Suetonius's Lives of the Caesars, "Gaius Caligula" 44-46. "Cal." may refer to Caligula, or perhaps to Sethus Calvisius as Milton's source for the date of A.D. 40.

sendsmessengers.title: sends Messengers
sendsmessengers.html: See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 2.12. See also Edwin of Northumbria and Rædwald of East Anglia.

sendsoverlupicinus.title: sends over Lupicinus
sendsoverlupicinus.html: Milton's margin here has: "Amm. L. 20." See Ammianus Marcellus, Roman History 20.1-2. Flavius Lupicinus was a Roman cavalry commander.

sendstoclaudius.title: sends to Claudius
sendstoclaudius.html: Milton follows Dio's narrative in Roman History 60.21.

sentback.title: sent back
sentback.html: Milton's margin here has: "Ingulf." See Pseudo-Ingulf, Historia.

senthither.title: Vitellius
senthither.html: Milton's margin here has: "69." 69 CE.was the year of Vitellius's triumph over Otho.

serpents.title: wondrous Serpents
serpents.html: See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 773 CE.

servileinmind.title: servile in mind
servileinmind.html: Milton's margin here has: "Gild. Bede." See Gildas, The Ruin of Britain 14, and Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 1.12.

setfoot.title: set foot
setfoot.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 865 CE.

sethimoff.title: set him off
sethimoff.html: See Monmouth, History of the Kings of Britain 8.17. See also Uther Pendragon.

setspeeches.title: set speeches
setspeeches.html: This principal of historiography probably comes from Polybius in his Histories 12.25a-b. But see above, where Milton quotes the supposed speech of Caractacus to Caesar at some length.

settingout.title: setting out
settingout.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." See Simeon, Historia Regum for 1063 CE.

severalgenealogies.title: several Genealogies
severalgenealogies.html: Milton's margin here has: "Mat. Westmin." The Flores Historiarum lists "Creodda" as the first king of Mercia.

severalkings.title: living then
severalkings.html: Milton's margin here has: "Primord. p. 444." Milton's authority for this claim that Gildas lived in Armorica is Ussher, De Primordiis 5.13.

severalplaces.title: several places
severalplaces.html: Milton's margin here has: "Ninn." See Nennius, Historia Brittonum 50: "Then it was, that the magnanimous Arthur, with all the kings and military force of Britain, fought against the Saxons. And though there were many more noble than himself, yet he was twelve times chosen their commander, and was as often conqueror....The twelfth was a most severe contest, when Arthur penetrated to the hill of Badon. In this engagement, nine hundred and forty fell by his hand alone, no one but the Lord affording him assistance." See also 56, a few paragraphs down.

severus.title: Julius Severus
severus.html: See Dio, Roman History 69.13. Dio writes that Hadrian dispatched Sextus Julius Severus from his role as governor of Britain to quell a rebellion in Judaea in 133 CE.

shipwrack.title: Shipwrack
shipwrack.html: Milton's margin here has: "Tacit. an. L. 2. Year after the Birth of Christ, 16." See Tacitus's Annals 2.24.

shornamonk.title: shorn a Monk
shornamonk.html: In other words, he became a monk, having his head shaved for a traditional tonsure.

shortreign.title: short reign
shortreign.html: Milton's margin here has: "Dion." See Dio, Roman History 74.14-16.

sickens.title: sickens
sickens.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun. Mat. West." See Simeon of Durham, Historia Regum for 1014 CE. See also the Flores Historiarum for 1014 CE. See also Sweyn Forkbeard.

silures.title: Silures
silures.html: The Silures were an ancient tribe of Britons in southeast Wales.

simeonaffirmsthat.title: Simeon affirms
simeonaffirmsthat.html: See Simeon of Durham, Historia Regum for 1016 CE: "Verum illi testante Deo falsum perhibuerunt testimonium, et fraudulenter mentiti sunt."

simeondurham.title: Simeon
simeondurham.html: Milton's first mention of Symeon of Durham whose Historia Regum Anglorum only became available to him in 1652, the year he went blind. See Symeonis Dunelmensis Opera et Collectanea.

simeonsays5.title: Simeon
simeonsays5.html: See Simeon of Durham's Historia Regum for 794 CE.

simeonwrites.title: Simeon writes
simeonwrites.html: Milton's margin here has: "Camden." See Camden, Britannia, "Scotland" 20 where Camden identifies "Al-Cluyd" as the Clyde-side town of Dunbritton or Dunbarton. For Simeon of Durham's account, see Historia Regum for 756 CE. See also Dumnagual III of Alt Clut.

simeonwritesagain.title: Simeon Writes
simeonwritesagain.html: See Simeon of Durham, Historia Regum for 939 CE.

simonzealot.title: som say
simonzealot.html: Simon the Zealot, Joseph of Arimathea, Barnabas, Paul, and Peter are all evangelists mentioned in scripture. See also Camden, "Romans in Britaine" 65.

singlecombate.title: single Combate
singlecombate.html: See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.10.

sixyears.title: 6 years
sixyears.html: Milton's margin here has: "577." The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records the victory of Cuthwine and Ceawlin at "Deorhamme" or Dyrham in Gloucestershire.

skinsofbeasts.title: skins of Beasts
skinsofbeasts.html: Milton's margin here has: "Herodian." See Herodian's History 3.14.6.

slaughterdthem.title: slaughterd them
slaughterdthem.html: Milton's margin here has: "Bed. Epit." See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 5.24. See also Huntingdon, Historia Anglorum 4.

slayinginfight.title: slaying in fight
slayinginfight.html: Milton's margin here has: "Bed. l. 4. c. 15." See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 4.15. See also Andhun of Sussex.

slaysgratian.title: slays Gratian
slaysgratian.html: Milton's margin here has: "383." Gratian died in 383 CE.

slenderly.title: slenderly wall'd
slenderly.html: Milton's margin here has: "Asser." See Asser, Life of Alfred. See also Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.3.

slingsdarts.title: Slings, Engines, and Darts
slingsdarts.html: See Caesar, Commentaries 4.25. The speech of the tenth legion ensign is also in 4.25.

smallcastle.title: his defence

smallnumber.title: small number
smallnumber.html: Milton's margin here has: "Buch. L. 6." See Buchanan, History of Scotland 6.15.

soend.title: so end
soend.html: Wheeloc notes that his manuscript of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle ends with the entry for 1001 CE. Hereafter he follows what is now known as the Winchester MS.

sogreat.title: of him
sogreat.html: Milton's margin here has: "Dion. L. 66." Dio, in his Roman History 66.20 speaks of Agricola "having received triumphal honours from Titus," but Tacitus, in his Life of Agricola 40, says he received such honors from Domitian, with whom he had a troubled relationship. Dio claims that Domitian murdered him (66.20.3).

sohuge.title: so huge
sohuge.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 885 CE.

solinus.title: Beast, Bird, or Flower
solinus.html: Milton's margin here has: "Solinus." Gaius Julius Solinus, author of Collectanea rerum memorabilium, or Polyhistor; in English, Collection of Curiosities. See Arthur Golding's translation of Polyhistor (1587) chapter 34. Milton recommends reading Solinus in Of Education.

solitarylife.title: surest Authors
solitarylife.html: Milton's margin here has: "Gildas. Bed." See Gildas, The Ruin of Britain 25; and Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 1.16.

som.title: som say
som.html: Milton's margin here has "Suetonius vit. Cæs." Gaius Suetonius Tranquillus is most well known for his De Vita Caesarum, The Twelve Caesars. In chapter 47 of his "Life of Julius," Suetonius suggests that his chief motivation for invading Britain was a the hope of finding pearls.

somemanhood.title: some manhood
somemanhood.html: Milton's margin here has: "Annal. omn." The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records the battle at "Wodnes-burg" in 591 CE.

somemistakesimeon.title: some mistake
somemistakesimeon.html: See Simeon, Historia Regum for 1018 CE where he records the Battle of Carham ("Carrum"), and his entry for 1016, where he records the death of Uhtred.

someoffence.title: some offence
someoffence.html: Milton's margin here has: "Florent. Huntingd." See Flores Historiarum for 992 CE. See also Huntingdon, Historia Anglorum 5.

somepart.title: King in some part
somepart.html: Milton's margin here has: "Beda." Milton claims Bede as the oldest source for the story of King Lucius of Britain. Sources older than Bede exist. See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 1.4.

somesayat.title: some say
somesayat.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun. Malms." See Simeon, Historia Regum for 1040 CE, and Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.12.

somesayoxford.title: some say
somesayoxford.html: Though several sources testify to Alfred's promotion of education among the nobility, none directly assert that he recommended Oxford University to anyone. "The University of Oxford has no known foundation date. Teaching at Oxford existed in some form as early as 1096, but it is unclear when a university came into being."

somesaysay.title: some say
somesaysay.html: See Henry of Huntingdon, Historia Anglorum and Flores Historiarum for 834 CE.

somestop.title: some stop
somestop.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 845 CE.

sometimesmet.title: sometimes met
sometimesmet.html: The Pseudo-Ingulf, Historia claims "Vidi ego illam multo tiens ... & saepius mihi de scholis venienti de literis ac versu meo apponebat.".

somthink.title: som think
somthink.html: Milton's margin here has: "Camd. Uss. primord." Camden, "Hantshire" 2. Ussher, in his De Primordiis, identifies this king as Uther Pendragon. See also Monmouth, History of the Kings of Britain 8.17.

somwillhave.title: place whereof
somwillhave.html: Milton's margin here has: "Cassidor. chro. Buchanan." Cassiodorus was the Roman author of Chronica, a history of the world up to 519 CE. He also claimed the wall was 132 miles long (French Fogle, Yale Prose 5 [Part 1], 102 n. 51). George Buchanan's History of Scotland 4.38 places the wall "between the Firths of Forth and Clyd," the location of the Antonine wall rather than Hadrian's Wall. The Antonine Wall, completed by Lollius Urbicus in 142 CE, stretches 39 miles. Even more confusing, Buchanan claims that Severus's wall "where it is least distant, yet is eighty miles off from the Wall of Adrian." If he means to the south, that would be about the location of Hadrian's wall. He probably is misreading Hector Boece's History of the Scottish People 5.13 which cites the Augustan History claim that Hadrian's wall is "eighty miles" long.

sonofcador.title: Constantine
sonofcador.html: See Monmouth, History of the Kings of Britain 11.2. See also Constantine and Cador.

soonafter.title: soon after
soonafter.html: Milton's margin here has: "844." See Rædwulf of Northumbria.

soonafterended.title: soonafter
soonafterended.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 957 CE.

soonafterwhich.title: soon after

sortofgame.title: sort of Game

soterrible.title: so terrible
soterrible.html: Milton's margin here has: "186." Sextus Tigidius Perennis was executed by order of Commodus in 185 CE. Dio, in Roman History 73.9 gives the number of 1500 seditious soldiers.

spearthrown.title: spear thrown
spearthrown.html: Milton's margin here has: "Malms." See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.10: "holding in his hand a sword stained with the blood of a fellow whom he had dexterously slain, exclaimed 'Fly, wretches! fly! behold your king was slain by this sword." Malmesbury dates this at "about Rogation-day." The story about the wayward spear follows next.

speedwaspossible.title: The Emperor
speedwaspossible.html: Milton's margin here has: "423." "In 423 CE, the Western Emperor Honorius, Theodosius' uncle, died and the primicerius notariorum Joannes was proclaimed Emperor." The following year Theodosius II, the Eastern Emperor, made war on Joannes.

spunnot.title: spun not
spunnot.html: Milton's margin here has: "Strabo." See The Geography 4.5.2.

stableofclerks.title: stable of clerks
stableofclerks.html: See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.7: "a sty for secular canons."

stainleftbehind.title: stainnbleftnbbehind
stainleftbehind.html: For this story of Wine and simony, see Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 3.7: "Wini was also expelled from his bishopric, and took refuge with Wulfhere, king of the Mercians, of whom he purchased for money the see of the city of London, and remained bishop thereof till his death." See also Bishop Wine.

stamford.title: Stamford
stamford.html: Stamford is a town on the River Welland in Lincolshire.

stateofthings.title: state of things
stateofthings.html: Milton's margin here has: "311." Constantine toured Britain and Gaul in 311 CE while Maxentius prepared his rebellion.

stpeters.title: Monastery
stpeters.html: See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 1.33. See also St. Augustine's Abbey.

strangefluxes.title: strange fluxes
strangefluxes.html: Milton's margin here has: "Malms." Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.10, mentions no plague except that of Danish raids. The Flores Historiarum and Simeon of Durham, Historia Regum both report pestilence in 987 CE.

strengthenhisaffairs.title: strengthen his Affairs
strengthenhisaffairs.html: Milton's margin here has: "Camd. ex Nin. Eumen. Pan. 3." See Camden's Britannia, "Romans in Britaine" 4.71: "Carausius governed Britain with incorrupt and unstained reputation, and in exceeding great peace: against the the Barbarians, as writeth Ninnius the disciple of Elvodugus."

strenuous.title: strenuous
strenuous.html: Milton's margin here has: "Malms." See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.10. See also Dunstan.

strongcastle.title: Ambrosius
strongcastle.html: Milton's margin here has: "Ninn." See Nennius, Historia Brittonum 40-42 for the story of Vortigern's retreat to "a province called Guenet" and the episode of the fatherless boy, Ambrose. In Geoffrey of Monmouth's History of the Kings of Britain 6.17-19, the fatherles youth is name Merlin. See also Radnorshire.

struckoff.title: struck off
struckoff.html: Milton's margin here has: "Encom. Em. Ingulf." See the Encomium Emmae Reginae 2.15: "eique ictu valido caput amputavit." See also the Pseudo-Ingulf, Historia.

succeededhim.title: succeeded him
succeededhim.html: Milton's margin here has: "673." See Ecgfrith of Northumbria.

succeeding.title: succeeding
succeeding.html: Milton's margin here has: "70." The first year of Vespasian's undisputed rule as emperor, 70 CE.

successioncrown.title: succession
successioncrown.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 901 CE.

suchargument.title: unfortunate end
suchargument.html: Milton's margin here has: "Ethelwerd. Malms." See Æthelweard, Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 2.19. See also Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 1.2 for an account of Cyneheard's treachery. See also Cyneheard the Ætheling.

suetonius.title: Suetonius
suetonius.html: Suetonius was an ancient Roman historian of the Imperial period of the Roman Empire.

suetoniuswrites.title: Suetonius writes
suetoniuswrites.html: See Lives of the Caesars, "The Life of Claudius" 17.2.

sufficientaid.title: sufficient aid
sufficientaid.html: Milton's margin here has: "Claudian. de land. stil. l. 2 & de bello Get." Claudius Claudianus was a Latin poet closely associated with the general Flavius Stilicho. See Claudian's On the Consulship of Stilicho 2. 247-55. See also his The Gothic War lines 416-18. Flavius Honorius Augustus was the younger son of Theodosius I and his first wife.

superscription.title: superscription
superscription.html: Milton's margin here has: "Malmsbury L. 1. c. 1. p. 8." See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England; in book 1.1. There is no mention here of Aetius or letter sent to him. Because Milton includes a page number here, it is possible to identify the edition he used as one published in Frankfurt in 1601.

supposdson.title: suppos'd Son
supposdson.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." See Simeon, Historia Regum for 1035 CE. See also Sweyn Godwinson.

supreamking.title: inveigh against the English Writers
supreamking.html: Milton's margin here has: "Buch. L. 6." See Buchanan, History of Scotland 6.16.

surerauthor.title: surer Author
surerauthor.html: Milton's margin here has: "Bede." "731." See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 5.23: "All these provinces, and the others southward to the bank of the river Humber, with their kings, are subject to King Ethelbald." Milton tends to trust Bede more than the other sources available to him. Bede's accounts end with the year 731 CE.

surerauthors.title: surer Authors
surerauthors.html: This presumably includes Livy; see The History of Rome I.1. Also see Virgil's Aeneid

surmises.title: Huntingdon
surmises.html: See Henry of Huntingdon, Historia Anglorum. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records Cuthred's death in 754 CE.

swolnabove.title: swoln above
swolnabove.html: Milton's margin here has: "Mat West." See the Flores Historiarum.

tankard.title: Tankard, not a man
tankard.html: This jest appears in almost the same words in Camden, Britannia, "Romans in Britaine" 4. 69.

tempest.title: Tempest
tempest.html: Milton's margin here has: "Malms." See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.10. Simeon dates the return of Danish raids to 980 CE in Historia Regum.

templeapollo.title: Temple of Apollo
templeapollo.html: William Camden believed that an ancient temple dedicated to Apollo stood on the site where we now find Westmister Abbey. See also Geoffrey, History of the Kings of Britain 2.10 and Camden, Britannia: "London" 15.14.

templeasagod.title: Temple as a God
templeasagod.html: Milton's margin here has: "Tacit. an. 14. 44." Presumably 44 CE. Tacitus's Annals 14.31 mentions "A temple also erected to the Divine Claudius".

tenthdegree.title: tenth degree
tenthdegree.html: Milton's margin here has: "The Kingdome of Northumberland. Annal omn. Bed. Epit. Malmsb." See the Chronicle note above. See also Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 5.24: "In the year 547, Ida began to reign; from him the royal family of the Northumbrians derives its original; he reigned twelve years. And see Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 1.3, which claims that "during the space of ninety-nine years, the Northumbrian leaders, contented with subordinate power, lived in subjection to the kings of Kent." Milton's "nigh 180 years" below is surely a misprint for "nigh 100 years."

tenthyear.title: tenth year
tenthyear.html: Milton's margin here has: "Malms. Antiquit. Glaston." Milton refers here to William of Malmesbury's "On the Antiquity of Glastonbury" as quoted by Ussher in his De Primordiis 5.13.

tenyearsafter.title: ten years after
tenyearsafter.html: The Flores Historiarum dates the massacre in 1012. See also Massacre. Malmesbury, in his Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.10, also includes an account of this story, and is also confused about the dates.

tenyearsspace.title: ten years space
tenyearsspace.html: Milton's margin here has: "Bed. l. 4. c. 12." See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 4.12.

testudo.title: like a rooff
testudo.html: Milton describes the Roman military testudo formation.

thanetisle.title: Ile of Tanet
thanetisle.html: The Isle of Thanet, no longer an island, is the eastern-most point of Kent.

thatcondition.title: that condition
thatcondition.html: Milton's margin here has: "Eadmer." See Eadmer, Historia novorum in Anglia 5: "super regnum Angliae mulierem extraneam, inconsultis principibus, me nec debere, nec sine grandi injuriâ posse adducere noverit."

thatdignity.title: that dignity
thatdignity.html: Milton's margin here has: "Malms." See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 1.1, pages 11-12; he says that Hengist died 39 years after his arrival in Britain, which Milton reckoned as 450 CE. According to Malmesbury, Hengist's son, Eisc, ruled for "twenty-four years."

thatpart.title: that part
thatpart.html: Milton's margin here has: "Gildas. Bed. Ninn." See Gildas, The Ruin of Britain 23-25; Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 1.15; and Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 1.1, page 10, who also interprets "Gourong" as "Viceroy." See also Nennius, Historia Brittonum 56: "Hengist having died, however, his son Octha crossed from the northern part of Britain to the kingdom of Kent and from him are descended the kings of Kent." See also paragraph 38 for "Octa and Ebusa."

thatplace.title: Bishop of that place
thatplace.html: Milton's margin here has: "Mat. West." See Flores Historiarum for 958 CE. See also Ælfsige.

thattime.title: that time
thattime.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. ann." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for the year 628 CE.

the3rdyear.title: The third year
the3rdyear.html: Milton's margin here has: "789." The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 787 CE says that the invading Danes first arrived during the reign of Beorhtric of Wessex.

thearchbishop.title: the Archbishop
thearchbishop.html: Milton's margin here has: "Eadmer." See Eadmer, Historia novorum in Anglia: "crudeli custodiae per septum menses mancipatus."

thebastard.title: the mean while
thebastard.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." See Simeon, Historia Regum for 1036 CE.

thebeginningof.title: The beginning
thebeginningof.html: Milton's margin here has: "Huntingd." See Huntingdon, Historia Anglorum 5.

thecause.title: not approving
thecause.html: Milton's margin here has: "Malms. Ingulf." See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.10. See also the Pseudo-Ingulf, Historia.

theclergy.title: the Clergy
theclergy.html: See Gildas, The Ruin of Britain 66-69.

thecontestwasbetween.title: the contest was between
thecontestwasbetween.html: See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.12. See also Harthacnut.

thecustom.title: the custom
thecustom.html: Milton's margin here has: "Malmsb." See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 1.1, page 8.

thedaughter.title: the Sister
thedaughter.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an." The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records the expulsion of of Cenwalh by Penda in 645 CE and his baptism the following year. But see also Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 3.7.: "for he put away the sister of Penda, king of the Mercians, whom he had married, and took another wife; whereupon a war ensuing, he was by him expelled his kingdom, and withdrew to Anna, king of the East Saxons, where living three years in banishment, he found and received the true faith, and was baptized." See also Anna of East Anglia.

thedecease.title: the decease
thedecease.html: Milton's margin here has: "Florent." See the Flores Historiarum for 1016 CE. See also Edmund Ironside.

theenglish.title: the English
theenglish.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." See Simeon of Durham, Historia Regum for 998 CE.

thefirstauthor.title: the first Author
thefirstauthor.html: Milton's margin here has: "Hieronym." Eusebius Sophronius Hieronymus, better known as Jerome, in his "Letter 133: To Ctesiphon," wrote "For Britain, that province so fertile in despots, the Scottish tribes, and all the barbarians round about as far as the ocean were alike without knowledge of Moses and the prophets" (paragraph 9). Because Jerome mentioned Porphyry in the sentence before this, Gildas mistakenly attributed this remark about the British and Scots to him.

thefourthindia.title: Sighelm, Bishop of Sherburn
thefourthindia.html: Milton's margin here has: "Malms." See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.4.

theincitement.title: great sum of money
theincitement.html: Milton's margin here has: "Malms. Sax. an. Ethelwerd." See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 1.2: "thirty thousand marks of gold", and the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 694 CE: "cui viros triginta donabant." See also Æthelweard, Anglo-Saxon Chronicle: "thirty thousand shillings."

themonk.title: the Monk
themonk.html: Milton's margin here has: "661." See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 1.2.

themonkof.title: the Monk
themonkof.html: See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 1.1, page 11, and page 315.

themonmouthbook.title: the Monmouth Book
themonmouthbook.html: See Geoffrey of Monmouth, History of the Kings of Britain 8.18.

thenbesieged.title: then besieg'd
thenbesieged.html: Milton's margin here has: "402." The Visigoth invasion of Italy occurred in 402 CE. General Stilicho came to the defense of Honorius.

thencepeaceably.title: thence peaceably
thencepeaceably.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 879 CE.

thencereturning.title: Thence returning
thencereturning.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." See Simeon, Historia Regum for 1029 CE. See also Olaf II of Norway.

thenextyear3.title: the next year
thenextyear3.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." See Simeon of Durham's Historia Regum for 793 CE.

thenextyearagain.title: Shepey
thenextyearagain.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 832 CE where the town is called "Sceapige."

theninhabited.title: then inhabited
theninhabited.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." See Simeon of Durham's Historia Regum for 885 CE.

theother.title: the other
theother.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 681 CE.

thepatent.title: the patent
thepatent.html: See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 2.2. See also Asser, Life of Alfred.

thepreaching.title: the preaching
thepreaching.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sax. an." See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for the year 635 CE. See also Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 3.7: "AT that time, the West Saxons, formerly called Gewissae, in the reign of Cynegils, embraced the faith of Christ, at the preaching of Bishop Birinus, who came into Britain by the advice of Pope Honorius."

theprimacy.title: the Primacy
theprimacy.html: Milton's margin here has: "Asser. Men." Asser (Asserius Menevensis) was a monk of St. David's in Wales and author of a Life of Alfred.

theprime.title: the prime
theprime.html: Milton's margin here has: "Malmsb." See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 1.3.

thereforehaving.title: therefore having
thereforehaving.html: Milton's margin here has: "Sim. Dun." See Simeon, Historia Regum for 1030 CE.

therequest.title: the request
therequest.html: Milton's margin here has: "607." See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 2.2.

thesecalamities.title: commit incest
thesecalamities.html: Milton's margin here has: "Ninn. Malmsb." See Nennius, Historia Brittonum 39: "Vortigern, as if desirous of adding to the evils he had already occasioned, married his own daughter, by whom he had a son." See also Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 1.1, page 7.

thesecond.title: the second
thesecond.html: Milton's margin here has: "Malmsb. L. 1. c. 3." See Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England book 1.3.

theseevils.title: new divisions
theseevils.html: Milton's margin here has: "Bede. Constantius." See Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation 1.17. Constantius of Lyon wrote Vita Germani, Life of St. Germanus, in 480 CE; it details the story of Germanus's two missions to Britain to combat Pelagianism.

theseitake.title: these I take
theseitake.html: Milton's margin here has: "Pontan. hist. Dan. L. 4" Ponatnus, Rerum Danicarum Historia (Amsterdam, 1631; Fensburg, 1637) book 4.

thesemarching.title: these marching
thesemarching.html: Milton's margin here has: "Camd." See Camden, "Wiltshire" 10.8. See also Edington in Wiltshire.

thesequel.title: the sequel
